# Election 2026 Manifesto

## Full text (verbatim)

# Election 2026 Manifesto

## A message from our co-leaders

Most of us slow down for a duck crossing the road. We feel uneasy watching a truck of animals go past on the motorway. We love our dogs like family.

And yet, somehow, that care rarely makes it into our politics.

That’s the gap we exist to fill.

Every year in this country, around 27 million sheep, cows, and pigs are killed for food. 120 million chickens. Billions of fish[1](#2d6d1b75-98ba-4f54-a148-93ad32806472). Many of them never see daylight, never feel grass, never get to do what comes naturally to them. And almost no one in parliament is talking about it.

We are.

We also know life is tough right now. Food costs too much. People are worried about their health, their jobs, the state of our rivers. Farmers are under real pressure. These things matter to us too, because the way we treat animals is tangled up with all of it.

Sheep and cattle alone account for nearly half of New Zealand’s greenhouse gas emissions[2](#b4bad5a9-4236-48a1-a1a6-ef4bd90f0a28). Ninety-five per cent of our waterways in farming areas are exceeding safe limits for contamination[3](#ca8d9314-5142-4115-9b64-1d30a6f06d76). The health costs of our current food system run into the billions. These aren’t abstract problems. They’re showing up in people’s lives.

Here’s what we’re working to change.

---

#### A politics you can trust

New Zealanders are tired of politics that serves donors and sidesteps hard questions. We’re committed to getting money out of politics, protecting whistleblowers, and supporting the kind of open, peaceful democratic participation that keeps power honest. We say what we mean.

---

#### Ending factory farming

Most New Zealanders, if they could see inside an intensive farming operation, wouldn’t be comfortable with what they saw. We want to ban the most harmful farming and fishing practices, and we want to support farmers to make that transition properly, with real funding and time to adjust. Change that leaves rural communities behind isn’t good change.

---

#### Pound reform

In Auckland, 60%[4](#562720e4-ed4e-420e-a778-cd2e649ec235) of dogs impounded last year were killed rather than rehomed.

That is not because these dogs were beyond help. It is because the system around them is broken: short timeframes to claim a dog, upfront costs many families cannot pay in one go, and shelters running well past capacity.

We want rehoming and no-kill to be the default, nationally, not the exception. That means fixing the system so fewer dogs end up unclaimed in the first place, and giving every dog who does the best possible chance of finding a home.

---

#### Vet costs and the bonds that matter

For many people, their animal companion is their closest relationship. Vet bills have become genuinely unaffordable for a lot of families. We’ll push for fairer access to veterinary care, and we support bereavement leave when someone loses an animal they love, because that loss is real.

---

#### Giving animals legal standing

Right now, animals are property under New Zealand law. That makes it very hard to protect them in any meaningful way. We want the law to catch up with what most people already feel: that animals are individuals who can suffer, and that matters.

---

#### An independent voice for animals

Animal welfare is currently overseen by the same ministry that promotes the farming industry. That’s a conflict of interest, and it shows. We want an Independent Commissioner for Animals with real powers, answerable to the public.

---

#### Smarter conservation, not a war on cats (or other animals deemed ‘pests’)

New Zealand’s indigenous species deserve real protection, and we’re fully behind that. But mass killing of cats is not the answer, especially when there’s no reliable way to tell a ‘feral’ cat from someone’s companion or a community cat that neighbours have cared for for years.

Cats didn’t put themselves in the wild. Humans did. So that’s where the solution has to start: nationwide desexing programmes, Trap-Neuter-Return, habitat restoration, and predator-proof fencing. Conservation that actually works, and that we can be proud of.

---

#### Healthier food, lower costs

More plant-based food in schools, hospitals, and public institutions would cut costs and improve nutrition. Estimates suggest a shift toward plant-rich diets could save New Zealand’s health system up to $22 billion in prevented chronic disease.[5](#77b9673a-ba40-41d8-8739-1c0c9c3d17a9) We’ll also push for clearer food labelling so people can make informed choices. Our circular and sharing economy policies reduce waste and help keep money in communities. None of this is radical. It’s just good policy.

---

#### Compassionate education

We want empathy, critical thinking, and environmental awareness to be genuinely central to how we raise children in this country, not an add-on, but a foundation. Kids who grow up understanding their connection to the natural world and to other living beings are better equipped for the future we’re all heading into.

We’re here because the animals don’t have a vote, and someone needs to speak up for them honestly and without apology.

If that sounds like your kind of politics, we’d love your support.

Danette Wereta and Rob McNeil\
Co-Leaders, Animal Justice Party\
\
\
Want more detail on our policies? [Read our 2026 policy summary](https://animaljustice.org.nz/policies/policy-summary/) or the [policy platform PDF](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1U0yXwLQojMLxFXFI1EwWoX7132f86Lag/view?usp=sharing).

# Abolish all farming of animals

> Archive note: Web text is the policy post body from animaljustice.org.nz/wp-json/wp/v2/policies; the PDF version linked from the page (if any) follows, extracted with pdftotext -layout.

## Full text (verbatim)

### Web page text

The Animal Justice Party Aotearoa NZ (AJP) advocates for the complete abolition of animal farming. All animals used in farming, regardless of the intended product or purpose, have an equal right to live free from suffering, exploitation and neglect. AJP supports a transition to a system that respects animal rights, protects the environment and promotes public health through plant-based, cellular and sustainable agriculture.

# AJP Animal Policies Overview

## Full text (verbatim)

### Web page text

The Animal Justice Party Aotearoa envisions a future rooted in compassion, non-violence, and strict legal protection for non-human animals. Guided by the precautionary principle and a commitment to systemic reform, our policies outline actionable pathways to abolish exploitation, protect wild ecosystems, and transition toward a humane, sustainable society.

Protecting the rights of farmed animals
The Animal Justice Party Aotearoa New Zealand (AJP) asserts that all forms of animal
farming are ethically indefensible, fundamentally unjust, and must end. Every animal,
regardless of the product they are exploited for, has the inherent right to live free from
suffering, exploitation, and commodification. AJP is committed to driving a rapid
transition to a plant-based economy, recognising the urgent need to dismantle systems
that cause the greatest harm to animals. While working towards the complete abolition
of animal farming, we demand immediate reforms to eliminate the most severe suffering
and uphold the dignity and rights of all sentient beings.

In alignment with Te Tiriti o Waitangi principles, AJP affirms that protecting the rights of
animals requires genuine partnership with Māori. We honour the unique relationship
between tangata whenua and the natural world and commit to ensuring that policy
development and implementation incorporates Māori perspectives and knowledge
systems. Concepts such as kaitiakitanga (guardianship), mauri (life force), and
whakapapa (ancestral connection) offer powerful frameworks that challenge extractive
models of agriculture and envision a future grounded in respect, care and justice for all
living beings.

animaljustice.org.nz | party@animaljusticeparty.org.nz
3

Abolish all farming of animals
The Animal Justice Party Aotearoa NZ (AJP) advocates for the complete abolition of
animal farming. All animals used in farming, regardless of the intended product or
purpose, have an equal right to live free from suffering, exploitation and neglect. AJP
supports a transition to system that respects animal rights, protects the environment
and promotes public health through plant-based, cellular and sustainable agriculture.

The industrial farming of animals represents the largest source of animal exploitation
and cruelty globally. Every year in New Zealand, billions of animals, including fish, are
bred, confined and/or killed for food production. This includes, for example: 119.5 million
chickens, broiler chickens, (2022),1 4.67 million dairy cows (2023/24)2 and
approximately 72.7 million farmed fish and shellfish individuals (noting this is an
estimate as fish are not measured by number of individuals but by metric weight alone,
the stated figure of 109, 016 metric tonnes3 is equivalent to the weight of approximately
72,677 cars).

These animals endure significant physical and psychological suffering throughout their
abbreviated lives, treated as mere units of production. AJP recognises that these
animals are sentient, and have interests in living lives free from suffering, with
autonomy, and the freedom to express their natural behaviors. These interests are often
comparable to the similar interests of humans, and establish the legal personhood of
sentient animals, along with rights which must be protected in the law. These rights are
fundamentally incompatible with ownership or consumptive practices.

All forms of farming impose severe harms and infringe on the rights of animals. The
dairy industry, central to New Zealand's economy, subjects cows to annual pregnancies,
separation from their calves, and intensive milking that leads to painful conditions like
mastitis. Male calves, considered "surplus" to the industry, are typically killed within days
of birth. Chickens raised for meat (broilers) are genetically manipulated to grow at
unnatural rates, leading to painful skeletal disorders, while hens in the egg industry are
confined in crowded conditions and killed when their productivity declines. Male chicks
are killed by maceration within their first few days.

The fashion and textile industries also represent significant sources of animal
exploitation. In New Zealand, the wool industry alone involves approximately 25.3
million sheep (2022)4, while possum fur and leather production contribute to animal
suffering and death.

All farming operations, whether animals are raised for meat, milk, wool, leather, down,
or any other product, including emerging industries such as insect and eel farming,
prioritise profit over the welfare of sentient animals and infringe on their rights. While
different forms of farming vary in the severity of their cruelty, all animal farming
fundamentally denies animals their personhood, along with their rights to autonomy and
freedom from exploitation.

AJP also recognises that animal farming imposes an unsustainable burden on natural
ecosystems both in Aotearoa and globally. The environmental impact of animal
agriculture is far-reaching and deeply harmful. It is a major driver of greenhouse gas
emissions, particularly methane and nitrous oxide, which are far more potent than
carbon dioxide in terms of warming potential. Animal farming also requires vast
amounts of land for grazing and feed production, leading to deforestation and habitat
destruction that endanger native species and contribute to biodiversity loss. In New
Zealand, intensive dairying has been directly linked to the degradation of waterways,
with nutrient runoff and effluent polluting rivers and lakes, harming aquatic life and
undermining the health of entire ecosystems. Leather tanning creates toxic pollution and
wool farming contributes to land degradation and water pollution. Globally, the
conversion of forests to pasture and feed crops is one of the leading causes of
biodiversity collapse and a significant barrier to achieving climate goals. Transitioning
away from animal farming is therefore essential not only to reduce animal suffering but
to restore ecological balance and safeguard the planet's capacity to support life.

Furthermore, intensive animal farming presents a critical threat to global public health
by creating ideal conditions for the emergence of zoonotic diseases. This risk arises
through two major pathways. Firstly, the confinement of animals in overcrowded and
often unhygienic environments facilities the transmission and mutation of pathogens
that can jump from animals to humans. These facilities can act as breeding grounds for
new viral and bacterial strains, with the close contact between animals and workers
increasing transmission risks. Secondly, the routine use of antibiotics in animal
agriculture, often used preventatively due to unsanitary conditions and to promote rapid

4
https://www.stats.govt.nz/news/fewer-sheep-and-dairy-cattle-in-2022/

animaljustice.org.nz | party@animaljusticeparty.org.nz
5

---

growth, is fuelling the global crisis of antibiotic resistance. This overuse contributes to
the emergence of ‘superbugs’ - bacteria that are resistant to multiple antibiotics. The
World Health Organisation has identified identified antimicrobial resistance as one of the
top ten global public health threats facing humanity, warning that without urgent action,
we could enter a ‘post-antibiotic era’ where common infections and minor injuries may
once again become fatal.5

AJP affirms Te Tiriti o Waitangi as a foundational document and recognises the
importance of working in partnership with tangata whenua in the pursuit of justice for
animals and collective, intergenerational wellbeing. This includes supporting Māori-led
exploration of how kaitiakitanga can guide non-exploitative relationships with animals.
Māori frameworks such as kaitiakitanga, mauri, and wairua offer perspectives that
challenge dominant colonial-industrial relationships with animals.

We acknowledge the importance of Māori-led conversations around the future of food
systems, species protection and animal rights and that some traditional harvesting
practices form part of Māori identity and whakapapa. While AJP opposes all animal use
and advocates for a post-exploitative food system, we are committed to respectful,
Treaty-consistent dialogue with hapū and iwi.

In order to protect the rights of animals and dismantle exploitative industries, AJP
advocates for a systematic transition away from all forms of animal farming, including
for food, fibre and fashion, towards plant-based, cellular and sustainable alternatives.
This transition will eliminate the use of animals as commodities, dramatically reduce
environmental destruction, and promote public health. It must be managed carefully to
support farmers, rural communities, and affected industries through inclusive and just
transition strategies.

Key Objectives:

1. Establish a clear timeline for phasing out all forms of animal farming, with specific
targets for each industry sector.
2. Provide economic and technical support for farmers to transition to other
industries.
See AJP’s Plant-Based Transition policies for further objectives aligned with this
transition, including focusing on investment in plant-based and cellular agriculture

research and development and creation of comprehensive transition
programmes to support farmers in converting to plant-based agriculture or other
sustainable enterprises.
3. Prohibit the expansion, or the establishment, of animal farming operations.
4. Prohibit all forms of intensive animal farming.
5. Legislate transparency in all animal farming operations through increased
monitoring and enforcement and public reporting. See Regulatory Oversight and
Enforcement Policy.
6. Introduce consistent legislation that defines and acknowledges animal sentience,
ensuring legal protection from harm. See Legislative Foundations Policy.
7. Expand the application of the Animal Welfare Act 1999 to all species of any order
for which there is strong evidence of sentience in at least one species of that
order, following Birch et al. (2021)’s framework.6 See Legislative Foundations
Policy.
8. Require greater legislative protection of animal welfare. See Reducing Harm and
Mistreatment and Legislative Foundations Policies.
9. Work with Māori leaders, ethicists and communities to explore Treaty-grounded,
culturally inclusive pathways for protecting animal wellbeing.

The Animal Justice Party Aotearoa NZ (AJP) affirms that all animals used in farming,
whether for food, fibre, or fashion, possess inherent personhood, dignity and rights.
These policies apply equally to all farmed animals, land-based or aquatic, regardless of
the product or industry they are exploited for. Our interim policies seek to reduce harm
while working toward a future where no animal is treated as a commodity or object of
human use.

Independent Animal Welfare Governance to Reduce Harm
The Animal Justice Party (AJP) envisions a New Zealand where compassion,
sustainability and ethical practices guide our treatment of animals. While we advocate
for a complete transition to a plant-based farming system, we recognise that meaningful
societal changes require time and a ‘Just Transition’.7 In the interim, we are committed
to reducing the most severe harm and mistreatment of animals by improving oversight
of farming practices and strengthening legislation to provide stronger protections and
ensure higher welfare standards for all animals in Aotearoa.

New Zealand's animal welfare system must be free from conflicts of interest and bias.
Currently, the role of Minister for Animal Welfare is embedded within the Ministry for
Primary Industries (MPI), an institution heavily tied to the animal agriculture sector. To
address this, AJP calls for the establishment of an independent Commissioner for
Animals.8 This role would ensure impartial oversight and monitoring of animal welfare
and protection in Aotearoa New Zealand and more effective enforcement of, and
compliance with, the Animal Welfare Act 1999. See Regulatory Oversight and
Enforcement Policy.

The Animal Welfare Act 1999 outlines several needs (known as the “Five Freedoms”)
which must be provided for farmed animals:
- Proper and sufficient food and water.
- Adequate shelter.
- The opportunity to display normal patterns of behaviour.
- Physical handling in a manner which minimises the likelihood of unreasonable or
unnecessary pain or distress.
- Protection from, and rapid diagnosis of, any significant injury or disease.
While the Five Freedoms are insufficient to protect all the rights that sentient animals
are entitled to (such as the right to life), they represent the minimum legislative
standards to be adhered to. However, current farming methods and the codes of welfare
frequently do not meet these standards, especially in intensive animal farming.
Additionally, there is limited action or motivation from Government decision makers or
regulators to initiate and drive positive welfare law reform9 to align current farming

Emerging technologies, including artificial intelligence, are increasingly being used in
animal agriculture to monitor, manage or even conceal harmful practices. Without
ethical oversight and transparency, these tools risk entrenching cruelty and further
distancing the public from the realities of animal exploitation. AJP supports legislation to
ensure that any technological use involving animals prioritises their welfare and does
not enable or obscure mistreatment.

Ensuring Humane Transport Conditions

The Animal Justice Party (AJP) envisions a New Zealand where compassion,
sustainability and ethical practices guide our treatment of animals. While we ultimately
seek a complete transition away from animal agriculture towards plant-based and
cellular systems, we recognise the urgent need to reduce the suffering of animals who
are currently trapped in this system. One of the most severe and widespread breaches
of the five freedoms11 occurs during transport, particularly when animals are moved
between farms, saleyards and slaughterhouses.

Every year, millions of animals in New Zealand endure long and stressful journeys that
cause significant physical and psychological distress. The process of transport exposes
animals to unfamiliar environments, loud noises, rough handling, overcrowding and
prolonged confinement, often without adequate rest, food or water. Vulnerable groups
such as bobby calves and dairy cows are especially at risk. Despite existing regulations,
the current system prioritises cost-efficiency over animal wellbeing, with inadequate
limits on journey length, stocking density and handling standards.

Live export is one of the most extreme examples of suffering associated with transport.
Although New Zealand banned the export of livestock by sea for slaughter in 2023, this
ban is under threat from Government proposals in 2025 to overturn it, a move AJP
strongly opposes, see AJP Live Export policy. Furthermore, other forms of live export
continue, including the export of farmed species like eels by air, which also subjects
animals to prolonged and distressing journeys.

Transport regulations must be equally stringent for animals farmed for non-food
products, including alpacas, angora rabbits and other fibre-producing animals. These
animals often face similar or greater transport risks due to less established welfare
protocols and monitoring systems.

AJP calls for a complete overhaul of animal transport regulations to recognise the
specific needs of each species, regardless of their intended use. While animal farming
continues, we demand far stricter controls on journey times, space allowances, rest
periods and handling practices, as well as the retention and strengthening of the live
export ban. Our long-term vision remains the complete replacement of animal farming

afforded the highest possible level of protection.

Key Objectives:
1. Implement comprehensive reforms to strengthen the Animal Welfare (Transport
within New Zealand) Code of Welfare.
2. Establish stricter maximum journey times aligned with New Zealand's geographic
and agricultural context, particularly for vulnerable animals like bobby calves.
3. Extend the current ban on live export by sea to include all live animal exports,
including by air (noting the need for some exceptions, such as companion
animals migrating with their guardians).

Extending the Live Export Ban
Animal Justice Party Aotearoa New Zealand (AJP) will campaign to prevent the ban on
sending steers, heifers, cows and bulls (‘cattle’) and sheep, deer and goats by sea from
being repealed.

AJP will also campaign for an end to exporting live animals by air, except in the case of
companion animals relocating overseas and coming into New Zealand with their
families, zoo animals and horses requiring relocation. Refer to AJP’s Policy regarding
Horse Racing.

The Animal Welfare Act 1999 was amended in 2022 to state that after 30 April 2023 no
livestock may be exported from New Zealand by sea.12 Federated Farmers, ACT
Party13 and National Party14 have all made public statements in support of repealing this
amendment.

Although it is not well known, we also export millions of animals every year by air,
namely, goats, llamas, pigs, alpacas, bees, deer, horses, cats, dogs and day-old baby
chicks. In 2022 more than 2000 goats and 3.4 million day-old chicks were sent offshore
by plane. We also export aquatic species such as longfin eels even though they are ‘at
risk’ native animals15 and crayfish.16

Further, regardless of the method of transport, once the animals are exported, New
Zealand no longer has any control over how our animals are treated in the destination
country. For example, boiling crayfish alive in a restaurant is an offence in New Zealand
but similar rules do not necessarily apply overseas.17

Live export by sea

5,867 cows and 41 crew tragically died when Gulf Livestock 1 sank at sea in September
2020 which led to a temporary suspension of livestock export by sea from New Zealand.
After an independent review by Michael Heron QC, exports resumed with tighter
controls including increased voyage reporting and reduced stocking density on vessels.

Another 128 cows also died in 2020 during the usual course of transport and as a result
of the terrible conditions on board. Animal Genetics Trade Association spokesman
Dave Hayman has said “Deaths were most often from a broken leg or a joint injury.”

MPI have stated that the minimum pen area per head for cattle exported by sea is
strongly recommended to be 2m2 for the average 600 kg cow. Australian Dr. Lynn
Simpson is a veterinarian who has travelled on 57 long haul live export voyages. Dr.
Simpson has said “They’re pretty tight. They’re right up against each other, and they
have to choreograph and jostle around to find space. Generally in my experience they
can’t all lie down at the same time”.

A New Zealand veterinarian has described their experience on board a live export ship:
“The cramped nature of the pens and the effluent buildup (both on the floor and on the
coats of the cattle) reduced air flow around the cattle, which added to the heat stress. I
found it very difficult to alleviate the distress I observed during this period of the
journey.”
“Despite our best efforts to get all the cattle across the equator alive, two cattle died of
heat stress on the journey. Although the two cattle written down on our trip report
represent a low mortality rate attributable to heat stress, the pain and distress they and
the surviving cattle experienced still haunts me.”26

Live export by air

3.4 million day-old chicks travel internationally by air annually causing variable welfare
compromises to the day-old chicks. Day-old chicks are not able to regulate their own
temperature and are subjected to handling, loading, and transporting stress.

This industry takes advantage of the day-old chicks’ ability to survive for up to 72 hours
without food and water due to their residual yolk-sac which provides nutrients and
hydration, in the absence of feed and water. The composition and size of the yolk-sac
depends on various factors and some will last longer than others. While the yolk-sac
can provide up to 72 hours of nutrition and hydration, the rate of use is also affected by
factors such as genetics and environmental conditions. Some individual chicks will not
have adequate sustenance during their journey meaning inadequate nutrition and
dehydration which will contribute to their death.

The Ministry for Primary Industries does not routinely report mortality statistics for
day-old chicks, so we do not even know how many could not survive the journey. In
addition, the Ministry only applies voluntary guidelines to the trade, which are not
publicly consulted.

Ensuring Adequate Living Conditions and Environmental
Standards
The Animal Justice Party Aotearoa NZ (AJP) is working towards a future without animal
agriculture. In the meantime, we are committed to addressing the widespread neglect of
shelter, housing and environmental conditions that cause immense suffering to farmed
animals. Despite existing legal protections, animals across New Zealand are routinely
exposed to harsh weather, overcrowding and barren environments that deny them the
ability to express natural behaviours. AJP is calling for urgent reforms to ensure farmed
animals are afforded basic protections, dignity and care.

The Animal Welfare Act 1999 legislates that animals must be provided with "adequate
shelter" and "the opportunity to display normal patterns of behaviour." However, these
requirements are often poorly defined and inadequately enforced. Throughout New
Zealand, animals frequently lack protection from harsh weather conditions, with many
farms having removed natural shelter like trees that historically provided protection.

This is particularly concerning given New Zealand's varied and often extreme weather
pattern. For example the Code of Welfare: Dairy Cattle (2019) states “Dairy cattle in
New Zealand are exposed to extreme weather (heat, cold, rain, snow and wind)” and
that this can “create welfare risks, leading to hyper- or hypothermia.”31

Intensive winter grazing represents one of New Zealand's most pressing animal welfare
and environmental challenges, particularly in southern regions. This practice forces
animals to graze fodder crops in small allocated areas, often resulting in them standing
in deep mud for extended periods. Animals frequently lack adequate shelter, dry lying
areas or protection from harsh weather conditions. Pregnant and nursing animals are
especially vulnerable, facing increased risks of health issues and pregnancy
complications. The practice not only compromises animal welfare but also causes
significant environmental damage through soil degradation, waterway pollution and
increased greenhouse gas emissions.

Indoor housing systems, particularly in intensive pig and poultry farming, frequently
subject animals to poor air quality, excessive noise and overcrowding. These conditions
not only cause physical health issues but also prevent animals from expressing natural

Ensuring Adequate Nutrition and Health Standards
The Animal Justice Party Aotearoa NZ (AJP) is committed to transforming New
Zealand’s approach to animal nutrition and health in farming systems. While our
long-term goal is to end animal agriculture, immediate reform is needed to address the
widespread welfare harms caused by inadequate feeding practices, compromised
health management and overreliance on pharmaceuticals in industrial farming. AJP
supports stronger regulation, enforcement and a shift in priorities from production
efficiency to animal well-being.

Despite the Animal Welfare Act 1999 requiring proper and sufficient food and water for
animals, many farming practices in New Zealand compromise animals' nutritional
needs. This creates a notable contradiction between the feed restriction practices
permitted under industry-specific welfare codes and the broader principles of the Act
itself, which emphasises animals' right to proper nourishment and natural behaviors.

New Zealand's dairy industry presents specific nutritional challenges, with
high-producing dairy cows often struggling to meet their metabolic demands through
pasture alone. This can lead to conditions like milk fever and ketosis.32

Similarly, in intensive poultry and pig operations, animals may receive diets that
maximise growth or production at the expense of their overall health and welfare. For
example, the parent birds of meat (broiler) chickens are often placed on restricted
feeding programs to prevent them from becoming too heavy, which would impair their
reproductive capabilities.33 This creates welfare concerns as these birds have been
genetically selected for rapid growth and have strong appetites, yet are fed only about
25-50% of what they would eat if given free access to food.

The practice of winter break feeding on forage crops has drawn significant criticism due
to animal welfare concerns. This practice often leaves cattle and sheep standing in
deep mud for extended periods, without adequate shelter, creating both welfare and
environmental issues.34

Animal Breeding and Reproduction Reform
The Animal Justice Party Aotearoa New Zealand (AJP) is committed to transforming
animal breeding and reproduction practices to uphold the rights, personhood and
welfare of animals. While our long-term vision is to end all forms of animal agriculture,
we recognise the urgent need to reform current breeding practices, which often prioritise
production and profit at the expense of animal health, dignity and wellbeing. This policy
addresses the ethical, legal and welfare concerns associated with genetic manipulation,
reproductive control and growth-promoting technologies used in modern farming.

There are pressing issues arising from intensive breeding programmes and
reproductive technologies that have often prioritised productivity at the expense of
animal health and well-being. A prime example of this is the breeding of broiler
chickens, who have been genetically selected to grow at an unnaturally rapid rate,
leading to severe health problems such as skeletal disorders and heart failure. Our
policy advocates to reverse these trends.

Current breeding practices often involve invasive and problematic procedures, including
forced artificial insemination and semen collection. These practices subject animals to
significant psychological stress and physical manipulation without their consent. In dairy
farming, cows are repeatedly impregnated through artificial insemination to maintain
milk production. Similarly, in pig farming, boars are subjected to forced semen collection
for artificial insemination programs. These practices reduce animals to reproductive
machines, ignoring their sentience and dignity.

Bobby calves are a direct result of dairy industry practices. These male calves, typically
separated from their mothers within 24 hours of birth, face severe welfare concerns
including premature maternal separation, inadequate nutrition and early slaughter. AJP
has identified this as an inherent systemic issue requiring immediate reform. While
working towards the complete abolition of dairy farming, we will advocate for strict
interim measures alongside transparent reporting of bobby calf statistics, enhanced
monitoring of welfare standards and significant penalties for non-compliance.

The breeding of animals for fibre and skin products, such as sheep for wool and cows
for leather, presents similar ethical concerns. Selective breeding for traits like increased
wool yield or specific hide qualities often compromises animal welfare. For example,
merino sheep bred for fine wool production frequently suffer from increased flystrike

MPI Codes and Welfare Expectations

Under the Animal Welfare Act 199937, MPI Codes of Welfare set minimum care
standards for animals, including breeders and those selling animals. Codes for dogs
and cats specifically recommend desexing for animals not intended for breeding, noting
that desexing significantly reduces the number of unwanted animals entering shelters
and improves overall population control. MPI guidance makes clear that desexing
should be performed before puberty for dogs not used for planned breeding, and cats
should be desexed early to prevent unplanned litters38.

These Codes also outline responsible breeding practices and highlight the need to
consider the availability of suitable homes before breeding. However, enforcement
mechanisms and penalties remain weak, leaving gaps in protection and oversight.

SPCA and Responsible Regulation

SPCA New Zealand supports improved legislative tools to mitigate welfare harms
arising from unregulated breeding. This includes stronger regulation and inspection of
breeding establishments, mandatory microchipping and desexing prior to sale, and
licensing systems for breeders with enforceable welfare standards. SPCA opposes the
purpose-breeding of companion animals for sale in ‘pet’ shops and online retailers

Ensuring the welfare and protection of
aquatic species
Equitable Protection for Aquatic Animals
The Animal Justice Party believes that if we say animals matter, our laws need to protect them.
New Zealand already acknowledges in legislation that fish, crustaceans, and cephalopods are
sentient beings capable of suffering. What we don't yet have are the standards, the
enforcement, and the consistency to make that acknowledgement legally binding. We want to
close that gap, and ensure that aquatic animals receive the same protection under the law that
we extend to animals on land.
What is happening
New Zealand's Animal Welfare Act 1999 names fish, octopus, squid, crab, lobster, and crayfish
within its definition of 'animal', and since 2015 has explicitly recognised animal sentience in its
purpose. But recognition without enforcement is just words on a page. The Act and its codes of
welfare are applied selectively, with significant gaps in oversight and monitoring. For aquatic
animals, those gaps are particularly wide. There is no standalone code of welfare for fish in
commercial aquaculture or wild capture. Without species-specific standards or adequate
resourcing, aquatic animals are effectively left out of the protection that the law promises them.
The picture is even more woeful for decapod crustaceans such as shrimp and prawns, and
cephalopods such as cuttlefish, which currently fall outside the legal definition of 'animal' under
the Act. Scientists now have strong consensus that fish can feel pain,51 and the evidence for
sentience in many aquatic invertebrates continues to grow.52 Our law has simply not kept pace
with these developments.
This matters at scale. Globally, somewhere between 78 and 171 billion farmed fishes,53 1.1 and
2.2 trillion wild fin-fishes are killed each year for human consumption,54 alongside 25 trillion of
shrimp.55 What New Zealand does in its own waters, and the standards it holds its industries to,
is within our power to change.

International Marine Animal Protection
The Animal Justice Party believes our oceans deserve more than management. They deserve
protection. Aotearoa New Zealand is a Pacific nation, bound to the moana by culture, identity,
and geography. Our closest neighbours have already led the way: in 2024, Indigenous leaders
from Aotearoa, the Cook Islands, Tahiti, Tonga, Hawaii, and Rapanui signed He Whakaputanga
Moana, recognising whales as beings with inherent rights. We want New Zealand to honour that
vision with action, ending our complicity in international marine cruelty and becoming a genuine
champion for the animals who live in our shared ocean. This shift in the international animal
welfare and protection policy environment highlights the growing recognition of animal welfare
as a critical issue on the global stage.

What is happening

Commercial whaling has never stopped. Japan, Norway, and Iceland continue to kill whales
despite a 40-year-old international moratorium,57 using a regulatory loophole that allows for
lethal scientific research. Since that moratorium came into force, Japan alone has killed over
24,000 whales,58 Norway over 16,000,59 and Iceland over 2,000.60 61(International Whaling
Commission, 2024.) Norway's 2026 quota is set at 1,641 minke whales, an increase of 235 on
last year, when the quota was set at 1,406.62 63 Japan withdrew from the International Whaling
Commission in 2019 to resume coastal commercial whaling and added fin whales, a threatened
species, to its commercial hunt in 2024.64 This is not tradition. It is industry, subsidised by
governments and sustained by political manoeuvring.

Each year in Taiji, Japan, hundreds of dolphins are driven into a cove, selected for marine parks
or killed. In the 2024/25 season, 286 dolphins were slaughtered and 94 taken captive, according
to on-the-ground monitoring by the Dolphin Project and Japanese animal advocates.65 In the
Faroe Islands, similar slaughter and trauma happens each year in the ‘grind’, in 2026 over 700
dolphins were killed.66 Families are separated. Calves lose their mothers. The animals who are
released carry the trauma of what they have witnessed.

Sharks are killed by the millions globally, often for their fins, and in some places culled to protect
beachgoers despite evidence that shark culls are both ineffective and ecologically damaging.
Seal hunting continues in Canada, Namibia, and elsewhere, driven by commercial fur and skin

Eliminating the Use of Animals in Science
Ending Animal Testing
The Animal Justice Party of Aotearoa NZ (AJP) aims to ban all harmful forms of animal
experimentation. AJP will commit to promoting the use of compassionate research.
Animal experimentation often utilises harmful and invasive processes that routinely
involve subjecting animals to painful and stressful procedures. The rate at which
animal-based models of experiments fail to translate to human-based models is high.
This creates an opportunity to find alternative methods that can prove to be more
effective, accurate and ethical. For example, there are emerging alternatives to many
forms of animal experimentation, such as cell cultures and computer simulations. By
requiring the use of alternatives to animal testing wherever possible, we can foster a
culture of innovation and advancement in the scientific field that does not come at the
expense of animals.
According to New Zealand Anti Vivisection Society (NZAVS), Aotearoa’s primary
charity defending animals used in science, there are major problems with animal
testing:
Animals are unreliable and unscientific models for predicting outcomes in humans
because:
- Animal biology does not translate to human biology.
- What works in animals often does not work in humans.
- What is safe for animals can be dangerous for humans.
- What does not work in animals may save human lives.
- Animal experiments are expensive and time consuming.
Animal experiments are harmful to humans and animals alike. Animal-free methods
often outperform animal experimentation and these animal-free technological methods
of testing can enable innovative ways to overcome the limitations of animal research.
Key objectives:
1. Campaign for the phasing out the use of harmful animal experimentation and
invasive testing and research methods.
2. Campaign for funding towards the 3Rs (replacement, reduction and refinement)
in the use of animals for science.

3Rs Explainer:
Animal experiments are widely required to comply with the 3Rs principle (Replacement,
Reduction, Refinement) to provide a framework for ethical decision making. In essence,
the 3Rs principle demands that wherever alternative methods exist, they have to be
used (replace), the number of animals used has to be kept to the bare minimum to
achieve the objectives of the research (reduce) and the treatment of the animals has to
be improved with measures taken to mitigate any pain, suffering or distress (refine).1
Whilst the 3Rs principle is widely recognised internationally by scientists as a moral
obligation, it fails, however, to provide any legal protection for the animals being
subjected to the experiments2 or establish any legal principles governing what ethical
research conduct actually means.3 It is also of itself a barrier to change, given that it
begins from an animal testing standpoint."

The environmental impacts of animal-based research
The Animal Justice Party of Aotearoa New Zealand (AJP) aims to ban all harmful forms of
animal experimentation. AJP commits to promoting the use of compassionate research.

Animal experimentation often utilises harmful and invasive processes that routinely involve
subjecting animals to painful and stressful procedures. The rate at which animal-based models
of experiments fail to translate to human-based models is high. This creates an opportunity to
find alternative methods that can prove to be more effective, accurate and ethical, for example,
there are emerging alternatives to many forms of animal experimentation such as cell cultures
and computer simulations. By requiring the use of alternatives to animal testing wherever
possible, we can foster a culture of innovation and advancement in the scientific field that does
not come at the expense of animals.

However, the traditional, and still dominant, ethical view, which is mirrored in most animal testing
legislation and regulations, is that the use of animals in research is acceptable in order to
achieve scientific, public safety and medical goals, provided that animal suffering is minimised
and that the human benefits gained could not be obtained by utilising alternative methods. By
its very nature, animal testing required by law is in tension with the goal of animal welfare
legislation, which is to protect animals from violations of their welfare.

Animal-based research isn't just an ethical issue. It also has significant environmental impacts
that demand attention. The environmental cost of maintaining these practices contradicts
commitments to sustainability and climate action.
The main environmental impacts of animal experimentation include:
5. High Resource Consumption: Animal research facilities use large amounts of water,
electricity, and specialised food for the animals. The need to maintain specific environmental
conditions (e.g., temperature control and ventilation) further increases energy use.
Animal research requires significant energy resources. Research facilities consume up to
ten times more energy per square metre than office buildings74 due to stringent
requirements, including controlled ventilation, temperature regulation, pathogen barriers,
specialised lighting, and power-intensive equipment.
6. Waste Production and Pollution: Research generates substantial biomedical waste that
requires careful management and disposal. This includes both biological waste (animal
carcasses, excrement, bedding, and uneaten food) and hazardous materials (syringes,
needles, contaminated materials, and chemical waste).
When animals used in research are disposed of, their remains may be classified as
hazardous waste, depending on the type of studies they were involved in. This can include
exposure to chemicals, infectious agents, or radioactive materials.

A key concern is the gap in awareness and safety measures between laboratory personnel,
who are trained to handle such materials, and external waste management or transportation
services, which may not have the same level of knowledge about the risks involved. If these
third-party handlers are unaware of potential hazards, improper disposal could lead to
environmental contamination or public health risks.
Proper disposal methods often involve incineration or other resource-intensive processes.
During incineration, particulate matter, organic compounds, pathogens, and radioactive
materials may be released into the surrounding environment, posing significant human health
risks, including cancer and respiratory illnesses. Environmental concerns include air and
water pollution, acidification, and greenhouse gas emissions.
7. Carbon Footprint: The transportation of animals, supplies, and research materials
contributes to carbon emissions. Additionally, maintaining breeding colonies and research
facilities adds to the overall carbon footprint.
8. Land Use and Habitat Destruction: Large-scale breeding and housing of research animals
requires land, which could otherwise be used for conservation or more sustainable
purposes.
9. Chemical and Pharmaceutical Pollution: Animal testing is particularly used for safety
(toxicity) and efficacy testing of chemical compounds. Beyond toxicity testing, animals are
also used to assess the effectiveness of sanitation, disinfection, and sterilisation processes.
A key concern is that some chemicals used in these experiments may have unknown
hazardous or carcinogenic properties, posing risks not only to the animals but also to
researchers, waste handlers, and the environment. Many chemicals tested in
laboratories may not yet have fully understood toxicological profiles, potentially exposing
both animals and humans to unknown dangers.
Industries that conduct toxicity and pharmaceutical testing on animals can contribute to
groundwater and soil contamination if their waste management practices are
inadequate. Improper disposal of chemical agents, pharmaceuticals, and biological
waste can lead to hazardous substances leaching into the environment, causing
long-term environmental hazards and public health risks.

Ban Rodeo
The Animal Justice Party Aotearoa NZ (AJP) advocates a ban on using animals for
‘entertainment’ and profit, and is committed to an immediate and complete ban of rodeo

In New Zealand, approximately 30 rodeo events are held every summer, featuring
activities such as bareback bronc riding, saddle bronc riding, bull riding, steer wrestling,
barrel racing, team roping, and calf roping. These events involve significant risks to
animal welfare, resulting in injuries and fatalities.

To entertain the public, rodeo animals are subjected to chasing, grabbing, prodding,
tackling, wrestling, and roping. Their heads and tails are twisted, and normally gentle
animals are forced into bucking frenzies through the use of spurs and irritating flank
straps, both of which cause significant physical and psychological distress to the
animals.

During rodeo events, animals can suffer from torn ligaments, broken bones (often
requiring euthanasia), cardiac arrest, bruising, and internal damage. Even without
physical injuries, animals experience significant stress and fear, especially calves who
are particularly vulnerable. Additionally, there is a lack of transparency in rodeo training
sessions, suggesting that many more animals are likely injured away from public
scrutiny.

Rodeos inherently involve cruelty, and we believe that they cannot be made safe
through regulation. These events promote and normalise violence against animals,
dulling society’s sensitivity to animal suffering. This is particularly concerning for children
who learn a skewed perception of “acceptable” animal treatment, shaping their
long-term attitudes towards animal welfare.

AJP advocates for non-violent, community-friendly entertainment that aligns with
society’s progressive concerns and higher ethical and moral principles, and does not
exploit and undermine animals’ well-being.

Ban Recreational Hunting and Hunting Competitions

The Animal Justice Party Aotearoa NZ (AJP) is opposed to recreational hunting,
including hunting competitions, and is committed to a complete ban. Recreational
hunting and hunting competitions cause death and suffering to animals, and undermine
efforts to promote respect and compassion for all.

Recreational hunting involves the pursuit and killing of animals for ‘sport’. This practice
not only causes unnecessary suffering to animals but also fosters a culture of violence
and desensitisation towards animal life. Significant suffering is inflicted upon animals:
they may endure prolonged pain from injuries before dying, and non-target species
often become unintended victims.

Hunting competitions exacerbate ethical concerns by incentivising the rapid, large-scale
killing of animals for prizes and recognition. This pressure often leads to inhumane
practices and a disregard for animal welfare. Current practices in some New Zealand
schools encourage children to participate in the mass killing of animals, often framed as
a game or competition, in which violence is normalised and young minds become
desensitised to the suffering of living creatures. Activities like 'Toss the Poss' not only
disrespect animal life but also teach children to view certain species as disposable,
rather than as sentient beings with lives of inherent worth.

Hunting promotes and normalises violence against animals, dulling society’s sensitivity
to animal suffering. Instead of fostering a connection with nature and teaching
responsible environmental stewardship, hunting promotes a harmful and oversimplified
approach to wildlife management.

New Zealand allows the hunting of an arbitrary and wide range of animals including, to
name a few, deer, pigs, free-roaming cats, rabbits and various bird species. Seasonal
restrictions may apply or licences may be required.

animals are not killed instantly, resulting in painful wounds and prolonged suffering;
injured animals that escape often face a slow, agonising death and the use of certain
hunting methods, such as traps or particular types of ammunition, can increase the
likelihood of non-fatal injuries. In the case of duck hunting, a seasonal activity, an
estimated one million birds are affected annually, highlighting the scale of the issue.

The Future of Zoos and Aquariums

The Animal Justice Party (AJP) advocates for a fundamental reorientation of zoos and
aquariums away from entertainment-driven models toward facilities that exist to serve
the interests of animals themselves. Facilities that currently exhibit animals for public
display must transition toward roles centred on rescue, veterinary care, rehabilitation
and, where necessary, the provision of lifelong sanctuary.

Where animals cannot be returned to the wild, their environments must be designed to
approximate natural conditions as closely as possible, prioritising autonomy, social
needs and behavioural expression. Public access, if permitted, must be strictly
managed to ensure that it does not compromise animal wellbeing.

The AJP recognises that many species are not suited to captivity under any
circumstances. As such, the long-term objective is to significantly reduce and, where
appropriate, eliminate the keeping of animals in traditional zoo settings. Technological
alternatives, particularly immersive and virtual experiences, should replace the use of
live animals for education and entertainment.

Phase out practices that prioritise exhibition and profit, supporting the evolution

circumstances where approval is considered, require rigorous pre-licensing
assessments, including detailed evaluation of operator suitability, financial

3. End Breeding for Display
Ban captive breeding except where it forms part of independently assessed
conservation programmes that demonstrably benefit both species survival and
individual animal welfare.

Background and Rationale

Zoos and aquariums may unintentionally communicate that it is acceptable to confine
wild animals in small or unsuitable enclosures - sometimes in isolation from their own
species - for human education or entertainment. Yet such conditions can cause
significant harm, as many animals are unable to engage in their natural, species specific
behaviours.

The AJP’s approach is grounded in the moral significance of individual animals. Whilst
biodiversity and ecosystem protection are important, they must not be pursued at the
expense of the lives and wellbeing of individual sentient beings. Practices such as
forced breeding, confinement in inadequate conditions and the treatment of animals as
interchangeable components of conservation strategies are ethically indefensible.

Effective conservation must prioritise the protection and restoration of natural habitats.
Without suitable environments for animals to return to, captive breeding programmes
offer limited value and may, in some cases, perpetuate harm. Moreover, zoos tend to

The AJP envisions a future in which human engagement with animals is guided by
respect, responsibility and non-exploitation. Transforming zoos and aquariums is a
critical step toward this goal, ensuring that animals are no longer used for entertainment
purposes, but are instead protected as individuals with intrinsic value.

Defining Zoos and Sanctuaries

Facilities that house animals vary widely in purpose and practice, often using
overlapping terminology that obscures important ethical distinctions.

- Zoos and aquariums are typically commercial enterprises that display animals
to paying visitors, sometimes incorporating conservation or educational activities
alongside entertainment functions.

- Sanctuaries, by contrast, are dedicated to the protection and care of animals,
without breeding, trading, or exploiting them for profit. Whilst some may allow
visitors, animal interests must always take precedence.

Given the blurred boundaries between these categories, regulatory focus should be
directed toward the underlying purpose of the institution - whether it exists primarily for
animals or for commercial gain.

Protection of indigenous and
non-indigenous wild animals
The Animal Justice Party (AJP) recognises all wild animals (indigenous and
non-indigenous) as individuals with unique needs and value. We believe that within
Aotearoa New Zealand both native and introduced animals have a right to live their lives
unimpeded and unharmed by human activities. For the purpose of this document, ‘wild
animal’ refers to free-living animals who live outside captivity and without direct human
control, including feral animals.

AJP recognises there can be conflicts between endemic and introduced animals, while
emphasising the need for solutions that prioritise compassion and protection. We reject
divisive language, hunting and the glorification of trapping and killing animals for
conservation purposes. Fundamentally, wild animals deserve the same rights to liberty,
health, and freedom from harm as domesticated animals, and this should be reflected in
law by specifically including them under the protection of the Animal Welfare Act, rather
than considering them “pests” for eradication.

The health and integrity of these ecosystems are of value to New Zealanders and
necessary to uphold the Crown’s obligations under Te Tiriti o Waitangi, and are also vital
for the flourishing of wild animals. For these reasons, AJP supports compassionate and
just efforts to mitigate the threats that our ecosystems face.
AJP’s policies for the protection of wild animals would best be implemented alongside a
transition to a plant-based economy. This is important for three key reasons. Firstly,
much of the funding for ‘pest’ control is allocated specifically to protect animal
agricultural interests from disease vectors, particularly targeting possums and stoats
which can carry bovine tuberculosis that affects farm animals.84 This risk would naturally
be eliminated with the end of animal farming. Secondly, the focus on invasive species
neglects the devastating impact that habitat loss has had on native fauna, which was
primarily driven by the need to create pasture for animal farming.85 Eliminating animal

Ending trapping and hunting for population control
AJP opposes the trapping and hunting of wild animals as a part of so-called ‘pest
control’ activities. For AJP’s policy on hunting for entertainment, see: Hunting and
Fishing policies.
Common trapping practices include:
- Leg-Hold Traps: These devices are designed to capture animals by the limb,
restraining them until they are dispatched by trappers. The use of leg-hold traps
can result in severe injuries, including fractures, dislocations, and lacerations.
Animals caught in these traps can experience prolonged periods of distress and
pain before being euthanised.106,107
- Kill Traps: Intended to provide a swift death, even the most humane traps can kill
non-target species or cause non-lethal injury.108
- Live-Capture Cage Traps: These traps aim to capture animals without immediate
harm, allowing for relocation or euthanasia. Animals may experience stress,
dehydration and exposure to harsh environmental conditions while confined for
up to 24 hours, according to regulations. However, these regulations are not
actively enforced.109
A lack of enforcement for existing codes of conduct means that inhumane practices
persist with minimal accountability. This regulatory gap allows for the continuation of
trapping and hunting methods that cause unnecessary suffering to animals.
Children and young people in New Zealand are sometimes involved in trapping
activities without sufficient age restrictions.110 This exposure raises ethical concerns
regarding the normalisation of violence towards animals and potential desensitisation to
animal suffering. It also poses safety risks, as handling traps and captured animals can
be hazardous without proper training and supervision.
Current trapping practices, coupled with inadequate regulation and enforcement, often
result in significant, and unnecessary, animal suffering. Addressing these issues

Protect and restore natural habitats
AJP supports greater protection and restoration of natural habitats and ecosystems. We
recognise that the destruction or degradation of habitats and ecosystems causes direct
harm to wild animals, and that both humans and wild animals are sustained by natural
habitats and ecosystems.

forestry.113 In order to reverse this process, AJP would enable greater protection of

Protect wildlife from anthropogenic harms
Wild animals are frequently harmed due to the design of urban structures, roads, and
the activities of people who are often unaware of their impacts. To address these issues,
AJP wishes to see greater integration of wildlife considerations into urban planning,
road design and signage by way of impact assessments. This would require greater
collaboration between local councils, urban planners, conservation groups and
communities to develop wildlife-friendly infrastructure.
Many wild animals, native and introduced, inhabit towns and cities and are frequently
harmed by their human-centric design. For example, windows can be made with glass
that is more visible to birds, thereby reducing collisions.119 Human-wildlife conflicts can
be addressed in nonviolent ways, such as through nonviolent population control of
pigeons, rather than using spikes to restrict perching.120 Generally speaking, by
considering animals in the design of urban structures and areas, harms to wild animals
can be reduced or avoided altogether. This may often require collaboration between
local councils, urban planners, conservation groups and communities.
This is particularly important in the design of roads, which frequently kill and injure wild
animals. Measures such as wildlife crossings, barriers, and lower speed limits can
reduce these harms,121 and research into wildlife movement patterns can inform road
and urban planning that prioritises animal safety. While the Wildlife Act 1953 requires
permits for developments that may disturb or kill protected species, its focus remains on
species conservation and habitat protection rather than the welfare of individual
animals, leaving a gap between conservation law and animal welfare.
An important aspect of making urban areas friendly to wild animals is by the integration
of habitat. This may involve planting native species, connecting fragmented habitats
through wildlife corridors, or creating green roofs and pocket parks. Such measures not
only provide shelter and food for animals but also improve the quality of life for people.
Lastly, signs warning people of sensitive wildlife, or educating people about how to
behave around them, need to be informative, highly visible, and strategically placed to
maximise their effectiveness in both rural and urban areas.

Mitigate natural threats to wild animals
AJP recognises that wild animals often suffer from causes of natural origin. In many
cases, intervention can be appropriate to protect wild animals from threats that they are
not able to cope with.
There are many examples today of people and conservation agencies intervening to
protect particularly endangered or charismatic species. For example, stranded whales
or dolphins are often kept wet and efforts are made to refloat them;122 lost penguins are
transported back to Antarctica;123 underweight yellow-eyed penguin/hoihoi chicks have
been hand-reared until they can survive at sea;124 and following cyclone Gabrielle,
wildlife stranded in mud and floodwaters were rescued.125 However, non-threatened and
less charismatic species often suffer from similar threats. AJP wishes to see these
existing efforts increased and expanded to other species. Research is also needed to
understand the welfare of wild animals and how their flourishing can be ensured and
legally protected.
Wild animal populations are especially impacted by natural disasters. For example, the
Kaikōura earthquake disrupted marine ecosystems and seal colonies,126 while
increasingly frequent severe storms and flooding events have destroyed habitats and
nesting sites of birds like the endangered wrybill.127 Prolonged drought conditions have
reduced food availability for many species,128 and rising sea levels threaten coastal
wildlife.129 The increasing intensity of these events due to climate change compounds
the suffering of wild animals who have no means to escape these disasters.

starvation, disease, harsh weather, or threats from other species or members of their

Our position at a glance
We support a greater focus on the introduction of science-based, ethical methods to
manage the genuine tension between introduced species, including cats, and
indigenous species. We believe the primary driver of indigenous species decline in
Aotearoa is habitat loss, not introduced animals, and that this must be honestly named
and addressed proportionately.

What we believe: six policy pillars

1. All animals matter
Both indigenous and introduced species are sentient beings with a right to live
unimpeded by human activities. Cats did not choose to come here. Humans brought
them.

2. Language shapes thinking
We call for an end to unscientific, emotive and dehumanising terms to describe
introduced animals that are not useful to us. Language that vilifies animals makes killing
them easier to ignore. NZ has no hate speech laws pertaining specifically to animals -
while animals cannot be hurt directly by the attribution of malice or intentional damage
achieved by use of terms like ‘pest’, ‘invasive’, ‘stone-cold killer’, ‘utter killing
machines’,‘killers for fun’, the effect is to demonise and to make killing and cruelty more
acceptable.

3. Lethal eradication is not conservation
We oppose the use of 1080 poison on cats. Animal welfare scientists have found 1080
causes deaths averaging 9.5 hours of spasms and tremors. This is not humane. It is not
acceptable.

4. Innovation over violence
Immunocontraceptives, in-ovo sex determination, gene drives are real, proven or

restored right across present day Aotearoa with its permanent and growing population
and large scale agricultural economy, and that mainland eradication of introduced
predator and perhaps also competitor species is achievable using available and even
foreseeable technologies. We support a focus on strengthening and augmenting an
adequately sized, world class reserve system encompassing multiple habitats above an
unrealistic, overly-diffuse and ‘ad infinitum’ policy of eradication.

5. Address the real driver
Habitat loss is the primary driver of native species decline in Aotearoa. Focusing on

rights of animals as sentient beings, ensuring they are not subjected to exploitation,
harm or cruelty. It is imperative that animal welfare and protection legislation is
adequately resourced and equipped with robust compliance monitoring, appropriate
penalties and regulatory enforcement capabilities.

Animal welfare legislation should be drafted with the sole intention of recognising animal
sentience and protecting animals, without influence from industries that profit from their
exploitation. The principles enshrined in the Animal Welfare Act 1999 must be
enforceable, without loopholes that allow industries to evade responsibility by
self-regulation. Until adequate animal protection legislation is in place, AJP will also
campaign to remove and prohibit exemptions and inconsistencies that allow animal
cruelty to occur (for example, codes of practice for the “welfare” of farmed animals).

AJP supports a legal framework that reflects a societal commitment to valuing,
protecting and respecting animals, fostering responsible and compassionate treatment
in all contexts and industries. Without stringent, and enforceable, legal protection,
animals remain vulnerable to cruelty and exploitation, their welfare jeopardised by
profit-driven motives.

Empowering and resourcing authorities to share information and enforce legislation and
regulations is essential, ensuring individuals and organisations are held accountable for
infringements. Championing animal-centric legislation paves the way to a more just and
humane society where positive animal welfare136 is legally recognised and animals are
granted by the law the dignity and protection they deserve.

International Considerations
The shift in the international animal welfare and protection policy environment highlights
the growing recognition of animal welfare as a critical issue on the global stage.

It is no longer viewed as peripheral but has become integral to discussions in regional
and international policy forums.

This change is underscored by the emergence of an expanding framework of
science-based standards, conventions, treaties, regulations, directives, and
agreements.

Key trends in this evolving landscape include:

1. Science-Based Frameworks: Policy decisions are increasingly guided by robust
scientific research, which ensures that animal welfare measures are grounded in
evidence and best practices.
2. Global and Regional Agreements: International treaties and regional directives,
such as the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild
Fauna and Flora (CITES), the World Organisation for Animal Health (WOAH)
standards or EU directives on animal welfare, set benchmarks for practices
across borders.
3. Integration into Broader Agendas: Animal welfare is being linked with
sustainability, public health, biodiversity, and climate change, ensuring it receives
attention in broader policy contexts.
4. Stakeholder Collaboration: Governments, NGOs, scientists, and industry
players are collaborating more actively to develop and implement welfare
policies.

This evolving framework not only reflects a growing ethical commitment to animals but
also acknowledges their role in sustainable development and human wellbeing. Global
animal protection is, however, a complex challenge requiring collaboration across
countries, cultures, and legal systems.

While there are various treaties, conventions, and agreements addressing specific
aspects of animal welfare, there is no unified international instrument that broadly
regulates animal welfare across all contexts and provides holistic animal welfare
protections.

Key gaps include:

1. Limited Scope: Existing frameworks often prioritise conservation and
biodiversity rather than the welfare of individual animals. This leaves many
species, especially those not endangered or economically significant, without
legal protection.
2. Lack of Universal Standards and Jurisdictional Issues: Countries have
varying cultural, economic, and ethical views on animal welfare, making it difficult
to establish universally accepted standards. International frameworks may
conflict with national sovereignty, limiting their enforceability within domestic legal
systems.
3. Non-Binding Nature: Many international standards, such as the WOAH’s animal
welfare standards, are non-binding, leaving adoption and enforcement at the
discretion of individual nations.
4. Lack of Enforceability: Even binding agreements like CITES face challenges
with enforcement, as they rely on national governments to implement and
monitor compliance.
5. Species-Specific Gaps: Many frameworks focus on specific species or groups
(e.g., endangered species under CITES), leaving gaps in protection for other
animals, such as farmed or laboratory animals, despite these being the largest
groups of animals directly impacted by human activity.

Below is a proposed structure to guide the formulation of a policy to advocate for more
comprehensive and enforceable global animal protection frameworks:

law and policy instruments and challenge any provisions that undermine animal
protection.
2. Harmonising Standards: Creating internationally accepted benchmarks that
accommodate regional differences whilst maintaining high welfare standards for
imported animal products. As New Zealand has some of the most robust animal
welfare practices, compared to our trading partners, we have set the benchmark
for our primary industry and a framework for continuous improvement in animal
quality of life:
- AJP will campaign for uniform standards when importing animal products.

Animal welfare standards and known breaches

The Animal Welfare Act 1999146 outlines the needs of animals as follows:

- Proper and sufficient food and water.
- Adequate shelter.
- The opportunity to display normal patterns of behaviour.
- Physical handling in a manner which minimises the likelihood of unreasonable or
unnecessary pain or distress.
- Protection from, and rapid diagnosis of, any significant injury or disease.

These basic needs must be met by law and oftentimes they are not147, hence the need
for such a position as the Commissioner for Animals to be established. An independent
Commissioner for Animals should be equipped to propose changes to legislation and
enforcement where these basic requirements are being ignored or compromised.

Why do we need the Commissioner for Animals to be established?

New Zealand is the second largest exporter of animal products globally148, and while our
Animal Welfare Act may seem adequate, the accompanying Codes, shaped by the
animal agriculture industry, at times directly breach this Act. Because Aotearoa has
such a large export industry, it is crucial that ethics and standards are upheld. As This
industry is governed by stakeholders who do not have an impartial interest149, the rights
and welfare of animals is often not prioritised. Simple things like the right to adequate
shelter are being ignored and animals are suffering as a result150. New Zealand
promotes animal welfare as our ‘brand image’ and prioritises animal welfare as part of
our export story. It would seem that we are only capable of improving welfare standards

as a part of our export image but while there are animals being housed inappropriately,
enduring inadequate shade and shelter, and being denied basic freedoms, we can not
claim this image as truth151. The Commissioner for Animals would ensure a better
outcome for all animals including farmed animals, animals in entertainment, companion
animals, wild animals, and animals in research, testing and teaching.

Fireworks displays fundamentally contradict the conservation purpose of New Zealand's
core environmental legislation, including the Wildlife Act 1953, the Marine Mammals
Protection Act 1978, and the Fisheries Act 1996, by introducing noise, chemical
pollution and acute stress that compromises the well-being and habitat of legally

Broader Benefits
Adoption of this policy would position Aotearoa as a leader in compassionate and
responsible governance, prioritising the well-being of people, animals and the
environment and demonstrating that celebration and environmental responsibility are
not mutually exclusive. By ending private fireworks use, we would protect our unique
ecosystems, reduce animal suffering, and respond to clear public demand for change.

Professional fireworks displays, while more controlled than private use, still cause the
same environmental contamination and wildlife disturbance. Modern alternatives like
synchronised drone shows offer equally spectacular celebrations without any of these
harms.183

The policy recognises that when we know better, we must do better. Just as we no
longer permit smoking in cars with children, we must evolve our approach to
celebrations that cause significant preventable harms. This is a policy whose time has
come.

Key Objectives
1. Prohibit private sales of fireworks to individuals across all retail channels.
2. Legislate against private use of fireworks.
3. Phase out professional fireworks displays over a 1-2 year transition period.
