Artificial Intelligence and Animal Welfare
Introduction
The Animal Justice Party of Aotearoa New Zealand (AJP) recognises that artificial intelligence (AI) is
rapidly transforming how millions of animals are managed across farming, aquaculture and introduced
species control in Aotearoa New Zealand. While AI technologies offer potential to improve animal
welfare through enhanced monitoring and early disease detection, they also risk entrenching harmful
practices and creating new forms of harm if deployed without adequate governance systems.

AJP does not endorse the continued expansion of animal agriculture. Any use of AI in these systems must
demonstrate responsible development and genuine prioritisation of animal welfare and harm
minimisation. We oppose AI technology systems designed purely for economic efficiency that treat
animals as units of production rather than as sentient individuals with inherent value.

AJP calls for immediate integration of animal welfare and protection considerations into AI governance
frameworks before harmful practices become economically entrenched and impossible to reform. The
long-term policy direction of AI must prioritise transition away from animal farming, not the
technological optimisation of it.

Context
The Scale of AI Deployment
AI technologies are already deployed across Aotearoa New Zealand's animal management systems at
unprecedented scale. Over 400,000 cattle are currently managed using AI-powered virtual fencing
systems, whilst millions more animals in dairy, beef, sheep, chicken, aquaculture systems and introduced
species control are increasingly likely to be subject to AI-driven management decisions.

AI systems are being rapidly integrated into the management of these animals, making autonomous
decisions about their welfare, health and lives.

Current AI applications include:

- Virtual fencing and herding: AI-integrated wearable technology using sounds and vibration to
control animal movement, with systems learning and predicting individual behaviour patterns
- Slaughterhouse automation, Computer vision, machine learning and robotics for carcass grading,
meat inspection, automated restraint, and cutting, optimising yield and throughput.
- Health monitoring: Computer vision and machine learning analysing gait patterns, body
condition and behaviour to assess welfare
- Automated feeding and milking: AI-optimised systems managing nutrition and dairy production
- Aquaculture management: Machine learning for biomass measurement, feeding optimisation
and water quality monitoring
- Introduced species control: AI-powered cameras in traps using species recognition, and
autonomous drones identifying and poisoning target animals

animaljustice.org.nz | party@animaljusticeparty.org.nz
118

---

The Regulatory Gap
The Animal Welfare Act 1999 was enacted before AI technology existed and contains no provisions for
AI-driven animal management and welfare. This creates a critical regulatory time lag where technology is
reshaping human-animal relationships faster than legislation and regulation can adapt.

Aotearoa New Zealand's AI Strategy (July 2025), positions agriculture as a key adoption sector but
contains no animal welfare considerations. The accompanying Responsible AI Guidance for Businesses
covers cybersecurity, privacy and intellectual property whilst omitting animal welfare entirely. The
Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment has been explicit that "unlike EU regulatory
approaches, our approach is dispersed. The Government doesn't intend to put in place an overarching AI
Act. AI risks should be managed in relevant legislation as they arise."(email correspondence Oct 2025).

This dispersed “light touch” approach is already being implemented in other sectors. 2025 changes to
the Commerce Act, address AI-facilitated anti-competitive conduct, ensuring companies are liable for AI
actions. Additionally, a Members Bill was introduced (2025) to amend the Harmful Digital
Communications and Crimes Act 1961 to address AI-generated harms such as deepfakes. These
examples confirm that rapid, targeted legislative response is possible.

Animal welfare requires the same urgency. Without explicit action to integrate welfare considerations
into relevant existing Acts, AI governance will continue to treat animal welfare as a low-priority
externality rather than a core consideration.

Without explicit regulatory requirements, AI systems will inevitably be designed solely for economic
efficiency rather than animal welfare and protection. Market forces alone cannot ensure welfare and
safety outcomes; only regulation can mandate that AI development prioritises animals' behavioural,
physical and mental needs rather than subordinating them to economic and productivity metrics.

Case Study: Virtual Fencing Regulatory Lag
Virtual fencing technology demonstrates the pattern of regulatory lag that affects AI systems
deployment. Despite operating commercially since at least 2020 and affecting hundreds of thousands of
cattle:

- Circa 2021: The National Animal Welfare Advisory Committee (NAWAC) recommended
safeguards for virtual fencing in its Code of Welfare Evaluation Report on Dairy Cattle, stating
these "should have more generic application than only virtual fencing and apply to any future
technology proposed for animal management"
- Early 2024: A petition called for a parliamentary inquiry into virtual fencing technology
- December 2024: Veterinarians for Animal Welfare Aotearoa announced development of a code
of ethical conduct for virtual fencing, demonstrating industry concern whilst government action
remained pending
- April 2025: The Petitions Committee recommended inclusion of guidance in the Code of Welfare:
Dairy Cattle update

animaljustice.org.nz | party@animaljusticeparty.org.nz
119

---

- July 2025: The government noted that virtual fencing presents "an opportunity to review the
standards" but provided no timeline for implementation
- Late 2025: NAWAC's work programme plans to provide a revised recommendation, with no
certainty about when actual regulatory guidance will be implemented

This five-year lag between commercial deployment and potential regulatory guidance illustrates the
systematic failure to apply anticipatory regulation principles to animal welfare contexts, despite on-going
advocacy by the Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals (SPCA). Without proactive intervention,
each new AI technology will follow this same pattern: commercial deployment, widespread adoption,
entrenchment in industry practice, then belated regulatory consideration of animal welfare and safety.

Global Context and Market Pressures
Globally, most AI governance frameworks have overlooked animal welfare. The OECD's AI Principles and
most national AI strategies focus exclusively on human-centred concerns such as privacy, bias,
transparency, data integrity, accountability and safety. However, a significant breakthrough occurred in
July 2025, when the EU's General-Purpose AI Code of Practice explicitly listed "risk to non-human
welfare" as a systemic risk, alongside threats to democratic processes, financial stability and
environmental harm. This represents the first time a major jurisdiction has formally recognised that AI
governance must consider animal welfare, achieved through successful advocacy by animal welfare
organisations during the drafting stage.

Beyond the EU, Serbia's AI framework explicitly states AI systems "must be in line with the well-being of
humans, animals, and the environment." These examples demonstrate that inclusion of animal welfare
in AI governance is both achievable and is increasingly being recognised as necessary.

The AI animal health market is projected to grow from approximately $1.4 billion in 2024 to over $8
billion by 2034, with the farmed animal sector expected to see the fastest growth. This rapid investment
is occurring without systematic regulatory oversight of welfare outcomes, creating substantial risk that AI
systems will entrench rather than improve current harmful practices.

Welfare Risks of Unregulated AI
- Intensification of harmful practices: AI technology makes existing harmful practices more
efficient rather than more humane. It integrates best with intensive, cage-based systems that
have the worst welfare conditions, enabling higher stocking densities and more intensive
confinement, whilst appearing to ensure individualised care.
- Economic prioritisation: Data collection prioritises economic metrics over welfare indicators. AI
systems optimise measurable parameters (e.g. milk yield, growth rate, feed conversion) whilst
potentially missing qualitative welfare aspects such as emotional wellbeing, behavioural
freedom and social relationships.
- Reduced human oversight: Fewer human caregivers enable larger-scale operations, removing
human-animal relationships and reducing opportunities for animals to receive individualised
attention and compassionate care.

animaljustice.org.nz | party@animaljusticeparty.org.nz
120

---

- Degraded human-animal relationship: humans become algorithm supervisors rather than carers
risking moral injury and loss of empathy. Sentient beings are viewed as data streams.
- Technological dependency: System failures could leave animals without care. Farms become
vulnerable to hacking, sabotage and corporate espionage. Adverse weather conditions may
impact camera-based systems.
- Welfare washing: AI systems create the appearance of individualised care whilst facilitating
intensive systems. Companies can claim "precision welfare" or "AI-monitored health" whilst
maintaining fundamentally harmful practices.
- Automated lethal control: AI-powered introduced species control technologies operate without
direct human oversight of individual animal deaths, making life-or-death decisions
autonomously. This raises serious ethical questions about delegating such decisions to
algorithms designed for efficiency rather than compassion.

Economic Scale and Digital Divide
High AI technology implementation costs will create a digital divide where smaller operations cannot
access technologies that larger commercial operations use for both efficiency and welfare monitoring.
This risks creating a two-tiered system where animal welfare outcomes depend on economic scale rather
than consistent regulatory standards, with larger operations able to demonstrate compliance through AI
systems monitoring, whilst smaller farms lack resources for equivalent compliance systems.

The Window for Action
Despite AI technology deployment already underway across Aotearoa New Zealand's animal
management systems, the window for proactive policy intervention still remains open. While systems
already affect hundreds of thousands of animals, harmful practices have not yet become so economically
entrenched that reform is impossible.

The government has demonstrated capacity for rapid legislative response when circumstances require it.
In May 2025, Parliament passed the Wildlife (Authorisations) Amendment Bill under urgency to clarify
authority for killing protected wildlife during development projects, responding within months to a High
Court decision. This swift action demonstrates that regulatory speed depends on political prioritisation
rather than legislative capacity.

Connection to Existing AJP Policies
Several existing AJP policies already provide a foundation for addressing AI systems and improving
animal welfare:

- Commissioner for Animals: An independent Commissioner would provide necessary impartial
oversight to manage inter-agency coordination on AI governance and ensure animal welfare and
protection remains central to technological development
- Sentience and Legal Status: AJP's existing advocacy for abolishing the classification of animals as
property, extended species coverage and defining sentience clearly in the Animal Welfare Act

animaljustice.org.nz | party@animaljusticeparty.org.nz
121

---

1999 directly supports the need for AI systems to recognise animals as sentient individuals rather
than productive units
- Worker Rights and Safety: Existing policies on Health and Safety at Work align with the
recommendation to include animal welfare in automated system safety assessments
- Transparency and Whistleblowing: Policies protecting those who expose cruelty support the
need for accountability in AI-managed systems

However, the unique challenges posed by AI systems require specific additional measures beyond these
existing governance frameworks.

Key Objectives
1. Amend the Animal Welfare Act 1999 to explicitly address AI applications affecting animals, including:

- Specific welfare and protection provisions for AI systems in both farming and introduced species
control contexts
- Mandatory independent validation of AI welfare monitoring systems before commercial
deployment
- Requirements for human oversight alongside AI systems automation, ensuring that critical
welfare decisions are not delegated entirely to algorithms
- Mandatory welfare impact assessments for new AI technologies before deployment at
commercial scale
- Prohibition of AI systems that conceal, normalise or facilitate harm or cruelty
- Clear accountability frameworks establishing who is responsible when AI management systems
decisions cause animal harm or welfare failures

2. Update Codes of Welfare to include AI-specific guidance, beginning with the Code of Welfare: Dairy
Cattle to address virtual fencing and AI-driven monitoring systems. All Codes should include:

- Generic safeguards applicable to any future technology proposed for animal management
- Standards for AI-enabled welfare monitoring to ensure systems genuinely improve outcomes
rather than simply measure declining welfare more precisely
- Requirements for validated welfare benefits before widespread adoption
- Mandatory human competency and oversight requirements

3. Establish an animal-centred design framework for AI systems affecting animals, requiring that:

- Systems must be explicitly designed for animal welfare, competence and protection, not merely
economic efficiency
- Design processes incorporate the Five Domains Model of positive animal welfare (Nutrition,
Environment, Health, Behavioural Interactions, Mental State)
- Systems actively enhance animals' choice, control, variety, complexity and competence rather
than simply monitoring their decline
- Welfare outcomes are validated independently before and after deployment
- Animals' behavioural, physical and mental needs are prioritised above productivity metrics

animaljustice.org.nz | party@animaljusticeparty.org.nz
122

---

- Beneficial AI research and development is supported, including non-lethal, humane alternatives
for managing human-wildlife conflict, and technologies that facilitate transition to plan-based
food systems.

4. Create an Inter-agency AI-Animal Welfare Working Group chaired by the Commissioner for Animals,
with representatives from agencies, including (but not limited to) the Ministry for Primary Industries,
Department of Conservation, Environmental Protection Authority, Civil Aviation Authority and
Commerce Commission, to:

- Develop consistent guidelines and protection mechanisms across existing legislation and
regulation
- Coordinate enforcement protocols and information sharing between agencies
- Apply One Welfare principles integrating animal welfare, human wellbeing and environmental
considerations before AI systems are deployed
- Report annually on AI systems developments, regulatory gaps and welfare outcomes
- Monitor emerging AI technologies and assess their welfare implications before widespread
deployment

5. Build regulatory capacity to assess and monitor AI technologies by:

- Develop AI literacy programmes for Ministry for Primary Industries inspectors and Department
of Conservation staff, enabling them to evaluate AI-based animal management systems
- Create farmer and animal manager education programmes ensuring those who deploy AI can
interpret outputs, recognise system failures and maintain appropriate human oversight
- Develop assessment tools and criteria for evaluating AI-based welfare systems
- Provide agencies with ongoing resources to understand rapidly evolving AI technologies and
improve governance frameworks

6. Leverage existing legislative frameworks to address AI-animal welfare intersections immediately,
without waiting for new legislation, including:

- Privacy Act 2020: Extend data protection to animal-derived biometric data, ensuring commercial
interests cannot exploit animal data without welfare safeguards and protection
- Fair Trading Act 1986: Strengthen enforcement against misleading welfare claims, particularly
"welfare washing" where AI systems monitoring is marketed as welfare improvement without
evidencing genuine benefit to animals
- Consumer Guarantees Act 1993: Ensure AI animal management systems meet
fitness-for-purpose standards when welfare outcomes are promised
- Resource Management Act 1991: Include animal welfare and protection in environmental impact
assessments for AI systems
- Health and Safety at Work Act 2015: Include animal welfare considerations in automated system
safety assessments

- Hazardous Substances and New Organisms (HSNO) Act 1996 and Agricultural Compounds and
Veterinary Medicines (ACVM) Act 1997: Require welfare impact assessments for AI systems for
all new technological interventions
- Biosecurity Act 1993: Integrate welfare standards into AI-powered introduced species control

- Civil Aviation Act 1990: Mandate welfare protocols for drone-based animal operations, including

- Wildlife Act 1953: Establish ‘humane’ standards for AI-enabled introduced species control

- Conservation Act 1987: Ensure the Department of Conservation's AI systems deployment

- Mandatory public reporting of AI deployment scale, including the number of animals affected

- Accessible data on welfare outcomes, system failures and interventions
- Clear pathways for reporting, and addressing, welfare concerns related to AI systems
- Protection for whistleblowers who expose AI systems-related welfare failures
- Public registers of validated AI welfare management systems
- Consolidated national statistics on introduced species control methods, kill numbers and welfare

- Enable increased stocking densities or more intensive confinement
- Reduce human-animal contact below minimum welfare standards
- Make autonomous lethal decisions without human oversight
- Prioritise economic optimisation at the expense of animal welfare and protection
- Conceal or normalise practices that would otherwise be recognised as harmful or cruel

- Expand explicit species coverage in animal welfare legislation to reflect current scientific

- Regulate AI systems affecting aquaculture and commercial fishing with the same rigour as

- Require that AI design processes acknowledge and respond to positive species-specific

Interim Measures

While comprehensive legislative amendments are developed and implemented, AJP supports immediate

10. Issue urgent guidance under existing legislation to all research facilities, farms and conservation

## Full text (verbatim)

### Web page text

Climate change and habitat loss pose urgent threats to both people and non-human animals, driven by fossil fuels, ecosystem destruction, and intensive animal agriculture. The Animal Justice Party advocates for decisive, systemic change – putting the wellbeing of all sentient beings at the forefront of environmental policy and legal protection.

Note: Read our dedicated policy page detailing the AJP’s commitment to a just transition to a plant-based economy that respects sentient life, protects public health and supports farmers.

Urgently addressing Climate Change
The AJP is the only political party in Aotearoa New Zealand with a serious commitment to
tackling major sources of emissions in ways which are credible, compassionate and aligned
with climate science. We support a rapid reduction in animal agriculture (which is
responsible for around half of Aotearoa New Zealand’s emissions) by transitioning to a
plant-based economy, supporting farmers to grow produce instead of farming animals and
addressing the profoundly detrimental impact of climate change on animals. Additionally,
animals are extremely vulnerable to the storms, flooding and fires we continue to see in
Aotearoa New Zealand as a result of climate change.
We support policies that reduce emissions, avoid unnecessary animal suffering, improve
human and non-human animal health, and restore and expand our waterways, forests and
wildlife. We reject ineffective solutions that aim to perpetuate the status quo. We are
committed to supporting animals of all kinds to adapt to the changes in climate that are
already underway, and that which are predicted, in order to create a sustainable future
Core Principle
Climate change is a symptom of the metacrisis, a planetary emergency requiring a
whole-of-government response that addresses root causes, not symptoms. We must move
beyond the failed approach of leaving token climate action to environment ministries while
economic policy continues business-as-usual. This systemic approach protects animals by
preventing the habitat destruction, ocean acidification, extreme weather events, and
ecosystem collapse driven by climate change, while ending the economic pressures that
force expansion of industrial animal agriculture and fossil fuel extraction into remaining
wildlife territories.

animaljustice.org.nz | party@animaljusticeparty.org.nz
2

---

Climate leadership
The AJP calls for climate leadership that protects sentient beings. Climate change threatens
all life in Aotearoa and across the Pacific as well as globally. Effective climate leadership
must embed sentient animal protection into all domestic frameworks, working to prevent
further climate change while strengthening enforcement and accountability. Climate risk
assessments and adaptation plans must explicitly consider the welfare of animals and the
health of ecosystems, alongside human infrastructure and communities, ensuring that policy
decisions reduce harm and build ecological resilience.
New Zealand has a responsibility to partner with Pacific Island nations as tangata whenua of
Te Moana-nui-a-Kiwa. Supporting Pacific-led solutions, including climate-safe migration
pathways and sanctuary networks, protects both human and non-human communities.
Ending fossil fuel financing, intensive agriculture, and creating regional climate coalitions
ensures biodiversity, marine life and habitats are safeguarded. By linking domestic climate
action with regional cooperation, New Zealand can lead in protecting animals, ecosystems
and communities from the escalating impacts of climate change.
Key Objectives
1. Enforce robust National Adaptation Plan commitments, with binding timelines and
penalties for departments that fail to protect animals and habitats.
2. Extend domestic climate risk assessments to regional impacts, ensuring wildlife,

Comprehensive Waste Minimisation at Source
The AJP is committed to eliminating waste creation at the source rather than managing
waste streams after environmental damage has already occurred. We acknowledge that
current approaches focus on end-of-pipe solutions while ignoring the resource extraction and
manufacturing processes that destroy wildlife habitats to create products destined to become
waste.

Every product manufactured requires raw materials extracted from ecosystems where
animals live. Mining operations destroy underground habitats for countless invertebrates and
soil organisms as well as the ecosystems at the surface. Forestry operations fragment and
destroy territories used by native birds, bats and ground-dwelling species. Manufacturing
processes consume enormous quantities of water that animals depend upon whilst
generating toxic byproducts that contaminate the environments where wildlife must survive.

The most effective way to protect animal habitats is to dramatically reduce the volume of
products manufactured in the first place. When we require manufacturers to design out
waste, extend product lifespans and take responsibility for entire product lifecycles, we
directly reduce the pressure on natural systems that sustain wildlife populations.

The AJP prioritises eliminating waste at its source to protect wildlife habitats and reduce
resource extraction. Every tonne of waste not created avoids trucks driving through wildlife
corridors, prevents processing facilities from being built on productive land and keeps
disposal sites from contaminating watersheds that native species rely on. By requiring
products to be designed for longevity, repairability and responsible end-of-life management,
these policies minimise environmental harm while keeping recovery systems as a back-up
for what cannot be designed out.

innovative packaging solutions, prevents countless plastic-related deaths of marine animals,
reduces toxic contamination of seafood, and establishes New Zealand as a global leader in

Urban Biodiversity and Natural Infrastructure
The AJP is committed to restoring native ecosystems within urban environments, creating
corridors for wildlife movement and habitat regeneration that support both indigenous
species and community wellbeing. We acknowledge that urban development has
fragmented natural habitats, isolating native species populations and reducing their
resilience to climate change and other pressures.

Urban areas house 86% of New Zealand's population14 but often function as ecological
deserts where native wildlife cannot survive or move between remaining habitat patches. Yet
cities also represent a great opportunity for rapid biodiversity gains. Urban forests in New
Zealand, such as those in Auckland's parks, can sequester carbon at rates comparable to
natural vegetation. A study by Schwendenmann and Mitchell (2014) found that a 27-year-old
planted forest stored a total of 45.9 megagrams of carbon per hectare, equating to an
average annual carbon sequestration rate of 1.7 megagrams per hectare.15 This rate is
within the range reported for New Zealand shrublands. Despite challenges like poor-quality
soil and contamination, urban forests can sequester carbon at similar rates to natural
vegetation in New Zealand. By providing both carbon storage and connectivity, these forests
support biodiversity while contributing to climate mitigation.

Green infrastructure provides multiple benefits: native plantings filter stormwater whilst
creating habitat, tree canopy reduces urban heat whilst providing nesting sites, and
biodiversity corridors connect fragmented ecosystems whilst offering communities
opportunities to engage with native wildlife. Research shows that urban biodiversity supports
human mental health16 whilst creating resilient ecosystems that can adapt to climate change.

International examples demonstrate what's possible. Singapore’s “City in a Garden” initiative
has transformed dense urban areas into functional habitat networks. Its green corridors and
restored parks support over 60 bird species, as well as bats, butterflies, and other native
fauna, allowing them to move safely across the city and access feeding and breeding sites.17
These corridors turn urban spaces from ecological deserts into interconnected habitats that
sustain animal populations.

Melbourne’s Urban Forest Strategy, which plants over 3,000 trees annually, not only
improves air quality and urban resilience but also creates canopy networks and stepping
stones that allow native birds, bats, and insects to navigate and survive in the city
landscape.18 By integrating animals’ needs into city planning, these initiatives show that
urban greening is essential infrastructure for biodiversity, not just human amenity. Uk

Protecting Insects from Human-Caused Harms
Insects, particularly pollinators, are in global decline, with studies showing terrestrial insect
abundance dropping by about 9 % per decade.19 Although long-term monitoring is lacking in
New Zealand, around 54 % of assessed native insect species are currently listed as
threatened or at risk, underscoring the urgent need for conservation.20 Habitat loss,
monoculture farming, and pesticide use are major drivers of these declines.
There is also growing scientific evidence of sentience of different insects. For example, a
2022 review of the evidence for pain in insects found “strong evidence” for the orders
containing flies and cockroaches, “substantial” evidence for the orders containing beetles
and butterflies, and “no good evidence that any insects failed a criterion”.21 Since these
species are largely under-studied, a precautionary approach requires that we grant
protection even when such evidence is incomplete.22
Key threats to insects are:
- The expansion of urban areas and intensive farming has led to the destruction of
natural habitats, reducing the availability of nesting sites and food sources for many
insect species.
- The widespread use of chemical pesticides has had devastating effects on insect
populations, particularly bees, butterflies, and other pollinators. Many pesticides
disrupt the nervous systems of insects, leading to mass die-offs.
- Industrial agricultural practices, including large-scale monocultures, reduce plant
diversity and limit food sources for insects, further contributing to population declines.
- Rising temperatures, shifting weather patterns, and pollution disrupt insect life cycles
and reduce the availability of suitable habitats.
Protecting insects is essential for maintaining a thriving environment. AJP will continue to
advocate for policies that safeguard pollinators, restore ecosystems and promote
sustainable land-use practices.
Key Objectives:
1. Safeguard and restore natural ecosystems, such as forests, meadows, wetlands and
waterways, which are vital for the survival of bees, butterflies, and other insects.
2. Implement stricter regulations on pesticide use, including restrictions on high-toxicity
chemicals during key insect activity periods, in areas where insects forage, breed, or
migrate, and promote adoption of non-toxic alternatives.
3. Support research and development of non-toxic alternatives to chemical pesticides.
4. Promote mixed farming practices over monocultures to enhance habitat diversity and
insect-friendly landscapes.

Strengthening Environmental Enforcement in Aotearoa
The AJP is committed to robust enforcement of environmental protections to ensure
industries cannot profit from destroying ecosystems that animals depend on for survival.
While New Zealand has an Environmental Protection Authority (EPA), current enforcement
and penalties are often inadequate, and monitoring resources are limited. This can result in
some companies treating fines as a minor business cost rather than a meaningful deterrent
to harmful behaviour.

Weak enforcement allows ongoing degradation of marine habitats, freshwater ecosystems
and native wildlife populations. Some companies discharge pollutants, destroy sensitive
habitats or operate without full compliance because penalties are too low or violations go
undetected. When penalties represent only a small fraction of profits, destructive practices
become economically rational. The result is systematic environmental degradation that
threatens the survival of native species whilst communities bear the health and economic
costs.

International best practice demonstrates effective enforcement works. Countries with strong
environmental agencies, substantial penalties and comprehensive monitoring achieve
significantly better environmental outcomes. In Germany, the Federal Environment Agency
(UBA) imposes substantial fines and criminal penalties for environmental violations,
reinforced by public reporting and court decisions emphasizing climate and ecosystem
protection.23 In the Netherlands, environmental authorities enforce a “duty of care,” issuing
administrative sanctions and remedial orders to prevent harm, holding both companies and
individuals accountable.24 These approaches show that independent authorities, meaningful
penalties, and executive liability significantly improve environmental outcomes.

The AJP believes that robust environmental enforcement is essential for protecting the
ecosystems that sustain all life in Aotearoa. Strong enforcement will deter environmental
destruction, ensure polluters pay the full costs of their impacts and create market incentives
that reward companies protecting rather than exploiting natural systems.

Key Objectives:

1. Strengthen and expand the powers of the New Zealand EPA, enabling immediate
stop-work orders and higher penalties for serious environmental violations.
2. Implement penalty structures exceeding potential profits from environmental
violations, ensuring harmful activities are never economically rational.
3. Create personal liability provisions making corporate directors and executives
criminally responsible for serious environmental crimes
4. Fund comprehensive environmental monitoring systems, including satellite
technology, remote sensing and community reporting networks.

Economy Within Ecological Limits
The AJP recognises that infinite economic growth on a finite planet is incompatible with
human wellbeing, wildlife protection, ecosystem resilience, and animal welfare. The
economy must operate within ecological limits, prioritising community abundance, meeting
everyone’s basic needs and safeguarding the habitats that sustain nonhuman animals.
Humanity has long exceeded the planet’s safe ecological limits. Scientific evidence shows
that at least six of the nine planetary boundaries (climate change, biodiversity loss,
land-system change, freshwater use, nitrogen and phosphorus cycles, and chemical
pollution) are already beyond safe thresholds. This overshoot drives habitat destruction,
fragments ecosystems and reduces wildlife to vulnerable populations, while intensifying
suffering for farmed animals through industrial, resource-intensive systems.
Transitioning to a post-growth, sufficiency-based economy ensures that resource use stays
within planetary limits, protects ecosystems and prioritises the welfare of all sentient beings
while meeting human needs.

- Integration with schools to provide children with access to diverse learning
opportunities
- Reduced tax rates for worker cooperatives and community-owned enterprises
- Tax advantages for businesses prioritising people, planet, and animals over profit
maximisation
- Simplified regulations for community-owned sharing services and cooperative
ventures
- Public procurement preferences for cooperatively-owned businesses serving
community needs

This approach directly reduces pressure on animals and their habitats. Manufacturing fewer
products means less resource extraction destroying wildlife homes. Shared transport
reduces urban sprawl that fragments habitats. Community food production can focus on
plant-based options, eliminating demand for factory farming while building food security.

When people's essential needs are met through public investment rather than private
accumulation, they're less vulnerable to economic pressures that might force them into
exploitative employment, including jobs that harm animals. Economic security creates space
for making ethical choices about consumption, work, and lifestyle.

The AJP believes that pursuing private sufficiency and public luxury is a transformative
approach that can begin now in pilot communities while building towards broader social
change. It will create better quality of life with dramatically reduced environmental impact,
build the social infrastructure necessary for a cooperative society, and reduce the economic
pressures that perpetuate harmful industries while creating abundance through sharing
rather than individual accumulation.

Key Objectives:

1. Establish demonstration communities showcasing the private sufficiency, public
luxury model with shared facilities and sufficient private space for all residents
2. Invest in world-class public amenities (libraries, transport, workshops, and cultural
facilities) that surpass what individuals could access through private ownership

animaljustice.org.nz | party@animaljusticeparty.org.nz
20

---

3. Create comprehensive community sharing networks for tools, vehicles, and
equipment that reduce manufacturing demand while improving access to high-quality
resources
4. Transform urban planning to prioritise shared spaces over individual storage, freeing
land for wildlife corridors and community gardens
5. Support cooperative ownership models ensuring communities control their shared
resources while building local economies based on cooperation rather than
competition
6. Integrate with housing policy to ensure everyone has secure private space while
building communities around extraordinary shared amenities that foster connection
and reduce environmental impact
7. Establish community land trusts specifically to prevent land speculation that converts
wildlife habitat and small-scale plant-based farming into industrial animal agriculture
operations.

animaljustice.org.nz | party@animaljusticeparty.org.nz
21

---

Circular Economy and Community Resilience
The AJP is committed to fostering sharing economies and circular systems that reduce
waste, strengthen communities, and minimise our environmental footprint. We acknowledge
that current economic models based on individual ownership and constant consumption
drive the resource extraction and habitat destruction that devastate wildlife across Aotearoa
New Zealand.

Moving beyond ownership models towards community-based sharing reduces pressure on
natural systems whilst building stronger neighbourhoods. When communities share tools,
vehicles, and resources, we dramatically reduce the manufacturing demand that destroys
habitats for native species. Car sharing alone can remove up to 15 private vehicles from our
roads, freeing urban space for green corridors that native birds and insects desperately
need.25

Community repair initiatives extend product lifecycles, reducing the 252,000 tonnes of
e-waste New Zealand generates annually—much of which contains toxic materials harmful
to wildlife. Libraries evolved from book repositories to community hubs can become centres
for sharing everything from tools to toys, reducing the material throughput that drives
environmental degradation.

Research from the Ellen MacArthur Foundation shows circular economy approaches can
reduce material extraction by up to 80% while creating more jobs than linear systems.
Worker cooperatives focused on repair and reuse create meaningful employment that builds
community wealth whilst protecting the environment that sustains all life.

The AJP believes that sharing economies represent an immediately implementable
approach to reducing environmental harm whilst strengthening communities. These systems
will reduce habitat destruction, support local employment, and create the social infrastructure
necessary for building a society that values cooperation over competition.

Key Objectives:

1. Expand nationwide networks of community repair cafés and tool libraries to extend
product lifecycles and reduce manufacturing demand
2. Support car-sharing cooperatives to reduce urban vehicle numbers and free land for
native habitat corridors
3. Transform library infrastructure into multi-purpose community hubs that facilitate
resource sharing and reduce individual consumption
4. Fund worker cooperatives specialising in repair, reuse, and sharing services that
create meaningful local employment
5. Create public banking options offering preferential rates for cooperative enterprises
focused on plant-based production, animal sanctuary operations and habitat
restoration projects
6. Support community ownership of renewable energy systems, ensuring profits from
clean energy stay local rather than flowing to extractive corporations that often fund
habitat destruction

## Full text (verbatim)

### Web page text

Practices that harm animals also harm people – from environmental degradation and public health risks to the social costs of ethical desensitisation. The AJP believes that human wellbeing is significantly enhanced when we make compassionate choices. Our policies outline actionable legal and social reforms that safeguard human health, support rural workers, promote social justice, and build a harmonious coexistence with the natural world.

People Category
Policy framework
The AJP seeks to create a society where the welfare, and ability to thrive, of both
humans and other animals is at the forefront, guided by compassion, inclusivity, just
governance, and a commitment to sustainability. As responsible stewards for future
generations we must consider the impact of our actions today on animals, the planet
and by extension ourselves.

We acknowledge the intrinsic connection between humans and other animals,
recognising the welfare of one directly impacts the other. When animals lead better
lives, the result is not only reduced suffering and exploitation, but also an overall
improvement in the health of our ecosystems, contributing to a healthier planet, and
in turn, fostering healthier communities.

Practices such as factory farming and cruel treatment of animals not only raise moral
and ethical questions but can also desensitise and harm individuals, and lead to
environmental degradation creating further harm. We believe the wellbeing of people
can be enhanced through ethical and compassionate choices in how we use, protect
and interact with animals.

Te Tiriti o Waitangi holds profound significance for Aotearoa New Zealand, shaping
the nation's foundation and fostering principles of justice, inclusivity, and cooperation.

The AJP embraces this treaty and acknowledges its importance in guiding a
compassionate, just and equitable relationship with animals. The treaty's
commitment to non-violent conflict resolution aligns with the AJP’s advocacy for
compassionate conservation, emphasising ecological sustainability and social
responsibility.

A just transition to a plant-based Aotearoa New Zealand reflects the essence of Te
Tiriti o Waitangi, promoting harmony and respect for all beings within the nation's
diverse tapestry.

The AJP is committed to improving the well-being of people by creating a better
world for non-human animals.

The current economic system perpetuates harm to non-human animals whilst
contributing to the exploitation and detriment of human well-being within these
industries.

animaljustice.org.nz | party@animaljusticeparty.org.nz 2

---

People employed in exploitative animal industries often endure hazardous working
conditions, low wages and psychological distress due to the inherently violent nature
of the work. Whilst equally people employed in organisations that care for and
protect animals face burnout and compassion fatigue from constantly witnessing and
responding to animal distress. The ongoing detrimental risks for humans include
antibiotic resistance and the spread of zoonotic diseases.

We wish to address these interconnected issues to prioritise the advancement of
both non-human animal wellbeing and human wellbeing.

We also advocate for increased nutritional knowledge and affordable access to a
healthy diet and exercise opportunities for everyone.

We support a compassionate approach to all our interactions with each other, human
or non-human animal.

animaljustice.org.nz | party@animaljusticeparty.org.nz 3

---

People policies summary
The AJP believes that creating a better world for animals begins with building a more
just, compassionate, and democratic society for all people. When humans are free
from economic exploitation, can participate meaningfully in democratic processes,
and are educated to value empathy and ethical decision-making, we create the
conditions necessary for extending that same compassion to all sentient beings.

These policies address the interconnected systems that currently perpetuate harm to
both humans and animals—from economic inequality that traps people in exploitative
industries, to democratic deficits that allow wealthy interests to block necessary
reforms, to educational systems that fail to nurture our natural capacity for
compassion.

Honouring Te Tiriti o Waitangi forms the bedrock of our political platform. Grounded
in kaitiakitanga (guardianship) and genuine partnership, our commitment to Te Tiriti
shapes and informs each of the five core policy areas below.

1. Democratic Reform and Participation

Creating a democracy that truly serves all beings by ensuring every voice can be
heard equally, regardless of wealth or political connections. These reforms will
strengthen democratic processes, improve representation for marginal communities,
and build the participatory systems needed to address complex challenges facing
our society.

2. Worker Rights and Just Transition

Supporting people to transition away from industries that harm both workers and
animals, while recognising the full humanity of all workers through comprehensive
rights and support systems. These policies create pathways to meaningful,
non-violent employment.

3. Economic Justice and Fairness

Building an economy that serves community wellbeing rather than enabling extreme
wealth concentration and corporate manipulation of public opinion. These policies
create ethical and legislative boundaries on wealth accumulation and corporate
influence while supporting the transition to a more compassionate society.

4. Protection and Advocacy Rights

Protecting vulnerable people and animals from harm while safeguarding the
democratic rights of those who speak up for others. These policies ensure that
animaljustice.org.nz | party@animaljusticeparty.org.nz 4

---

exploitation and abuse cannot be hidden behind legal barriers, and that people can
escape dangerous situations without abandoning the nonhuman animals they love.

5. Education and Community Building

Transforming education to nurture empathy, ethical awareness, and respect for all
living beings from early childhood through to tertiary study. This foundation creates
the next generation of citizens equipped with the compassion and critical thinking
skills necessary for building a just society that values all sentient beings.

animaljustice.org.nz | party@animaljusticeparty.org.nz 5

---

Strengthening Partnership with Tangata Whenua
The Animal Justice Party Aotearoa NZ (AJP) recognises that our history is both rich and at
times turbulent. AJP accepts Te Tiriti o Waitangi as the founding document of Aotearoa, and
commits to the principles of non-violent conflict resolution, compassionate conservation for
ecological sustainability, social responsibility towards all of our peoples, and a just transition
to a plant-based Aotearoa.

We believe in compassion, equality and non-violence therefore, we believe Māori and
mātauranga Māori should be respected and embraced. While AJP predominantly focuses on
animal rights and issues, we recognise Māori have an important role as kaitiakitanga
(guardians) of the whenua (land), moana/awa/roto (seas/rivers/lakes) and kararehe
(animals) of Aotearoa. To foster strong and respectful relationships between our party and
the tangata whenua (people of the land) of Aotearoa, we are committed to upholding the
rights of Māori to have a meaningful voice in decisions that directly impact them and their
whenua (land). We recognise the importance of partnership and advocacy in ensuring that
issues affecting Māori are addressed with fairness, inclusivity, and respect.

We acknowledge the role of Māori as tangata whenua (people of the land) and recognise the
importance of kaitiakitanga, manaakitanga, and tino rangatiratanga in shaping a just
transition. We understand that decolonisation is essential for creating the conditions where
both Māori ways of being and environmental restoration can flourish, recognising that
colonial structures have harmed both tangata whenua and the natural world they are
connected to as kaitiaki.

Key Objective:

- Work towards establishing genuine partnerships with tangata whenua to create
robust policies that will heal the environment and restore animal habitats whilst
honouring mātauranga Māori.
- Support the establishment of strong kaitiakitanga frameworks to enable capabilities
for Māori to protect kararehe, whenua, and moana/awa/roto through culturally
appropriate conservation practices.
- Advocate for the protection efforts of tangata whenua in the use and care of natural
resources, ensuring Māori have decision-making authority over ancestral lands and
waters.
- Integrate mātauranga Māori into conservation science and animal welfare practices,
recognising the value of indigenous knowledge systems in creating sustainable
solutions.
- Restore degraded ecosystems through collaborative approaches that honour both
scientific understanding and traditional ecological knowledge.

animaljustice.org.nz | party@animaljusticeparty.org.nz 6

---

Addressing Colonial Impacts on Māori Health and Food
Systems
The AJP recognises that colonisation and the establishment of intensive animal agriculture
have created systemic injustices that continue to impact Māori health, land rights, and food
sovereignty. We are committed to addressing these intersecting challenges through a just
transition that honours Te Tiriti principles and supports Māori-led solutions.

The colonial transformation of Aotearoa into "the dairy farm of the British Empire" displaced
traditional Māori food systems and imposed Western dietary patterns high in animal
products, contributing to disproportionate health inequities that persist today. 123Animal
farming continues to degrade waterways4 and ecosystems that are fundamental to Māori
identity and wellbeing, with many Māori communities bearing the brunt of environmental
pollution and land-use pressures.

We recognise that for many New Zealanders, including both Māori and Pākehā, there are
strong cultural and historical ties to animal farming. For Māori, these ties are often rooted in
whakapapa and a deep ancestral relationship with the land, while for Pākehā, the connection
has developed more recently through settler-colonial history. Understanding these different
histories is essential as we navigate a just transition away from animal-based systems.

AJP recognises that colonial systems have created structures of domination and exploitation
that affect multiple communities and beings. We will support systemic changes that address
these root causes whilst respecting the distinct nature of different liberation movements.

Key Objective:

- Ensure that Māori landholders are not disproportionately impacted by the transition
away from animal agriculture and are supported in exercising kaitiakitanga, whilst
prioritising Māori leadership in land-use decision-making to redress colonial injustices
and support tino rangatiratanga.(Transition to a Plant Based Economy policy
objectives)
- Support Māori food sovereignty through funding māra kai (community gardens),
traditional food systems, and indigenous plant-based industries such as kūmara and
native crops, recognising practices such as maramataka (Māori lunar planting cycles)
as integral to sustainable food production. (Transition to a Plant Based Economy
policy objectives)

1. Democratic Reform and Participation
Getting Money Out of Politics - Restoring Democratic
Equality
The AJP is committed to creating a democracy where all voices are heard equally,
regardless of wealth or corporate connections. We acknowledge that money
currently dominates our political system, giving wealthy industries—particularly those
that exploit animals—vastly superior access to decision-makers compared to
ordinary citizens and community advocates. We propose comprehensive reforms to
eliminate financial advantages in politics, ensuring democratic participation is based
on ideas and community support rather than economic power.

Unregulated lobbying creates a two-tier democracy where wealthy interests
dominate decision-making while ordinary citizens and advocacy groups are shut out.
The revelations in August 2025 about the then Fisheries Minister Shane Jones
receiving over $100,000 from fishing industry donors while rolling back
environmental protections illustrate this problem perfectly.5 Companies like Talley's
Group strategically split donations to avoid disclosure thresholds, while fishing baron
Craig Boote admitted to spending $30,000 across parties before securing exclusive
access to ministers.6 This isn't democracy - it's a system where money buys policy
outcomes.

Although Federated Farmers does not make direct political donations,7 influence
can flow through other channels. Andrew Hoggard’s career path illustrates the
concern: after nearly a decade in Federated Farmers leadership roles, including
serving as president until May 2023, he joined ACT New Zealand the very next day.8
Following the 2023 election, he was appointed Minister for Biosecurity and Food
Safety, and Associate Minister of Agriculture (Animal Welfare, Skills)9 and for the
Environment, portfolios directly affecting farming and animal welfare. This revolving
door between industry leadership and political office underlines the urgent need for
reform: mandatory lobbying registers, cooling-off periods, and stronger transparency
rules to ensure that public decision-making serves the wider public interest.

The connection to animal welfare is direct and profound. Industries that exploit
animals (factory farming, commercial fishing, entertainment using animals) rely
heavily on political influence to maintain harmful practices. By eliminating their

financial advantages, we create space for evidence-based policy that considers
animal welfare alongside human and environmental concerns.

When wealth can't buy political influence, policy debates focus on ideas, evidence,
and community values rather than corporate interests. This creates conditions where
animal welfare advocates can participate on equal terms with industry
representatives, leading to policies that reflect genuine public concern for animals
rather than industry profit margins.

The AJP believes that getting money out of politics is a fundamental step that can be
taken now to restore democratic equality and ensure all voices are heard. It will
create policy-making processes that serve community wellbeing rather than
corporate profits, reduce the political power of industries that exploit animals, and
establish the democratic foundations necessary for building a compassionate society
where the interests of all beings are properly considered.

Key Objectives:

Transparency & Electoral Finance

1. Limit total donations and loans from any single individual to a maximum of
$30,000 per electoral cycle (or $10,000 per year) to curb excessive influence.
2. Reduce the threshold for publicly disclosing a donor's identity from $5,000 to
$1,500 per year, preventing the "splitting" of donations.
3. Permit only New Zealand citizens or permanent residents registered to vote to
make political donations, removing corporate/industry "entity" donations.
4. Remove the mechanism that allows large donations to be funneled
anonymously through the Electoral Commission.

Lobbying & Institutional Integrity

5. Implement comprehensive lobbying transparency with real-time public
disclosure of all meetings and communications between industry
representatives and government officials
6. Create meaningful cooling-off periods preventing the revolving door between
industry leadership and political positions
7. Establish independent oversight with strong enforcement powers to
investigate breaches and maintain democratic integrity
8. Protect public interest advocacy organisations from government retaliation
while ensuring equal access to democratic processes

Democratic Participation & Campaign Equality

9. Establish maximum membership fee caps for all political parties with
low-income options, preventing wealthy parties from creating financial barriers
while ensuring participation is based on community support rather than wealth
10. Level broadcasting allocation between parties, distributing funding more
evenly rather than concentrating it among established parties, and expand

Democratic Representation for All Voices
The AJP is committed to reducing the MMP party vote threshold from 5% to 3.5% to
ensure that diverse voices, including those advocating for animals, environment, and
social justice, can meaningfully participate in parliamentary democracy.10 We
acknowledge that the current 5% threshold excludes significant portions of the
population from representation, particularly those supporting smaller parties focused
on ethical issues that major parties often ignore or compromise on.

An independent review of New Zealand's electoral system has concluded a major
shake-up of MMP is needed to ensure a fairer and more accessible democracy. The
current threshold means that parties receiving up to 4.9% of the vote—potentially
representing over 120,000 voters—receive no parliamentary representation
whatsoever. This creates a democratic deficit where substantial communities
advocating for animal protection, environmental justice, and other ethical concerns
are systematically excluded from decision-making processes.

International comparisons reveal New Zealand's threshold is unnecessarily high. In
Bolivia the threshold is 3%, in Germany 5% for federal parliament, while some
European nations operate effectively with thresholds as low as 2%. The Electoral
Commission recommended lowering the 5 percent party vote threshold to 3.5
percent as part of comprehensive electoral reforms designed to enhance democratic
participation.11

Reducing the threshold would enable parties focused on animal welfare,
environmental protection, and social justice to gain parliamentary representation with
community support levels that already demonstrate significant public backing. This
change would force major parties to engage seriously with ethical issues they
currently marginalise, knowing that specialist parties could hold balance-of-power
positions.

The AJP believes that lowering the party vote threshold is a fundamental democratic
reform that will amplify voices advocating for those without political power—including
animals. This change will ensure that ethical concerns receive proper parliamentary
consideration, create more responsive governance, and build the inclusive
democracy necessary for addressing complex challenges facing all beings in our
society.

Key Objectives:

2. Campaign for broader electoral reforms that enhance democratic participation

Participatory Democracy for Complex Societal Issues
The AJP is committed to creating a democracy that truly serves all beings by
ensuring citizens can meaningfully participate in complex decision-making
processes. We acknowledge that current democratic systems often fail to address
challenging issues due to polarisation, partisan politics, and the dominance of vested
interests over genuine public deliberation. We propose strengthening participatory
democracy to build the foundations of a more thoughtful, inclusive, and
compassionate society.

Participatory democracy goes beyond traditional voting by involving citizens directly
in decision-making on complex issues. It includes methods like citizens' assemblies,
where randomly selected groups of people learn about an issue, hear from experts,
and deliberate together to make recommendations.

Ireland's Citizens' Assembly on abortion provides a powerful example.12 In 2016, 99
randomly selected citizens spent five months examining this issue, hearing from
medical experts, legal scholars and people with lived experiences. Their thoughtful
recommendations led to a referendum that legalised abortion - a result many thought
impossible through traditional politics alone.

Research shows deliberative democracy works. An OECD study of citizens'
assemblies found that over half of the recommendations were implemented by public
authorities in 76% of cases reviewed, and all recommendations implemented in 36%
of cases.13 In Aotearoa New Zealand, we already have 15+ examples of successful
deliberative democracy at local level, proving our communities are ready for this
approach.14

The AJP believes that empowering citizens to engage deeply with complex ethical
questions is an effective step that can be taken now to build a more compassionate
democracy. It will lead to better policy outcomes that consider the interests of all
affected beings, break through political polarisation and create the democratic
culture necessary for addressing the greatest challenges facing our society and
planet.

Comprehensive Wellbeing Data Framework
The AJP is committed to creating evidence-based governance that measures what
truly matters for thriving communities. We acknowledge that current data systems
focus primarily on economic indicators while ignoring social, environmental and
ethical dimensions of wellbeing, making it impossible to track whether our policies
actually improve lives for all beings. We propose establishing comprehensive
wellbeing data systems that capture the full spectrum of what makes communities
healthy and compassionate.

You can't improve what you don't measure. While New Zealand still has wellbeing
tools like the Living Standards Framework (including the LSF Dashboard)15 and the
He Ara Waiora framework,16 recent changes, such as removal of certain wellbeing
requirements in the Public Finance Act and the discontinuation of the branded
Wellbeing Budget1718 have weakened mandatory reporting and accountability. This
leaves gaps in our ability to track whether policies are improving people’s lives or to
identify where interventions could have the greatest impact.

A proposal for a comprehensive wellbeing data system is not without precedent. The
Kingdom of Bhutan, for instance, pioneered the concept of Gross National
Happiness (GNH), which deliberately elevated the wellbeing of its citizens above
Gross Domestic Product (GDP) as its central development philosophy. The resulting
GNH Index is a robust, multidimensional measurement tool that guides policymaking
across nine domains, including ecological resilience, cultural vitality and time use.19
This international example of embedding social, environmental and ethical
dimensions into a mandated policy-screening framework demonstrates a successful
model for the “compassionate governance” and full-spectrum measurement we are
committed to achieving in New Zealand.

The AJP believes that implementing comprehensive wellbeing data is an effective
step that can be taken now to build accountability for compassionate governance. It
will lead to better policy decisions that consider the interconnectedness of human,
animal, and environmental health, provide clear evidence of what interventions work
best and create the foundation for a society that values the wellbeing of all beings.

Key Objectives:

1. Review existing wellbeing indicators from other jurisdictions and national
datasets to identify best practice methodologies

2. Worker Rights and Just Transition
Mental Health Support and Just Transition for Workers
in Violent / Exploitative Industries
The AJP is committed to creating a society where no person is forced into work that

many industries founded on systematic harm, including, but not limited to, animal

Making Work Fair for All
The AJP is committed to rebuilding worker rights in Aotearoa New Zealand,
recognising that exploitative employment conditions not only harm workers but
create the economic desperation that drives animal exploitation industries. Decades
of neoliberal policies have systematically weakened collective bargaining,
suppressed wages and created precarious employment conditions that trap workers
in harmful industries while undermining their capacity to make ethical choices. We
acknowledge that strong worker rights are fundamental to a just society for all
beings, enabling fair distribution of economic gains while ensuring workers have
genuine voice in transitioning away from industries that exploit animals. We propose
comprehensive labour law reform that puts workers' collective power at the centre of
employment relations and supports the transition to a compassionate economy.

Worker empowerment through collective organisation is essential for creating an
economy that serves all beings rather than concentrating wealth among employers
and shareholders who profit from animal exploitation. Strong unions and worker
rights provide the foundation for reducing inequality, improving workplace safety, and
enabling workers to transition away from industries that harm animals without facing
economic destitution. When workers have economic security and collective power,
they are better positioned to resist participating in animal exploitation and to
advocate for ethical alternatives. Improving work-life balance while maintaining
productivity and enabling workers to participate more fully in community life enables
ethical consumption choices and the reduction in animal exploitation.

Many of the most harmful animal exploitation industries - from factory farming to
animal testing - rely on precarious employment conditions that trap workers in jobs
they may find morally troubling. Economic desperation forces workers to participate
in systems of animal cruelty, while weak labour protections prevent them from
speaking out about animal welfare violations they witness. The AJP will establish just
transition support for workers moving from animal exploitation industries to
compassionate alternatives, including retraining programmes, income support during
transition periods, and priority hiring in emerging plant-based and cruelty-free
industries.

The AJP believes that restoring worker rights through comprehensive employment
law reform is essential for creating a society where workers can choose
compassionate careers without sacrificing their economic security. This approach will
reduce inequality, strengthen democracy in workplaces, and create the economic
foundations for a society that values the wellbeing of all beings over profit
maximisation from animal exploitation.

Ethical Advertising Standards - Protecting

The AJP is committed to creating advertising standards that serve community
wellbeing, rather than corporate profits, recognising that current marketing practices
actively undermine efforts to build a compassionate society. We acknowledge that
advertising for harmful products, particularly animal products, fossil fuels, and
excessive consumption, manipulates people into choices that damage their health,
exploit animals, and destroy our environment. We propose phased restrictions on
harmful advertising, starting with the most damaging sectors and moving towards an
advertising landscape that informs rather than exploits.

Modern advertising is fundamentally about manufacturing desires for things we don't
need, often at tremendous cost to animals, people, and planet. The industry spends
billions convincing people that happiness comes from consuming animal products,
burning fossil fuels, and buying endless goods, directly contradicting the urgent need
to reduce harm and consumption for a sustainable future.

Children are particularly vulnerable, with food marketing creating lifelong preferences
for processed animal products while normalising cruelty as entertainment. By the
time a child reaches school age, they've been exposed to thousands of
advertisements promoting consumption patterns that cause immense animal
suffering and environmental destruction.

France has led globally by banning fossil fuel advertising since 2022,41 while
Amsterdam became the first city to ban meat and dairy advertising on public
transport in 2024.42 These pioneering approaches demonstrate that restricting
harmful advertising is both achievable and effective in shifting social norms towards
sustainability and compassion.

The connection to animal welfare is direct and profound. Animal product advertising
deliberately obscures the reality of factory farming, presenting false images of happy
animals while promoting products that cause immense suffering. By restricting this
misleading marketing, we create space for honest conversations about our food
choices and their impact on sentient beings.

Background
Aotearoa New Zealand has the second largest proportion of homes with companion
animals47. It is clear that companion animals are a huge part of our society and as
such we have a responsibility to ensure they are adequately cared for. This includes
ensuring private rental homes and social housing for those with companion animals
are readily available. Companion animals are more often than not considered an
integral part of the family unit, with research demonstrating numerous benefits of
companion animal guardianship.48 At the same time, they rely on us to meet their
needs.

In Aotearoa New Zealand, the high cost of purchasing housing has led to an
increasing number of people turning to the private rental market for their
accommodation needs. The median house price in Aotearoa has risen significantly
over the past decade49, making homeownership increasingly unattainable for many.
This, coupled with factors such as student loan debt, changing job markets, lifestyle
preferences, climate crisis impacts and immigration50, has contributed to a growing
renter population. According to recent statistics, approximately one-third of Aotearoa
households are living in rental accommodation.51 This translates to over 600,000
households, representing a significant portion of the population who are directly
affected by rental policies and regulations.

landscape, highlighting the importance of creating fair and inclusive policies that
consider the needs of both tenants and landlords. The right to live with companion

Universal Veterinary Care - Ensuring Wellbeing for All
Animals
The AJP is committed to establishing veterinary care as a fundamental right for all
animals, recognising that access to medical treatment should never depend on their
guardian's wealth or their status as companion, free-living, or wildlife. We
acknowledge that the current system fails countless animals who suffer needlessly
due to financial barriers, geographic inequities, and a veterinary workforce pushed to
breaking point by commercial pressures and inadequate support. We propose
comprehensive reforms to create a universal veterinary care system that prioritises
animal wellbeing over profit, ensuring no animal is denied treatment because of
economic circumstances.

The veterinary care crisis in Aotearoa reflects broader societal failures to value
animal lives equally. Countless companion animals live in households struggling with
the cost of living, where a sudden illness or injury forces impossible choices between
veterinary bills and basic necessities. Meanwhile, injured wildlife, including our
precious native species, suffer without treatment, and free-living cats and dogs
continue breeding due to lack of accessible desexing services, perpetuating cycles
of suffering that overwhelm rescue organisations and community groups.

This crisis is not inevitable, it is a direct consequence of treating veterinary medicine
as a luxury commodity rather than essential care. The current system concentrates
services in wealthy urban areas while rural and regional communities face severe
shortages, leaving both animals and their human carers without local access to
critical treatment. Veterinarians themselves suffer under this model, with crushing
student debt, unsustainable workloads, and moral injury from having to deny care
based on payment capacity driving concerning rates of burnout and mental health
struggles within the profession.

The economic barriers are deliberately constructed. GST on veterinary services
treats animal healthcare as discretionary spending, while limited university places
and high fees create artificial scarcity that drives up costs and restricts workforce
growth. Emergency procedures can cost thousands of dollars, forcing people to
choose between insurmountable debt or euthanasia, while preventative care like

communities already facing economic hardship.

suffers without veterinary intervention because there's no guaranteed funding for
wildlife care reveals the hollowness of our claimed concern for biodiversity and our
taonga species. Every free-living cat or dog who continues breeding because

native wildlife.

This policy also addresses the exploitation of veterinary professionals themselves.
The current system transforms dedicated animal carers into gatekeepers of
treatment based on payment, creating profound moral distress that drives people
from the profession. By removing financial barriers and adequately resourcing
veterinary services, we create conditions where practitioners can focus on healing
rather than billing, reducing the psychological harm that comes from denying
necessary care to animals in their most vulnerable moments.

Beyond individual animals, lack of accessible veterinary care undermines community
resilience and ecological health. Undesexed companion animal populations strain
rescue networks, SPCA resources, and council pounds. Untreated injuries in
free-living animals can lead to infection and disease spread that affects both
domestic and native species. The absence of preventative care creates more
expensive emergency interventions that people still cannot afford, perpetuating
cycles of suffering, guilt, and animal abandonment.

The current model also perpetuates inequality between communities. Whānau in

determines whether they receive treatment, fundamentally contradicting any
meaningful commitment to animal welfare.

The AJP believes that establishing universal veterinary care is an essential

preventable suffering, support carers in providing responsible care regardless of
income or location, and create a veterinary profession where practitioners can fulfil

is recognition that animals' right to medical care should not depend on economic

4. Protection and Advocacy Rights
Comprehensive Whistleblower Protection and Peaceful
Protest Rights
The AJP is committed to protecting the fundamental democratic rights of
transparency, accountability, and peaceful protest that are essential for exposing and
addressing animal cruelty. We acknowledge that industries profiting from animal
exploitation are increasingly using legal strategies, such as ag-gag laws, to silence
critics, hide their practices from public scrutiny, and criminalise those who seek to
document or protest against animal abuse. We propose comprehensive protections
for whistleblowers and peaceful protesters to ensure that the voices of animals and
their advocates cannot be silenced.

Ag-gag laws are anti-whistleblower laws that forbid undercover filming or
photography of activity on farms without consent, specifically targeting
whistleblowers of suspected animal rights abuses. These dangerous bills, pushed by
the animal agriculture industry, are designed to silence whistleblowers revealing
animal abuses on industrial farms.

Since 2011, twenty-five US states have introduced ag-gag laws, with six passing
legislation that falls into three categories: agricultural interference laws (prohibiting
recording without consent), agricultural fraud laws (prohibiting obtaining access
under false pretences), and agricultural terrorism laws.67

The threat extends beyond the US. In Australia, ag-gag laws seek to hinder animal
advocates by preventing them from recording operations of commercial agricultural
facilities. Meanwhile, both NSW and Queensland governments, as well as the
Australian federal government, are ramping up laws against animal activists who
trespass on farming properties.68

The assault on democratic rights extends to peaceful protest. Five Australian states
(NSW, Queensland, South Australia, Tasmania and Victoria) have introduced
anti-protest regulations, with South Australia's new laws increasing maximum fines
from $750 to $50,000 along with potential jail time. 69 The former Australian

- Training for teachers in using advanced, animal-free educational technologies
- Development of New Zealand-specific resources featuring native wildlife and
ecosystems

Tertiary Education Transformation:

Animal Science Programme Reform:

- Mandatory courses on animal sentience, cognition, and welfare science for all
animal science students
- Ethics components examining the moral implications of different animal use
practices
- Emphasis on animal-free research, teaching and testing methods and
plant-based alternatives to animal agriculture
- Career pathway support for students interested in companion animal care,
wildlife rehabilitation, and plant-based food systems

Professional Development Requirements:

- Continuing education requirements for teachers on compassionate education
methods
- Training programmes for educators on recognising and addressing
speciesism in curricula
- Support for teachers to develop animal-friendly lesson plans that avoid
treating animals as disposable commodities. Eg. https://www.faunedge.com/

Research and Graduate Studies:

- Funding prioritisation for research into animal-free education methods
- Graduate programmes focusing on animal welfare, conservation biology, and
sustainable food systems
- Legislated ethical review requirements for any research involving animals,
with animal testing only to be used as a last resort where non-animal methods
are not available

Specialised Education Centres:

Animal Welfare Education Hubs:

- Establishment of dedicated centres teaching about animal behaviour,
cognition, and welfare without using live animals
- Interactive exhibits using technology, models, and observation of animals in
natural settings
- Programmes for school groups, families, and community organizations
- Training facilities for educators in compassionate teaching methods

Wildlife Education Sanctuaries:

- Observation-based learning about native species behaviour and conservation
- Teaching about ecosystem relationships and the impacts of human activities
on wildlife
- Programmes specifically addressing compassionate approaches to introduced

Public Awareness Campaigns:

- Community programmes teaching responsible companion animal
guardianship
- Public education about the welfare needs of farmed animals and plant-based
alternatives to animal agriculture
- Workshops on compassionate approaches to wildlife conflicts
- Integration of animal welfare education into adult education and community
college programmes

Professional Training:

- Continuing education requirements for veterinarians, farmers, and animal care
workers
- Public education campaigns about career opportunities in plant-based food
production and animal welfare

Teacher Support and Resources:

- Development of comprehensive, age-appropriate compassionate education

Professional Support:
