The AJP believes that implementing compassionate education is a transformative
step that can be taken now to build a generation of citizens who value and respect all
living beings. It will create students equipped with the empathy and critical thinking
skills necessary for addressing complex ethical challenges, reduce unnecessary
animal suffering in educational settings, and establish the foundation for a society
that extends compassion to all sentient beings while preparing young people for
careers in a plant-based economy.

Key Objectives:

1. Implement mandatory compassionate education curricula across all
educational levels that teach respect for animals, environmental stewardship,
and ethical decision-making
2. Eliminate harmful animal use in educational settings by replacing dissection

# AJP Transition to a Plant-Based Economy Policies Overview

> Archive note: Web text is the policy post body from animaljustice.org.nz/wp-json/wp/v2/policies; the PDF version linked from the page (if any) follows, extracted with pdftotext -layout.

## Full text (verbatim)

### Web page text

True climate action requires transforming our agricultural system. The AJP’s vision for a plant-based economy provides a clear roadmap to move away from animal exploitation while ensuring a supportive, financially secure transition for farmers, workers, and rural communities. By incentivising crop farming, food-tech innovation, and ecological restoration, we can build an economy that respects sentient life and honors our guardianship/kaitiakitanga of the land.

Download the AJP Transition to a plant-based economy policies pack PDF below

### PDF version: https://animaljustice.org.nz/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/AJP-Transition-to-Plant-based-economy-policies.pdf

animaljustice.org.nz | party@animaljusticeparty.org.nz 1

---

Just transition to a plant-based economy
The AJP is committed to transitioning Aotearoa New Zealand to a wholly plant-based
economy, where animal farming has been eliminated and no animals are used for
economic gain. We acknowledge the role of Māori as tangata whenua (people of the
land) and recognise the importance of kaitiakitanga, manaakitanga, and tino
rangatiratanga in shaping a just transition. This transformation must be guided by
partnership with iwi and hapū, respecting mātauranga Māori and supporting Māori
economic aspirations through sustainable land-use practices. We want to create a more
prosperous, sustainable and secure economy that is underpinned by compassion for all.

A transformation approach is required. We recognise that our current economic model
is deeply reliant on the exploitation of animals for food, other products and exports. And
that for many New Zealanders, including both Māori and Pākehā, have strong cultural
and historical ties to animal farming. For Māori, these ties are often rooted in
whakapapa and a deep ancestral relationship with the land, while for Pākehā, the
connection has developed more recently through settler-colonial history and
generations of farming. Understanding these different histories is essential as we
navigate a just transition away from animal-based systems.

However, our current agricultural model has significant environmental impacts, including
biodiversity loss, freshwater degradation and greenhouse gas emissions, while also
inflicting unnecessary suffering on millions of sentient beings. It is also inherently risky
as an on-going economic strategy, as environmental tipping points, new technologies,
consumer preferences, societal concerns and changes in global trade threaten to
reduce long term demand for animal products alongside increasing regulatory burdens.
New Zealand is currently in a ‘chaos and emergence’ phase where existing systems are
being questioned and new alternatives are emerging.1

We appreciate transitioning to a plant-based economy will take time, and that to be
sustainable it must happen alongside support for farmers and the development of
attractive and affordable alternatives for both farmers and consumers alike. There are,
however, steps we can take now that will make a huge positive impact. These include
banning factory farming, tougher laws, regulations and enforcement mechanisms,
supporting farm livelihood transitions, engaging with Māori leadership, supporting
innovation in food tech, and promoting and incentivising more compassionate and

1
Klerkx, L., Turner, J., & Percy, H. (2023) Navigating the rapids of agrifood systems transformation:
reflections on Aotearoa New Zealand’s emerging mission oriented agrifood innovation system

animaljustice.org.nz | party@animaljusticeparty.org.nz 1

---

healthy dietary choices. He ara kai pai ake mō te tinana, te wairua me te taiao (healthier
and more sustainable food pathways for the body, spirit, and environment).

Shifting to a plant-based economy is the single most impactful change we can make to
reduce animal suffering whilst also addressing many of our most urgent economic,
social and environmental challenges. Our vision is for a radically different economy. Our
policy focuses on practical steps that can be implemented now to make this future
possible.

Four overarching objectives
Our policy for transitioning to a plant-based economy is focussed on shifting away from
animal agriculture and animal-based foods, and replacing these with sustainable and
compassionate alternatives. It is centered around four objectives, each supported by
specific proposals:

1. Increase consumption of plant-based foods. Use a variety of policy levers to
increase consumption and market demand for healthier, kinder, more sustainable
food options that align with kai ora (healthy food) principles

2. Use land and water sustainably and compassionately. Use regulation and
incentives to shift from animal to plant-based farming and other sustainable land
and water uses.

3. Support farmers, workers and communities to transition. Engage and
collaborate to support a fair and inclusive transition with economic opportunities
for all.

4. Develop long-term economic alternatives. Invest in new technologies,
products and markets - to replace animal farming and provide prosperity and
jobs.

To achieve these objectives, the Government should urgently develop a National Action
Plan to implement the proposals set out in this document. While animal agriculture
currently remains economically significant, there are both environmental and market
pressures that suggest the potential for transition. Given this context, transitioning to a
plant-based economy should be a national priority and the Government must play a
critical role in making this happen.

The ‘value’ of animal exploitation to New Zealand’s economy
Despite its well documented negative impacts, animal agriculture occupies a prominent
position in New Zealand's economy and national identity. While agriculture is often
described as the foundation of New Zealand's economic prosperity, contributing to GDP,

animaljustice.org.nz | party@animaljusticeparty.org.nz 2

---

exports and employment, the combined agricultural and fishing sectors represent
approximately just 5% of GDP.
The dairy sector accounts for 3% of this (>$11BN) and provides an estimated 55,000
jobs. Dried milk powder is one of our most significant export commodities, with the
dairy export trade earning around $1 in every $4 of New Zealand’s foreign exchange
income.2 However, the expansion of dairy farming has led to economic vulnerabilities,
including significant trade imbalances and a high reliance on imports. It has also
resulted in environmental challenges, particularly regarding water quality.
Shifting away from these industries will be a significant challenge. New Zealand's
agricultural identity, established during colonisation as the dairy farm of the British
Empire, continues to shape its global economic position and national politics. A just
transition requires redressing these injustices by prioritising Māori leadership in
land-use decision-making, ensuring economic benefits are equitably distributed, and
honoring Māori aspirations for self-determined food and land systems. The close
alignment between agricultural and state interests has historically been reflected in
strong rural sector representation in Parliament.3 This deep institutional and political
entrenchment, combined with significant industry influence over policy making, means
that developing viable economic alternatives will require substantial time, innovation and
investment.
It is imperative that we begin the transition to a plant-based economy with urgency. This
is critical not only to protect the environment, our health, and millions of sentient beings,
but also for our long-term economic prosperity. As consumers change dietary habits; as
countries such as China prioritise food independence; and as innovation in food
technology increasingly provides cruelty-free alternatives, there is a very real possibility
that future market demand for New Zealand’s animal products will decline. Shifting
away from animal agriculture offers opportunities to diversify, build resilience, food
security, and secure long-term economic prosperity.

Impacts on animals
Millions of farmed animals are slaughtered in New Zealand every year. Data from
StatsNZ reveals that around 27 million ‘livestock’ were killed in 2023, including 21
million lambs and sheep, 4.6 million cows and 600,000 pigs, heifers, bulls, steers and
calves. In addition, it is estimated that 120 million chickens are slaughtered annually.4
Between 953 million to 5.94 billion wild-fish were killed for food (2016, Our World in
Data), this estimate does not include unrecorded fish capture, such as bycatch and

2
For an industry perspective see: Sense Partners. (2023). Dairy’s economic contribution to New
Zealand. https://www.dairynz.co.nz/media/0oibxesz/solid-foundations-4-september-2023.pdf
3
Federated Farmers. (2023). From the back paddock to the Beehive. Farmers Weekly.
https://www.farmersweekly.co.nz/politics/from-the-back-paddock-to-the-beehive/
4
See: https://figure.nz/chart/3MTXwpL6IC7HriMp (sheep), https://figure.nz/chart/sTN0HlwsCBAbVCFz
(livestock), https://figure.nz/chart/MvEo5sIoSRn18Ofd (cattle), https://figure.nz/chart/tkWQS2fpbiLVpF7N
(pigs) and https://animalsaotearoa.org/learn/how-chickens-suffer-at-slaughter/ (chickens).

animaljustice.org.nz | party@animaljusticeparty.org.nz 3

---

discards. Farmed fish, including salmon, mussels and oysters are killed in their
hundreds of millions annually.
However, the impact on farmed animals cannot be captured by numbers alone. Poor
conditions and cruel practices are widespread. New Zealand’s animal welfare laws are
inadequate even when they are adhered to, but in practice we know that legal minimum
standards are often not met - with negative consequences for the sentient beings that
are powerless to resist. Whilst high welfare standards are better than low / no
standards, ultimately the only ethically justifiable course of action is to phase out animal
farming altogether.

Impacts on the environment
Animal farming is a major driver of climate change. Globally it is responsible for
between 10% and 20% of global GHG emissions, and it is one of the leading causes of
deforestation.5 48.6% of New Zealand’s total emissions in 2022 came from sheep and
cattle, of which 25.7% was from dairy cattle, 12.4% from sheep and 10.5% from beef
cattle.6 The inefficiency of producing food through animals also means that shifting to
plant-based foods has the potential to release large tracts of land for ecosystem
restoration and reforestation - critical parts of the solution to climate change.7 In New
Zealand around half of all land is used for agriculture, the vast majority of which is for
grazing.8
Animal farming also has severe effects on rivers and waterways - degrading
ecosystems, killing animals and reducing water quality. Many Māori communities bear
the brunt of these effects, with degraded rivers, pollution, and land-use pressures
disproportionately affecting Māori land and resources. In New Zealand the Ministry for
the Environment has estimated that 95% of waterways whose catchments included
areas of farmland exceed guideline values for water turbidity or dissolved nutrients; and
that 24% of total river length in those catchments had E. coli levels that were greater
than would be expected under natural conditions.9 Algal growth in streams and rivers -
caused by fertiliser runoff - is widespread, leading to impairment of water for swimming,
drinking and fish and other wildlife.

Impacts on human health

The rise in consumption of animal products over the past decades correlates with
increasing rates of chronic disease in New Zealand and globally. Research
demonstrates clear associations between high consumption of animal products and
5
Estimates vary depending on a variety of assumptions and methodological approaches. For a recent
summary see this article by The Breakthrough Institute (2023).
6
https://www.nzagrc.org.nz/news-and-events/race-on-to-reduce-emissions-from-new-zealand-livestock/
7
For a summary of animal agriculture and global land use see:Poore & Nemeck (2018) Reducing food’s
environmental impacts and https://ourworldindata.org/global-land-for-agriculture.
8
See: https://www.ehinz.ac.nz/assets/Factsheets/Released_2021/Agricultural-Land-Use_FA.pdf
9

animaljustice.org.nz | party@animaljusticeparty.org.nz 4

---

adverse health outcomes. Specifically, red and processed meat consumption is linked to
increased risk of colorectal cancer, with the World Health Organisation classifying
processed meat as a Group 1 carcinogen, alongside alcohol and tobacco.10 High
consumption of animal products is associated with increased risk of cardiometabolic
diseases, certain cancers, and all-cause mortality.11
Conversely, scientific evidence consistently shows that plant-based diets play both
preventative and therapeutic roles in managing major chronic conditions including
cardiovascular disease, type 2 diabetes, obesity, and certain cancers. Studies indicate
that replacing animal-based foods (such as red meat, processed meat, eggs, and dairy)
with plant-based alternatives (including legumes, nuts, whole grains, and olive oil)
improves cardiometabolic health outcomes.12
Plant-based diets are demonstrated to be safe and nutritionally adequate across all life
stages, from pregnancy and lactation through to elderly care, when appropriately
planned.. Beyond individual health benefits, transitioning toward plant-based agriculture
could significantly reduce the growing burden on our healthcare system. Shifting toward
predominantly plant-based diets is not only feasible but could substantially improve
public health outcomes, reduce healthcare costs by $11 to 22 billion,13 and help address
ethnic health inequities,14 as Māori and Pacific communities bear a disproportionate
burden of diet-related diseases. This transition presents an opportunity to move from a
healthcare system focused on treating chronic diseases to one centered on prevention
through dietary change.
In a plant-based economy, the risk of food-borne illnesses, pandemics and antibiotic
resistance would be significantly reduced, creating a safer and more resilient food
system. Industrial animal agriculture is a breeding ground for dangerous pathogens,
with cramped, unsanitary conditions allowing bacteria and viruses—such as Salmonella,
E. coli, and even pandemic-causing influenza strains15—to spread rapidly. Additionally,
the heavy use of antibiotics in livestock farming fuels the rise of antibiotic-resistant

animaljustice.org.nz | party@animaljusticeparty.org.nz 5

---

superbugs, threatening human medicine.16 By shifting to a plant-based food system, we
remove these high-risk environments, reducing the likelihood of zoonotic disease
outbreaks and preserving the effectiveness of life-saving antibiotics. A future built on
plant-based foods is not only kinder to animals and the planet but also crucial for global
public health.

Other voices for change

The AJP is not alone in advocating for a transition to a plant-based economy.
The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change has said that shifting to more
sustainable diets is a major opportunity to reduce global GHG emissions, with a
theoretical global shift to wholly plant-based diets saving up to 8Gt CO2e p/a (~13% of
total current global emissions).17
At the national level some countries are now implementing measures to support a
reduction in animal based foods. For example the Netherlands has a goal to reduce
meat consumption by 50% by 2030,18 in October 2023 the Danish government
published a national plant-based action plan with its strategy to transition Denmark
towards a richer plant-based diet and boost plant-protein production 1920 and France’s
Climate and Resilience law (2021) encourages school canteens to serve more
vegetarian meals.21
At a regional level, California's Plant-Based School Lunch Act (2022) provides additional
reimbursements to schools serving plant-based meals, incentivising more plant-based
options in school cafeterias22 and New York City hospitals offer plant-based dishes as
the default option since 2022. 23 Most large schools and universities in the U.S., France
and Germany offer regular meatless meal options.24

as-primary-dinner-option-for-inpatients-at-all-of-its-11-public-hospitals/

animaljustice.org.nz | party@animaljusticeparty.org.nz 6

---

Civil society initiatives, such as the Plant Based Treaty,25 provide ways for individuals,
organisations and communities to shift towards plant-based diets. The AJP supports the
Plant Based Treaty, and become a signatory in 2024.

A Treaty-Based Approach to Economic Transition
The AJP recognises that the transition to a plant-based economy must be grounded in
Te Tiriti o Waitangi me ngā mātāpono o te ao Māori (the Treaty of Waitangi and Māori
worldviews), ensuring that Māori are central partners in shaping Aotearoa’s future. By
integrating mātauranga Māori, supporting indigenous food sovereignty, and investing in
Māori-led agricultural transformation, we can create a truly sustainable, compassionate
and equitable economy for all. This includes recognising practices such as maramataka
(Māori lunar planting cycles) and māra kai (community food gardens) as part of broader
environmental restoration and food sovereignty initiatives.
The Government has a critical role in ensuring this transition is just, inclusive, and
reflective of Aotearoa’s unique bicultural identity. By working in genuine partnership with
Māori, we can create an economic model that protects the environment, enhances
well-being, and upholds the principles of Te Tiriti o Waitangi.
"Me whai kia whakamana te reo Māori, mātauranga Māori, me ngā tikanga tuku
iho i roto i tēnei huringa ōhanga. (We must ensure that te reo Māori, Māori
knowledge, and customary practices are upheld throughout this economic
transition.)”

25
https://plantbasedtreaty.org/

animaljustice.org.nz | party@animaljusticeparty.org.nz 7

---

Objective 1: Increase consumption of plant-based foods
Make plant-based foods the default option for public
institutions

The AJP proposes to increase the availability of plant-based foods in schools, hospitals
and other public institutions and events - by making nutritious plant-based foods the
default option.

At the current time our public institutions offer little in the way of alternatives to
animal-based foods, even in settings like hospitals where health and nutrition alone
should be a strong motive for change. Increasing the availability and visibility of
delicious plant-based foods is a low-cost high-impact way of increasing demand for
these products and supporting more sustainable, healthy and compassionate consumer
choices. This in turn has the potential to create a ripple effect beyond public institutions
by influencing broader community eating habits and private organisations.

Similar initiatives have been implemented with success elsewhere in the world. For
example in New York in 2022 plant-based meals were made the default option across
11 public hospitals. The initiative was introduced to address both health and
environmental objectives. By early 2024 over 1.2 million plant-based meals had been
served with an 80%+ satisfaction rate, and with discharged patients receiving a free
booklet of plant-based recipes to try at home. This also led to an estimated 36%
reduction in planet-heating greenhouse gas pollution, pointing to the contribution these
initiatives can make towards organisational carbon reduction efforts.26

To implement these initiatives in Aotearoa, we will also encourage the use of rooftops,
courtyards, and other green spaces in public institutions to create edible gardens.
These gardens can supply fresh, seasonal ingredients directly to institutional kitchens -
the ultimate in "farm to plate" - while also providing educational and therapeutic value.
Patients, students, staff, and visitors observing or participating in these gardens may be
inspired to grow food at home, creating a ripple effect beyond the institution. Globally,
edible landscapes are being successfully used in hospitals,27 schools,28 and community
centres29 to reconnect people with food, promote sustainability and enhance wellbeing.

26
NYC Health and Hospitals (2024) - Hospitals celebrate 1.2 million plant-based meals served
27
https://www.bmc.org/nourishing-our-community/rooftop-farm
28
https://www.ediblegardencity.com/key-projects
29

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2018/may/09/incredible-edible-yorkshire-towns-food-growing-scheme-
takes-root-worldwide

animaljustice.org.nz | party@animaljusticeparty.org.nz 8

---

To implement these initiatives effectively, we will work with hauora Māori (Māori health
providers), tohunga kai (food experts), and food suppliers to develop culturally
appropriate guidelines and menus that prioritise plant-based options. We will engage
with communities to cultivate buy-in and develop solutions that reflect the needs of all
New Zealanders.

AJP believes that instigating plant-based food by default in public institutions is an
effective low-regrets step that can be taken now and that will support a shift away from
animal-based foods. It will lead to better health and environmental outcomes and
reduce demand for products that cause immeasurable animal suffering.

Key Objectives:
1. Introduce plant-based menus at all public institutions and events, with
plant-based food the default option (animal-based options available on request).
2. Use public procurement to increase demand for plant-based foods and reduce
demand for animal-based foods.
3. Support the Plant Based Treaty.

animaljustice.org.nz | party@animaljusticeparty.org.nz 9

---

Ensure fair and transparent labelling

The AJP proposes to mandate fair and transparent food labelling that provides
information about the environmental, health and animal welfare impacts of food and
drink products.

At the current time very little information is provided to consumers about the impacts of
the food and drink products they buy. Even when there is strong scientific evidence - for
example that processed red meats cause cancer - this is not communicated on
packaging, in contrast to other harmful products like tobacco. Furthermore, many of the
marketing terms used on food and drink products are not standardised (such as ‘natural’
and ‘less dairy’) - and thus can be misleading to consumers.

By introducing a new mandatory system of labelling we will ensure that consumers have
access to the information they need to make more sustainable, healthier and
compassionate choices. This will also support producers who achieve higher standards
and help to drive a broader transformation of food supply chains.

Looking internationally, there are examples of good-practice approaches to labelling that
communicate information to consumers in a simple, transparent and high impact way.
For example in the UK a red-amber-green traffic light system is used to show nutritional
information such as levels of salts, fats and sugars. Research has found that this type of
mandatory labelling can be effective in encouraging healthier consumer choices.30

The AJP believes that consumers have the right to information about the health, animal
welfare and environmental impacts of the food and drink products they buy, and that
standardised, fair and transparent labelling has an important role to play.

Key Objectives:
1. Adopt a nutrition-based traffic-light labelling system for food and drink products.
2. Mandate the use of clear warnings of health risks where robust evidence exists
e.g. cancer warnings on processed red meats as per the World Health
Organisation rankings.31
3. Introduce greenhouse gas emission labelling on all food and drink products.

30

Introduce plant-based eating initiatives and improve
guidelines

The AJP proposes to launch a range of plant-based, healthy eating initiatives that
reduce harm to animals by promoting the consumption of healthy plant-based foods and
decreasing consumption of animal-based foods. While improving public health is a
valuable outcome, our primary focus is on preventing animal suffering through dietary
change. These initiatives will be based on the best-available science, and communicate
information in ways that promote transparency and inspire change.

New Zealand's food environment poses challenges for promoting healthier, plant-based
choices. While the national dietary guidelines (last updated 2020) make some positive
recommendations around plant proteins and limiting red meat, they maintain a strong
emphasis on dairy products, likely reflecting industry influence. Educational initiatives
like ‘Garden to Table’ demonstrate the potential for teaching children about growing and
preparing fresh food, but operate in only a fraction of schools due to limited government
funding.

Meanwhile, the public faces a constant barrage of meat-heavy fast food marketing, with
major chains dominating the advertising landscape through sports sponsorship, outdoor
advertising and prime-time TV spots. Children in particular are vulnerable targets for
food companies, as they struggle to distinguish marketing from fact. While adults are
also susceptible to marketing influence, children represent both current customers
through their impact on household purchasing decisions and valuable future customers.
Adults ultimately control food budgets, but research shows children significantly
influence family food choices, making them strategic marketing targets despite not
having direct purchasing power themselves.32 The constant flow of advertising makes it
virtually impossible for young people to avoid unhealthy food marketing, effectively
normalising unhealthy consumption patterns.

We propose a three-pronged approach:

First, we will launch public media campaigns to build awareness about the health
benefits of plant-based foods and the animal welfare concerns associated with animal
products. These campaigns will disseminate recipes and information on how to cook
nutritious plant-based meals, highlight ethical issues with animal-based foods, and
reflect the diversity of New Zealand society and current health inequalities.

Improve access to nutritious food

The AJP proposes to improve access to nutritious food for all New Zealanders through
a package of policy measures. While improving access to healthy food is a valuable
outcome, our primary focus is on preventing animal suffering through dietary change.
These measures will reduce costs, improve access to plant-based foods, support
communities to take a lead role, and tackle inequalities and health disparities.

Food access inequities exist across Aotearoa, disproportionately affecting Māori
communities.38 Lower-income areas often have a higher concentration of fast food
outlets and fewer fresh food retailers, while transport barriers and distance to
supermarkets create additional challenges, particularly in rural areas.

Many communities rely on local dairies (convenience stores) which typically stock
limited fresh food at higher prices. These access issues are compounded by the high
cost of healthy food. Fresh fruit and vegetables are notably expensive with significant
seasonal price fluctuations. Studies of healthy food baskets consistently show that
eating according to nutrition guidelines requires a substantial portion of a low-income
household's budget, while processed and energy-dense foods remain cheaper per
calorie than fresh, nutritious options.

New Zealanders are currently not eating the recommended servings of fruit and
vegetables. In 2023/24, 47.1% adults ate the recommended amount of fruit and only
9.1% ate the recommended amount of vegetables per day. For children aged 2 to 14
years the figures are 70.5% and 8.2% respectively39.

ability to obtain food; skipping meals or running out of food occasionally”,40 can lead to
an average educational achievement lag of up to four years for New Zealand

potentially life-long impacts.42 In 2023/24 rates of food insecurity were higher in

Objective 2: Use land and water sustainably and compassionately
Ban the most intensive and harmful forms of animal
farming and fishing

The AJP proposes to implement an absolute ban on the worst animal farming and
fishing practices.

We believe that all forms of animal farming and fishing should be phased out. There are
steps we can take now to eliminate the cruellest and most intensive practices, helping to
move towards our longer term objectives.

New Zealand’s Animal Welfare Act sets out obligations on people in charge of animals
(including farmed animals) to meet an animal’s physical, health and behavioural needs,
and to alleviate pain or distress. However in practice this does not happen. Minimum
standards contained in regulations and Codes of Welfare are inadequate, often
out-dated and reviewed according to the whims of Ministers, and frequently these
minimum standards are not met. In addition, monitoring and enforcement is stretched -
the Ministry for Primary Industries (whose main goals are productivity, export
opportunities and food safety50) employs around 30 inspectors for more than 160 million
farmed animals.51

We would undertake an urgent review of existing legislation, regulations and Codes of
Welfare and update these to strengthen a wide-range of requirements and minimum
standards. This would result in the following activities being banned:
- Intensive winter grazing (including feedlots and permanent indoor housing
systems)
- Breeding fast-growing chickens
- Intensive animal farming
- Live exports and long-haul animal transport
- Mutilations
- Bottom and conventional trawling

Introduce tighter standards and enforcement for
agricultural pollution

The AJP seeks to address the environmental harm caused by agricultural practices
while supporting farmers to transition to more sustainable and plant-based alternatives.
Through a combination of regulatory reform, targeted taxation and funding mechanisms,
we will create a path forward that ensures polluters pay for the damage they cause.
However, this will be no substitute for action which other AJP policies will drive in order
to reduce and eliminate the pollution.

Animal farming is a major polluter in Aotearoa, on land and at sea. It is responsible for a
48.6% of our planet-warming greenhouse gas emissions.52 It also causes effluent and
fertiliser run-off which is polluting our seas and rivers, making many of our waterways
unfit for aquatic life as well as for human swimming and drinking. Nutrient enrichment,
from fish farm releases, leads to eutrophication, promoting excessive algae growth that
depletes oxygen levels and harms marine ecosystems. Additionally, animal farming has
resulted in the destruction of much needed habitats for endangered species. This
pollution is allowed to occur largely unchecked. Regulations are insufficiently stringent,
often ignored and rarely enforced.

The huge costs from this pollution are not borne by the polluter - the animal farming
industry - but by nature and society at large. This is in effect a subsidy for one of the
dirtiest industries in the country.

One of the most urgent measures needed is to include agriculture into an Emissions
Trading Scheme (ETS). We would adopt the Climate Change Commission’s advice that
the current NZ ETS should focus on fossil fuel emissions. A separate, new
cap-and-trade ETS for biogenic emissions (including forestry) should be established,
which lowers gross methane emissions to agreed long-term flow.53 This should be
implemented as quickly as possible. We will also set separate gross (total emissions
produced) and net (emissions after offsets like forestry are considered) emissions
reductions targets and reform the ETS to ensure that gross agricultural emissions are
reduced, not simply netted off by forestry plantations.

To address other forms of agricultural pollution such as nitrogen run-off, the AJP
proposes an urgent review and strengthening of current standards such as the National

Objective 3: Support farmers, workers and communities to transition
Introduce a farm transition scheme

The AJP proposes to create a new national scheme that provides direct support to
animal farmers who wish to transition to plant farming and other economic activities.
This farmer-led, government-supported initiative will build momentum and knowledge on
viable approaches for diversifying beyond animal farming, while recognising and
honouring the unique considerations of Māori land and agricultural practices.

At the current time there are practical, financial and cultural barriers that prevent animal
farmers from diversifying their activities and moving away from animal farming.55 Whilst
there are examples in Aotearoa of farmers making positive changes, they are fighting
against the tide. The system as it stands is stacked against them, legacy policies and
institutional structures favour incumbent systems,56 and current adaptation strategies
often reinforce unsustainable, high-input systems.57

There are also knowledge gaps in terms of the most economically viable, sustainable
alternatives to animal farming, both in New Zealand and elsewhere in the world, which
need addressing urgently as the global food system changes.

However, this concentration into dairying in particular, is a relatively recent
phenomenon. Many regions were previously much more diverse, growing crops as well
as animals. Pig farming in this country is facing significant challenges as farmers
struggle to comply with new regulations and compete with floods of cheap overseas
pork from countries with lower animal welfare standards. Similarly, sheep farmers are
confronting problems due to climate change-induced weather patterns, an aging farmer
population, and decreasing value of mutton and lamb exports. The reluctance of
younger generations to enter these industries—including cattle farming—represents a
further challenge. These signs point to a broader decline in animal agriculture, creating
both urgency and opportunity for transition. The concentration of rural production into
animal agriculture means there is great opportunity for diversification in the future.

animaljustice.org.nz | party@animaljusticeparty.org.nz 28

---

Reskill workers within, and supporting, the industrial
animal system

The AJP proposes to create reskilling and training programmes for those currently
working in the animal farming, processing and food industries.

In New Zealand, DairyNZ estimates that around 55,000 people are employed in the
dairy industry, generating around $3.4BN in 2019. The Meat Industry Association
estimates that there are over 24,000 jobs in the meat processing sector. These jobs are
varied in nature but some - such as jobs in slaughterhouses - are seasonal, precarious,
and involve poor working conditions and increased risk of a range of mental health
issues.

As we shift away from animal agriculture towards a plant-based economy, some
animal-farming related jobs will be lost and other new jobs will be created in established
and emerging plant-based food and fibre industries. To ensure a just transition and
maintain public support, it will be essential for Government and local Councils to take a
proactive approach to ensure workers are reskilled and can access these new jobs.
Cultural identities and traditions can create resistance to change,62 solutions will also
need to be mindful of this and provide attractive opportunities.

To do this, we will create comprehensive worker training and reskilling programmes
developed in partnership with iwi and hapū, to honor the principle of tino rangatiratanga
(self-determination). These programmes will be:
- Publicly funded and implemented flexibly to recognise the specific skills and
needs of each participant.
- Available to young people who want to go directly into a career in plant-based
industries.
- Designed to incorporate mātauranga Māori (Māori knowledge) and tikanga Māori
(Māori customary practices) where appropriate.
- Designed to draw on learning from similar programmes from other economic
transitions such as the shift from fossil to renewable energy - including
comprehensive workforce mapping and a collaborative approach between
government, industry and workers.

62
Griffin, C., et al (2023). ‘As a farmer you've just got to learn to cope’: Understanding dairy farmers'
perceptions of climate change and adaptation decisions in the lower South Island of Aotearoa-New
Zealand. Journal of Rural Studies, 98, 147-158.https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jrurstud.2023.02.001

animaljustice.org.nz | party@animaljusticeparty.org.nz 29

---

The AJP believes that a successful transition to a plant-based economy must be fair to
all and that new opportunities for employment and prosperity must be provided to those
who lose their jobs in the animal-farming industry. Reskilling is essential to making this
happen. This transition must also uphold the principles of Te Tiriti o Waitangi and
support Māori aspirations for economic development and Kaitiakitanga (environmental
stewardship).

Key Objectives:
1. Create reskilling programmes, developed in partnership with Māori, to support
those currently working in the animal farming industry to access jobs and
opportunities in plant-based sectors.
2. Support a just transition that leaves no-one behind and honors Te Tiriti o
Waitangi principles.

animaljustice.org.nz | party@animaljusticeparty.org.nz 30

---

Objective 4: Develop long-term economic alternatives
Identify our biggest land-use and bioeconomy
opportunities

The AJP believes that the Government should convene a national process of
engagement and economic research to identify New Zealand's best opportunities to
diversify the economy away from animal agriculture into new land-uses, products and
markets.

At the current time our Government is taking a short-sighted approach to agricultural
policy. It is disproportionately influenced by the most regressive vested interests and is
now weakening environmental and animal welfare standards. Rather than take a
position of leadership to diversify the country’s agricultural sector away from animal
farming, the Government is doubling down on the status quo - an approach which is not
only bad for animals and the environment but also economically risky in a world of
changing technology and markets.

New Zealand’s approach to land-use urgently needs to change to deal with the
challenges of climate change, biodiversity loss and water quality.

To address these issues, the Government should lead a national programme to identify
the most promising economic opportunities for New Zealand’s bioeconomy and
land-use, taking into account future market demand, market size, jobs, GDP and export
potential. It should:
- Build on work undertaken by the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Enterprise
in 2023 that analysed 30 economic opportunities including land-based crops
such as pine nuts, hemp and bananas; water-based crops such as microalgae
and seaweed; forest based products such native botanicals and medicinal
mushrooms; and bioenergy, bioplastics and biochemicals.
- Investigate indigenous plant-based food as industries, such as kūmara, and other
native crops, which offer opportunities for Māori-led economic development while
ensuring alignment with tino rangatiratanga.
- Focus on region-specific opportunities suited to local land types, geographies,
climates and cultural contexts.
- Identify the key steps the Government can take to support these opportunities -
such as removing barriers, changing regulations and introducing incentives etc.

animaljustice.org.nz | party@animaljusticeparty.org.nz 31

---

- Involve a broad process of engagement and collaboration with farmers, land
managers, economists, academics, and the businesses and innovators that are
actively developing plant-based products.
- support local food63, prioritise ‘import-replacing’64 industries that build regional
resilience and self-sufficiency.65 66

We also advocate for the Government to develop a new comprehensive national
land-use strategy that considers the recommendations set out by the Parliamentary
Commissioner for the Environment in 202467. This strategy should support a shift away
from animal farming. It should include an integrated catchment approach to land-use
planning, devolved decision-making to regional and local authorities with meaningful iwi
partnership, and integrate with broader approaches to financial incentives such as
pricing biogenic methane and removing forestry from the Emissions Trading Scheme.
The Strategy will recognise the particular challenges faced by iwi with returned Crown
forestry land, create specific pathways for Māori landowners to gain economic benefits
from environmentally beneficial land uses and support iwi-led initiatives that align with te
ao Māori business frameworks and kaitiakitanga principles.

The AJP believes Aotearoa’s agricultural sector, and the way we use land, have huge
potential to be transformed to better meet the needs of both humans, animals and
nature. By embracing existing approaches and new technologies with regional control
and determination, we can build viable economic alternatives to replace animal
agriculture with a diverse portfolio of other products that go beyond an 'extractive
industries' model towards high-value, regionally controlled production centered on local
needs.

Key Objectives:
1. Identify the most promising region-specific economic opportunities for New
Zealand’s bioeconomy and land-use to shift away from animal farming, then
implement steps to make this happen.

63

https://www.resilience.org/stories/2024-11-05/the-globalized-industrialized-food-system-is-destroying-the-
world-we-urgently-need-to-support-local-food-economies/?mc_cid=e66bf4c222&mc_eid=36d5595f33
64
https://centerforneweconomics.org/publications/the-grace-of-import-replacement/
65

https://www.politico.eu/article/food-security-eat-less-meat-says-major-report-common-agricultural-policy-c
ap-eu-farming/
66

https://newsroom.co.nz/2024/11/12/the-case-for-feeding-our-5-million-first-before-first-tonne-is-exported/
67

https://pce.parliament.nz/media/qfxluadl/going-with-the-grain-changing-land-uses-to-fit-a-changing-landsc
ape.pdf

animaljustice.org.nz | party@animaljusticeparty.org.nz 32

---

2. Develop a new comprehensive national land-use strategy with devolved
decision-making that emphasises regional control of resources and financing and
supports a shift away from animal farming.
3. Ensure tangible support for Māori landowners to exercise kaitiakitanga and
rangatiratanga while achieving economic benefits.
4. Prioritise the development of local production for local needs, addressing the
supermarket duopoly and their centralised approach, strengthening regional
economies and reducing dependence on volatile export markets.

animaljustice.org.nz | party@animaljusticeparty.org.nz 33

---

Become a leader in alternative proteins

The AJP believes Aotearoa can become a world-leader in alternative proteins. The
Government should establish a National Centre for Alternative Proteins and dedicated
funding for research, innovation and commercialisation.

New Zealand must position itself proactively to avoid the economic vulnerability that
historically characterised its response to structural market changes, like the 1960s wool
price shock.68 Rather than treating the growing shift toward plant-based and cellular
agriculture as a temporary disruption, Aotearoa should leverage its existing agricultural
expertise, research capabilities and innovation systems to become a pioneer in this
emerging sector. Funding for alternative proteins grew by 85% in 2024 in Asia-Pacific69,

New Zealand has a long heritage of agricultural innovation and a strong foundation in
agricultural science and research. However at the current time much of this is being
directed towards the ongoing exploitation of animals, for example through the
development of vaccines, new genetic breeds and alternative feeds to reduce ruminant
methane emissions.

There is an opportunity for New Zealand’s science and research community to pivot
towards plant-based solutions that are better for the environment, the climate and
animals. Breaking free from the institutional inertia and path dependence that has
historically favored traditional primary sector activities70 noting New Zealand’s
institutional arrangements tend to favour the primary sector.71

The Vegan Society's Green Protein Report72 highlights that New Zealand has significant
untapped potential for plant protein production. According to the report, transitioning just
15% of animal farming land to plant protein crops could produce the same amount of
protein while reducing land use, greenhouse gas emissions, and water pollution.

68
Easton, B. 2023. Learnings from The New Zealand Economic History of Shocks . Wellington:
Productivity Commission.
69

https://www.greenqueen.com.hk/asia-pacific-agri-food-tech-funding-investment-agfunder-report/?utm_sou
rce=green-queen-future-food-weekly.beehiiv.com&utm_medium=newsletter&utm_campaign=china-grants
-regulatory-approval-for-animal-free-lactoferrin-future-food-weekly
70
Easton, B as above
71
New Zealand Productivity Commission. 2021. New Zealand firms: Reaching for the frontier. Final
report. Wellington: New Zealand Productivity Commission.
72
The Green Protein Report

animaljustice.org.nz | party@animaljusticeparty.org.nz 34

---

By making a decisive and well-resourced commitment to alternative protein
development - including cellular agriculture, precision fermentation, and plant-based
innovations - New Zealand can transform its agricultural comparative advantage into
leadership in sustainable protein production.

Cultivated meat and precision fermentation offer a transformative opportunity to create a
food system that is kinder to animals, healthier for people, and far less damaging to the
environment. By producing meat directly from animal cells, cultivated meat eliminates
the need for factory farming, sparing billions of animals from suffering while reducing the
risk of zoonotic diseases and antibiotic resistance. Precision fermentation allows us to
create dairy and other animal-derived proteins without the environmental toll of
industrial animal agriculture, slashing greenhouse gas emissions, water use, and
deforestation. These innovations provide the same tastes and textures people love, but
with dramatically lower impacts—offering a future where we can nourish the world
without harming animals or the planet.

This transition demands more than incremental policy changes; it requires substantial
investment in research and development, regulatory frameworks that enable innovation,
and coordinated support for alternative protein startups and scale-ups. Unlike previous
attempts at economic diversification that delivered "sub-therapeutic" results 73, the
alternative protein strategy must be backed by material resources and clear policy
frameworks to overcome the established institutional arrangements that favour
traditional agriculture.

We propose to establish a new National Centre for Alternative Proteins to focus on
these solutions - bringing together the best of New Zealand and international talent
across science, academia, the farming industry and the policy and finance communities.
This will be funded by redirecting the $400 million for R&D into agricultural climate
solutions74 away from animal-based towards plant-based solutions. It will be
complemented by a dedicated Research, Innovation and Commercialisation Fund that
supports New Zealand based innovators and scientists, and it will be targeted at
solutions that have high economic potential for the country.

The National Centre will have a Māori Alternative Proteins Advisory Board with
decision-making authority and a Māori Innovation Fund for iwi-led initiatives.
Mātauranga Māori will be embedded in research, and co-investment models will enable
iwi organisations to hold equity in ventures. Intellectual property protections and
benefit-sharing frameworks will safeguard indigenous knowledge, while targeted
73
Skilling, D. 2020. Frontier firms: An international small advanced economy perspective. Netherlands:
Landfall Strategy Group.
74
https://www.beehive.govt.nz/release/agriculture-come-out-ets

animaljustice.org.nz | party@animaljusticeparty.org.nz 35

---

programs will support Māori entrepreneurs and job creation in high-Māori-population
regions.

These initiatives will work across the public and private sectors from early stage R&D
through to scale-up and early commercial deployment. The National Centre will develop
a roadmap of steps New Zealand should take across major opportunity areas and
provide a range of grants and concessional finance support. It will also develop
innovation clusters that can overcome the path dependence that has reinforced New
Zealand's traditional economic trajectory and identify changes needed to the regulatory
framework to remove barriers and create market demand for new products.

There is huge potential for innovations in food technology to provide alternatives to
animal products (as we have already seen with the popularity of oat milk), and even to
provide ‘real’ animal products without farming animals. Whilst this must be done in an
ethical way, and should not distract from the very real imperative to reduce consumption
and animal farming now, it could make a real difference in reducing farmed animal
numbers and animal suffering.

This alternative protein strategy represents a material commitment to economic
diversification that acknowledges the institutional and historical barriers that have
previously prevented New Zealand from adapting to structural economic changes
before they become crises. With climate change advancing and almost fifty percent of
New Zealand's greenhouse gases coming from agricultural emissions, moving away
from animal agriculture now will help mitigate the size of the crisis. By ensuring Māori
are true partners in this journey, the strategy can support rangatiratanga and economic
self-determination while drawing on indigenous knowledge that may offer unique
insights and innovations in the alternative proteins space.

Key Objectives:
1. Support New Zealand to become a world-leader in alternative proteins through a
new National Centre and dedicated research, innovation and commercialisation
funding.
2. Redirect existing agricultural R&D funding from animal-based to plant-based
solutions.
3. Develop regulatory frameworks that enable rather than inhibit alternative protein
innovation.
4. Create institutional structures capable of overcoming the historical inertia that
has favored traditional primary sector activities.
5. Position New Zealand to proactively adapt to structural market changes rather
than treating them as temporary disruptions.

animaljustice.org.nz | party@animaljusticeparty.org.nz 36

While our long-term vision is to end all forms of animal agriculture, we recognise the urgent need to reform current breeding practices, which often prioritise production and profit at the expense of animal health, dignity and wellbeing. This policy addresses the ethical, legal and welfare concerns associated with genetic manipulation, reproductive control and growth-promoting technologies used in modern farming.

# Ending Animal Experimentation

> Archive note: Web text is the policy post body from animaljustice.org.nz/wp-json/wp/v2/policies; the PDF version linked from the page (if any) follows, extracted with pdftotext -layout.

## Full text (verbatim)

### Web page text

With many animal experiments being harmful or unreliable, we need further funding and research into more ethical scientific experimentation. The end goal is to replace all harmful animal experiments with alternative methods. As reported by the MPI during 2021.

Over 300,000 animals were used in experiments in the name of Research, Testing and Teaching. Many of these animals were killed both in these experiments and simply for no longer being useful to the industry. We know that animal experiments are unreliable in regards to biomedical research and yet, we continue to experiment with animals committing invasive procedures that too often do not yield anything valuable. It is completely unethical for research institutions to breed thousands of animals each year, to perform painful and distressing experiments, and then discard them.

[*The full policy for Ending Animal Experimentation can be found here.*](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1FgNFxOqqdj1sz0mq1r5CSYOsujP3-Tpi/view?usp=sharing)

# Commissioner for Animals

> Archive note: Web text is the policy post body from animaljustice.org.nz/wp-json/wp/v2/policies; the PDF version linked from the page (if any) follows, extracted with pdftotext -layout.

## Full text (verbatim)

### Web page text

Organizations such as SAFE, RNZSPCA, HUHA and NZAVS support the call for a Commissioner for Animals. These organisations are on the front lines, witnessing the inadequacies and are often powerless to act. Aotearoa prides itself on having high welfare standards but while there are animals housed inappropriately and being denied basic freedoms, we cannot claim this as truth.

AJPANZ proposes that the Commissioner for Animals will have the authority to undertake comprehensive reviews of the current system and work to repeal and amend any Codes that contradict the Animal Welfare Act 1999.

We propose that the Commissioner for Animals will have legal jurisdiction over animal well-being, enabling adequate monitoring of all sectors. We will allocate appropriate resources to organisations like MPI and RNZSPCA to ensure they have the capability to uphold the Animal Welfare Act 1999 and we will ensure these organisations enact effective administration of this Act.

**An independent Commissioner for Animals should be equipped to propose changes to legislation and enforcement where basic requirements are being ignored or compromised.**

[*The full policy for Commissioner for Animals can be found here.*](https://drive.google.com/file/d/16_ZMofNVB-LGHZKuy94fcBgVMrJsVywr/view?usp=sharing)

# Ban Recreational Fishing and Fishing Competitions

> Archive note: Web text is the policy post body from animaljustice.org.nz/wp-json/wp/v2/policies; the PDF version linked from the page (if any) follows, extracted with pdftotext -layout.

## Full text (verbatim)

### Web page text

The Animal Justice Party Aotearoa NZ (AJP) is opposed to recreational fishing and fishing competitions. We are committed to an immediate and complete ban on these activities.

Recreational fishing involves catching fish for “sport”. This practice causes significant distress and suffering to fish and other marine life. Fishing competitions exacerbate these issues by encouraging the mass capture and killing of fish for prizes and recognition.

Recreational fishing inflicts considerable suffering on fish, who can experience pain and distress from being hooked, handled, and often released back into the water injured. Non-target species, such as birds, turtles, and marine mammals, can also become unintended victims through bycatch, and entanglement in lost, abandoned or discarded equipment, leading to injuries or death.

Fishing competitions promote the capture of large numbers of fish in a short period, often resulting in unethical practices and significant harm to fish populations. Many fish caught in these events suffer prolonged pain and stress, and their survival rates upon release are low, contributing to ecological imbalance.

Recreational fishing and fishing competitions are ethically indefensible and cause significant suffering to marine life. AJP advocates for non-violent, community-friendly entertainment that aligns with society’s concerns and ethical and moral principles, and does not exploit and undermine animals’ well-being.

# Commissioner for Animals

> Archive note: Web text is the policy post body from animaljustice.org.nz/wp-json/wp/v2/policies; the PDF version linked from the page (if any) follows, extracted with pdftotext -layout.

## Full text (verbatim)

### Web page text

The Animal Justice Party Aotearoa NZ (AJP) believes that all animals in Aotearoa deserve adequate representation in Parliament, to ensure they are protected from exploitation and mistreatment.

To strengthen the voice of animals, we are advocating for the independent position of Commissioner for Animals to be established. Animal welfare is currently regulated by the Ministry for Primary Industries (MPI). This is the same Government department responsible for seizing export opportunities and overseeing agriculture productivity. Decisions on animal welfare policies are being driven by industry stakeholders who are invested in profiting from the use of animals.

# Economic sufficiency within planetary boundaries

> Archive note: Web text is the policy post body from animaljustice.org.nz/wp-json/wp/v2/policies; the PDF version linked from the page (if any) follows, extracted with pdftotext -layout.

## Full text (verbatim)

### Web page text

Policy category summary: The AJP recognises the profound impact of our lifestyles, economic metrics of success, dietary choices, and leisure activities on the environment. The core issue that urgently needs to be addressed is the current unsustainable trajectory, particularly in terms of environmental degradation. The AJP advocates for a paradigm shift in economic models, enabling an inclusion of externalities of the natural world, and a move away from short-term gain to long-term ecological sustainability, prioritising wellbeing over relentless growth, and emphasising the importance of sustainable and future focused change to ensure a balance between human activities and planetary boundaries.

\
We promote the adoption of circular economy principles, community-led initiatives, and local resilience measures to minimise negative impact on the ecological footprint. We envision a society that measures success, not only by economic metrics, but also by the health of ecosystems, the wellbeing of communities, and the ethical and moral treatment of non-human animals, aligning with a holistic and sustainable approach to living and thriving.

# Protecting ecosystems and biodiversity

> Archive note: Web text is the policy post body from animaljustice.org.nz/wp-json/wp/v2/policies; the PDF version linked from the page (if any) follows, extracted with pdftotext -layout.

## Full text (verbatim)

### Web page text

Policy category summary: The AJP envisions a world where ecosystems thrive, and biodiversity flourishes, fostering harmonious coexistence between humans and other animals. We aspire to a future where habitats are safeguarded, species abound, and the delicate balance of our planet’s natural systems endures for generations. The undeniable detrimental impact of animal agriculture and the current management of biodiversity and habitats necessitates urgent action. We advocate for a paradigm shift in agriculture towards efficient and productive land use without farming animals. This not only reduces ecological footprints but also creates opportunities for rewilding farmland, allowing natural ecosystems to flourish, and carbon sequestration. We support compassionate conservation measures, habitat restoration, and the implementation of policies to mitigate the impact of pollutants and pesticides, including ongoing and emerging environmental challenges.\

In honouring the Māori worldview, we embrace the concept of Kaitiakitanga, recognising our responsibility as guardians of the land. We look back to traditional practices that emphasise respect for nature and integrate these principles as we seek to preserve biodiversity and also respect the cultural connection between humans, non-human animals and the environment. In doing so, we aim to forge a sustainable path forward, where ecosystems are safeguarded, and the richness of biodiversity is cherished and protected.

# End the Private Sale and Use of Fireworks

> Archive note: Web text is the policy post body from animaljustice.org.nz/wp-json/wp/v2/policies; the PDF version linked from the page (if any) follows, extracted with pdftotext -layout.

## Full text (verbatim)

### Web page text

Fireworks cause preventable environmental damage, wildlife harm and animal distress across Aotearoa. The science is clear, and the public demand for change is overwhelming. This policy addresses the urgent need to protect our marine ecosystems, wildlife and companion animals from the harmful effects of explosive celebrations. \
The private use of fireworks in residential areas and sensitive environments creates unnecessary suffering and environmental contamination that is entirely preventable. By ending private fireworks sales and use, we can eliminate the majority of fireworks-related harm while transitioning to sustainable and animal friendly celebration alternatives.

*See our policy document [**PDF**](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1Z5bYYjypqhJ9DS-idX9t2lAezT_25AzV/view?usp=sharing) for the full policy.*

# Ending the Use of All Animals for ‘Entertainment’

> Archive note: Web text is the policy post body from animaljustice.org.nz/wp-json/wp/v2/policies; the PDF version linked from the page (if any) follows, extracted with pdftotext -layout.

## Full text (verbatim)

### Web page text

The exploitation of animals for entertainment stems from humanity’s long-standing belief in our dominion over other species. In these situations, profit often takes precedence over animal welfare. As a result, animals are routinely exposed to danger, forced to perform risky acts for human amusement and financial gain. This practice repeatedly jeopardises their safety, health, and lives, treating them as disposable commodities rather than sentient beings deserving of respect and protection.

This policy is a wide and generic policy providing breadth to support standalone policies for specific cases of animal use in entertainment, for example our *Ban Greyhound Racing* policy. This generic policy includes animals in zoos and aquaria, keeping cetaceans in captivity, agricultural and pastoral show animals (for example for riding), or chickens hatched to provide entertainment for children, and ensuring that animals are not reintroduced to circuses and all other uses.

AJP advocates for an end to animal exploitation for artistic, fashion, cultural, sporting  or entertainment purposes, and will work toward ensuring no animal is forced into a working life for ‘entertainment’ and/or gambling purposes.

**Key Objectives:**

Ban the use of animals for entertainment purposes.

*Interim measures, while we work towards the complete ban, include:*

1. Ban all forms of animal ‘entertainment’ that are funded through or support gambling.
2. Call for complete transparency of organisations that currently profit from animals in entertainment.
3. Ban the breeding of all animal species for ‘sporting’ performance.
4. Ban the forcing of animals to perform at high and peak levels.
5. Implement rigorous inspections of zoos, wildlife parks and aquaria to ensure their facilities and staffing numbers are optimum for the animals.
6. Support those needing help transitioning to alternative careers.

# Ending the use of lethal biological agents and poisons for population control

> Archive note: Web text is the policy post body from animaljustice.org.nz/wp-json/wp/v2/policies; the PDF version linked from the page (if any) follows, extracted with pdftotext -layout.

## Full text (verbatim)

### Web page text

AJP opposes the use of lethal biological and poisons to control introduced species, for example Rabbit Haemorrhagic Virus Disease (RHDV) and poisons like 1080 and Brodifacoum. Instead, AJP advocates for humane, non-lethal, and species-specific methods of population management.

Poisons and biological agents used for population control frequently cause intense and prolonged suffering, with some poisons and diseases taking hours or days to kill, leading to unnecessary animal distress. Research has shown that some commonly used poisons, such as those with a welfare impact score over 5.51, result in slow, painful deaths and must be reconsidered as part of a humane transition in wildlife management.

**Key Objectives:**

1. Ban the use of all lethal biological agents, including Rabbit Haemorrhagic Virus Disease (RHDV).

2. Cease the use of all poisons, including 1080 and Brodifacoum aerial drops.

3. Fund research into ethical, non-lethal alternatives for managing introduced species, such as: \
a. Immunocontraceptives for population control \
b. Fencing and habitat modification to prevent overpopulation \
c. Non-toxic deterrents and repellents

4. Ensure conservation efforts align with compassionate principles and recognise the sentience and intrinsic value of all animals.

# Ending trapping and hunting for population control

> Archive note: Web text is the policy post body from animaljustice.org.nz/wp-json/wp/v2/policies; the PDF version linked from the page (if any) follows, extracted with pdftotext -layout.

## Full text (verbatim)

### Web page text

AJP opposes the trapping and hunting of wild animals as a part of so-called ‘pest control’ activities. For AJP’s policy on hunting for entertainment, see: *Hunting and Fishing policies*.

A lack of enforcement for existing codes of conduct means that inhumane practices persist with minimal accountability. This regulatory gap allows for the continuation of trapping and hunting methods that cause unnecessary suffering to animals.

**Key Objectives:**

1. Amend the Animal Welfare Act to prohibit the unnecessary killing and suffering of all animals, requiring that population control be carried out with humane and non-lethal methods, and ensuring that greater accountability and stricter enforcement methods are upheld.

**Interim Objectives:**

While working toward long-term legislative change, AJP supports introducing more stringent regulations and safeguards to minimise harm to wild animals. These include:

1. **Mandatory live cameras on traps** to ensure compliance with animal welfare regulations and to facilitate immediate response once an animal is captured. Current legal requirements for trap checks every 12 hours are inadequate, and real-time monitoring would enable faster intervention to reduce suffering.

2. **Strict codes of conduct for hunting and trapping**, making ethical guidelines enforceable in legislation, rather than voluntary. AJP will advocate for uniform and legally binding standards across all hunting and trapping activities. (*aligns to Hunting and Fishing policies*)

3. **Age restrictions** to prohibit individuals under 18 from participating in trapping, hunting or any wild animal control activities that involve direct harm to animals.

4. **Stronger regulation of live trapping**, ensuring that any continued use of live traps adheres to high welfare standards, with a focus on transitioning toward non-lethal population management solutions.

### PDF version: https://animaljustice.org.nz/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Ending-trapping-and-hunting-for-population-control.docx.pdf

AJP Policy Document

Ending trapping and hunting for
population control
AJP opposes the trapping and hunting of wild animals as a part of so-called ‘pest
control’ activities. For AJP’s policy on hunting for entertainment, see: Hunting and
Fishing policies.
Common trapping practices include:
- Leg-Hold Traps: These devices are designed to capture animals by the limb,
restraining them until they are dispatched by trappers. The use of leg-hold traps
can result in severe injuries, including fractures, dislocations, and lacerations.
Animals caught in these traps can experience prolonged periods of distress and
pain before being euthanised.1,2
- Kill Traps: Intended to provide a swift death, even the most humane traps can kill
non-target species or cause non-lethal injury.3
- Live-Capture Cage Traps: These traps aim to capture animals without immediate
harm, allowing for relocation or euthanasia. Animals may experience stress,
dehydration and exposure to harsh environmental conditions while confined for
up to 24 hours, according to regulations. However, these regulations are not
actively enforced.4
A lack of enforcement for existing codes of conduct means that inhumane practices
persist with minimal accountability. This regulatory gap allows for the continuation of
trapping and hunting methods that cause unnecessary suffering to animals.

Children and young people in New Zealand are sometimes involved in trapping
activities without sufficient age restrictions.5 This exposure raises ethical concerns
regarding the normalisation of violence towards animals and potential desensitisation to
animal suffering. It also poses safety risks, as handling traps and captured animals can
be hazardous without proper training and supervision.
Current trapping practices, coupled with inadequate regulation and enforcement, often
result in significant, and unnecessary, animal suffering. Addressing these issues
requires comprehensive policy and legislative reform, including the development and
implementation of more humane control methods, stricter regulations and educational
initiatives to promote ethical practices in wildlife management.

Key Objectives:

1. Amend the Animal Welfare Act to prohibit the unnecessary killing and suffering of
all animals, requiring that population control be carried out with humane and
non-lethal methods, and ensuring that greater accountability and stricter
enforcement methods are upheld.

Interim Objectives:

While working toward long-term legislative change, AJP supports introducing more
stringent regulations and safeguards to minimise harm to wild animals. These include:

1. Mandatory live cameras on traps to ensure compliance with animal welfare
regulations and to facilitate immediate response once an animal is captured.
Current legal requirements for trap checks every 12 hours are inadequate, and
real-time monitoring would enable faster intervention to reduce suffering.
2. Strict codes of conduct for hunting and trapping, making ethical guidelines
enforceable in legislation, rather than voluntary. AJP will advocate for uniform
and legally binding standards across all hunting and trapping activities. (aligns to
Hunting and Fishing policies)
3. Age restrictions to prohibit individuals under 18 from participating in trapping,
hunting or any wild animal control activities that involve direct harm to animals.
4. Stronger regulation of live trapping, ensuring that any continued use of live
traps adheres to high welfare standards, with a focus on transitioning toward
non-lethal population management solutions.

# Ensuring adequate living conditions and environmental standards

> Archive note: Web text is the policy post body from animaljustice.org.nz/wp-json/wp/v2/policies; the PDF version linked from the page (if any) follows, extracted with pdftotext -layout.

## Full text (verbatim)

### Web page text

The Animal Justice Party Aotearoa NZ (AJP) is working towards a future without animal agriculture. In the meantime, we are committed to addressing the widespread neglect of shelter, housing and environmental conditions that cause immense suffering to farmed animals. Despite existing legal protections, animals across New Zealand are routinely exposed to harsh weather, overcrowding and barren environments that deny them the ability to express natural behaviours. AJP is calling for urgent reforms to ensure farmed animals are afforded basic protections, dignity and care.

While our long-term goal is to end animal agriculture, immediate reform is needed to address the widespread welfare harms caused by inadequate feeding practices, compromised health management and overreliance on pharmaceuticals in industrial farming. ### Web page text

The Animal Justice Party Aotearoa New Zealand (AJP) is committed to ending harmful animal handling practices and advancing a system of care that upholds the dignity,rights and welfare of all animals used in agriculture. While our ultimate goal is to abolish all animal farming, we call for urgent reforms to eliminate cruel procedures, ensure prompt access to veterinary care, and establish humane handling standards rooted in compassion and respect for sentient beings.

# Ensuring Humane Transport Conditions

> Archive note: Web text is the policy post body from animaljustice.org.nz/wp-json/wp/v2/policies; the PDF version linked from the page (if any) follows, extracted with pdftotext -layout.

## Full text (verbatim)

### Web page text

The Animal Justice Party (AJP) envisions a New Zealand where compassion, sustainability and ethical practices guide our treatment of animals. While we ultimately seek a complete transition away from animal agriculture towards plant-based and cellular systems, we recognise the urgent need to reduce the suffering of animals who are currently trapped in this system. One of the most severe and widespread breaches of the five freedoms1 occurs during transport, particularly when animals are moved between farms, saleyards and slaughterhouses.

AJP calls for a complete overhaul of animal transport regulations to recognise the specific needs of each species, regardless of their intended use. While animal farming continues, we demand far stricter controls on journey times, space allowances, rest periods and handling practices, as well as the retention and strengthening of the live export ban. Our long-term vision remains the complete replacement of animal farming with ethical, sustainable alternatives, but until that is achieved, animals must be afforded the highest possible level of protection.

# Extending the Live Export Ban

## Full text (verbatim)

### Web page text

AJP will campaign for an amendment to include animals that are exported by air; except for specific cases such as companion animals being relocated or relocation for conservation efforts. Not only are the transportation methods often dangerous, cramped and not up to the standards defined in The Animal Welfare Act 1999, we have no control over the management or care of animals once they reach their destination country. This allows for the treatment of animals we have raised and transported, to be substandard and not in accordance with our animal welfare laws and codes.
