# Policy Framework

## Full text (verbatim)

# Policy Framework

## Animals

The Animal Justice Party (AJP) believes in compassion and non-violence. Our unwavering commitment is focused on safeguarding and enhancing the lives of all animals. We believe that all animals, regardless of form, deserve the right to live and thrive. All sentient beings deserve recognition and protection under the law from harm or cruelty, guided by our commitment to the precautionary principle. This principle urges us to prioritise caution in the face of uncertainty, ensuring that all non-human animals are valued, and treated respectfully and with dignity, acknowledging their capacity for emotions, suffering, and joy.

\

Currently, animals face inadequate living conditions, exploitation in various industries, and practices that prioritise human interests over their inherent rights and well-being. This harms animals, us, and our planet, and it prevents the realisation of a harmonious coexistence between humans and non-human animals. Animal welfare is a significant issue of public concern.The solution lies in advocating for systemic change, just governance and legal and regulatory reforms and safeguards that prioritise the inherent rights and quality of life non-human animals deserve, making a positive difference through the application and improvement of animal welfare and protection law. By acknowledging the moral right that animals should not be treated as property, and guided by compassion and empathy, we can ensure that the wellbeing and protection of animals is enshrined in law, policy and practice.

\

This achievable future is not simply a goal; it’s a shared commitment to the wellbeing of non-human animals and a just and humane society. It is not just an aspiration, but a reality that we collectively create.

## Environment & Economy

The AJP is committed to a transition to a plant-based economy with respect for sentient animals at the core.

\

Climate change is one of the most urgent challenges we face. Driven by GHG emissions from fossil fuel use, the destruction of natural ecosystems and intensive animal farming, the world has now entered an era of rapid and unpredictable changes with profoundly detrimental consequences for both people and animals. The need for decisive action has never been clearer nor more urgent. But Aotearoa New Zealand’s political and economic system is failing to deliver the solutions we need, or to seize the enormous opportunities that climate action offers to transform our country for the better.

\

We are very concerned about the loss of wildlife habitat due to agricultural expansion, resource extraction, urban sprawl and exceeding planetary boundaries. The AJP believes humans can thrive while simultaneously reducing our adverse impacts on the environment. A central policy advocates for a phased transition to a plant-based economy, prioritising environmental protection, public health, and positive animal welfare, whilst ensuring a just and supportive transition for farmers and others working in the system.

\

Our vision has all sentient beings at the forefront of environmental and ecosystems considerations, emphasising their wellbeing and protection as essential to the collective welfare of the planet.

## People

The AJP seeks to create a society where the welfare, and ability to thrive, of both humans and other animals is at the forefront, guided by compassion, inclusivity, just governance, and a commitment to sustainability. As responsible stewards for future generations we must consider the impact of our actions today on animals, the planet and by extension ourselves.\
\
We acknowledge the intrinsic connection between humans and other animals, recognising the welfare of one directly impacts the other. When animals lead better lives, the result is not only reduced suffering and exploitation, but also an overall improvement in the health of our ecosystems, contributing to a healthier planet, and in turn, fostering healthier communities.\
\
Practices such as factory farming and cruel treatment of animals not only raise moral and ethical questions but can also desensitise and harm individuals, and lead to environmental degradation creating further harm. We believe the wellbeing of people can be enhanced through ethical and compassionate choices in how we use, protect and interact with animals.

[Browse Policies](https://animaljustice.org.nz/policy/our-policies/)

# Ban Greyhound Racing

> Archive note: Web text is the policy post body from animaljustice.org.nz/wp-json/wp/v2/policies; the PDF version linked from the page (if any) follows, extracted with pdftotext -layout.

## Full text (verbatim)

### Web page text

Greyhound racing involves greyhounds chasing a motorised lure at high speed around or along a specialised track while spectators place bets on particular dogs to win. The inherently risky nature of racing, coupled with the industry’s dependence on over-breeding, gambling revenue and the incentive to win prize money, has led to a situation where the welfare of racing greyhounds is compromised. Over 40 percent of racing greyhounds suffer injuries while racing; some serious, some lethal. This is the case wherever it occurs, and as a result, greyhound racing remains legal in only a handful of countries.

We do not believe that the greyhound racing industry can be safely regulated for the animals. We also acknowledge the negative impacts of gambling on human mental health, domestic relationships, and financial stability. Over the past decade, three reviews have shed light on concerning practices within the greyhound racing industry in New Zealand, following which the industry has lost its social licence.

AJP advocates for non-violent, community-friendly entertainment that aligns with society’s progressive concerns and higher ethical and moral principles and does not exploit and undermine animals’ well-being.

**Key Objectives:**

1. Ban all forms of greyhound racing in Aotearoa NZ.

*Interim measures, while we work towards the ban, include:*

2. Promote full transparency and accountability in relation to deaths and injuries of all greyhounds born into the racing industry, both on and off the track.
3. Recommend immediate restrictions to curb the breeding of greyhounds.
4. Call for a reduction on the number of greyhounds each racing kennel is permitted to own.
5. Support the SPCA’s ‘Good Life’ Recommendation.
6. Support the animal advocacy agencies (SPCA, SAFE, HUHA, Dogwatch) who are committed to finding loving homes for greyhounds when a ban is enacted.
7. Reallocate government funding and subsidies to transition those employed by the industry into non-exploitative jobs and careers.

# Ban Horse Racing

> Archive note: Web text is the policy post body from animaljustice.org.nz/wp-json/wp/v2/policies; the PDF version linked from the page (if any) follows, extracted with pdftotext -layout.

## Full text (verbatim)

### Web page text

The Animal Justice Party Aotearoa NZ (AJP) is opposed to all forms of horse racing and is committed to eliminating the use of animals for human ‘sport’ and ‘entertainment’.

Horse racing for profit includes flat racing, jumps racing, and harness racing. Horse racing in New Zealand is less associated with a sense of glamour of the past and is increasingly controversial owing to the inherent cruelty and risks involved. Every year, despite efforts to improve safety and regulate the industry, hundreds of horses suffer pain, stress, injuries, and even death as a result of being raced.

Contrary to popular belief, horses do not willingly participate in racing; many have to be coerced into the starting gates, highlighting the inherent lack of consent in the activity.

AJP advocates for non-violent, community-friendly entertainment that aligns with society’s progressive concerns and higher ethical and moral principles, and does not exploit and undermine animals’ well-being

**Key Objectives:**

1. Ban all forms of horse racing in Aotearoa NZ.

*Interim measures, while we work towards the ban, include:*

2. Ensure full transparency and accountability by having a public birth to death registry  for all horses born into the racing industry, whether these horses perform in official events or not.
3. Decrease the number of race meetings to alleviate the pressure on horses and reduce the frequency of injuries and fatalities associated with racing.
4. Prohibit cruel practices and tools, such as the use of whips, tongue ties and spurs.
5. Prohibit the racing of horses under three years of age.
6. End the slaughter of ex-racehorses.
7. Provide ex-racehorses with proper care, rehabilitation and rehoming for fulfilling post-racing life.
8. Reallocate government funding and subsidies to transition those employed by the industry into non-exploitative jobs and careers.

# Humane management of introduced species

> Archive note: Web text is the policy post body from animaljustice.org.nz/wp-json/wp/v2/policies; the PDF version linked from the page (if any) follows, extracted with pdftotext -layout.

## Full text (verbatim)

### Web page text

AJP recognises that animals from both native and introduced species are sentient, and have rights to life and welfare. AJP further recognises that humans are responsible for the introduction of non-endemic species to Aotearoa, and as such it is our responsibility to implement the most compassionate solutions where such species pose ecological threats. These should be framed and carried out in the spirit of Te Tiriti o Waitangi.

AJP supports valuing individual animals because they are sentient, not because of their species status as native or non-native. We oppose the demonisation of introduced species, and promote an understanding of them as animals living here as the direct result of human actions. With this in mind, AJP will work to raise awareness of the cruelty of current methods of controlling introduced species.

At the same time, AJP recognises the threat that particular introduced species, alongside habitat destruction and ecological damage caused by humans, pose to our native ecosystems. AJP therefore advocates for humane methods of population control, and the redirection of funds from current ‘pest control’ initiatives, such as Predator Free NZ, towards research and development of nonviolent forms of population control, such as contraceptives.

**Key Objectives:**

1. Call for government and government-funded entities to cease the use of unscientific, emotive and vilifying terms (e.g. ‘pests’) to describe animals and the requisite amendments made to the Animal Welfare Act.

2. Establish higher welfare standards for population control methods.

3. Fund research into nonviolent alternatives to current methods of population control.

4. Create a special task force to plan the phasing out of violent population control methods and work alongside environmental protection agencies to implement humane management of all species, endemic and introduced. This group would be responsible for developing policies that prioritise humane alternatives while balancing ecological concerns.

5. Implement educational programmes in schools, universities, and communities to promote compassionate management of introduced species.

# Ban Recreational Hunting and Hunting Competitions

> Archive note: Web text is the policy post body from animaljustice.org.nz/wp-json/wp/v2/policies; the PDF version linked from the page (if any) follows, extracted with pdftotext -layout.

## Full text (verbatim)

### Web page text

Recreational hunting involves the pursuit and killing of animals for ‘sport’. This practice not only causes unnecessary suffering to animals but also fosters a culture of violence and desensitisation towards animal life. Significant suffering is inflicted upon animals: they may endure prolonged pain from injuries before dying, and non-target species often become unintended victims.

Hunting competitions exacerbate ethical concerns by incentivising the rapid, large-scale killing of animals for prizes and recognition. This pressure often leads to inhumane practices and a disregard for animal welfare. Current practices in some New Zealand schools encourage children to participate in the mass killing of animals, often framed as a game or competition, in which violence is normalised and young minds become desensitised to the suffering of living creatures. Activities like ‘Toss the Poss’ not only disrespect animal life but also teach children to view certain species as disposable, rather than as sentient beings with lives of inherent worth.

Hunting promotes and normalises violence against animals, dulling society’s sensitivity to animal suffering. Instead of fostering a connection with nature and teaching responsible environmental stewardship, hunting promotes a harmful and oversimplified approach to wildlife management.

New Zealand allows the hunting of an arbitrary and wide range of animals including, to name a few, deer, pigs, free-roaming cats, rabbits and various  bird species. Seasonal restrictions may apply or licences may be required.

Hunting practices cause significant suffering across various species. For example: many animals are not killed instantly, resulting in painful wounds and prolonged suffering; injured animals that escape often face a slow, agonising death and the use of certain hunting methods, such as traps or particular types of ammunition, can increase the likelihood of non-fatal injuries. In the case of duck hunting, a seasonal activity, an estimated one million birds are affected annually, highlighting the scale of the issue.  These problems are not limited to any single species but are inherent risks in many forms of hunting.

The practice of hunting also disrupts local ecosystems and harms other wildlife in several ways: It can lead to habitat destruction or modification as hunters create access points or use methods that impact the environment; Non-target species may be accidentally injured or killed and the presence of hunters and their equipment can cause stress and behavioral changes in animals, affecting their natural patterns. Importantly, these harmful practices are unnecessary for wildlife management. New technologies,such as wildlife contraception, more humane methods for managing wildlife populations that do not involve lethal means which tend to be more effective in maintaining long-term ecological balance.

Recreational hunting and hunting competitions are ethically indefensible and cause significant animal suffering. AJP advocates for non-violent, community-friendly entertainment that aligns with society’s progressive concerns and higher ethical and moral principles, and does not exploit and undermine animals’ well-being.

**Key Objectives:**

1. Ban all forms of recreational hunting.
2. Ban hunting competitions.

*Interim measures, while we work towards the ban, include:*

3. Strengthen enforcement of existing animal welfare laws.
4. Call for an immediate ban on duck shooting.
5. Call for an immediate ban on the hunting of feral cats.
6. Enforce regulations to prevent children from participating in hunting activities, including ‘school gala days’.

# Improving the well-being of people

> Archive note: Web text is the policy post body from animaljustice.org.nz/wp-json/wp/v2/policies; the PDF version linked from the page (if any) follows, extracted with pdftotext -layout.

## Full text (verbatim)

### Web page text

Policy category summary: The AJP is committed to improving the well-being of people by creating a better world for non-human animals. The current economic system perpetuates harm to non-human animals whilst contributing to the exploitation and detriment of human well-being within these industries. People employed in exploitative animal industries often endure hazardous working conditions, low wages and psychological distress due to the inherently violent nature of the work. Whilst equally people employed in organisations that care for and protect animals face burnout and compassion fatigue from constantly witnessing and responding to animal distress. The ongoing detrimental risks for humans include antibiotic resistance and the spread of zoonotic diseases.\

We wish to address these interconnected issues to prioritise the advancement of both non-human animalwellbeing and human wellbeing. We also advocate for increased nutritional knowledge and affordable access to a healthy diet and exercise opportunities for everyone. We support a compassionate approach to all our interactions with each other, human or non-human animal.

# Independent Animal Welfare Governance to Reduce Harm

## Full text (verbatim)

### Web page text

The Animal Justice Party (AJP) envisions a New Zealand where compassion, sustainability and ethical practices guide our treatment of animals. While we advocate for a complete transition to a plant-based farming system, we recognise that meaningful societal changes require time and a ‘Just Transition’. In the interim, we are committed to reducing the most severe harm and mistreatment of animals by improving oversight of farming practices and strengthening legislation to provide stronger protections and ensure higher welfare standards for all animals in Aotearoa.

# International Considerations

> Archive note: Web text is the policy post body from animaljustice.org.nz/wp-json/wp/v2/policies; the PDF version linked from the page (if any) follows, extracted with pdftotext -layout.

## Full text (verbatim)

### Web page text

The shift in the international animal welfare and protection policy environment highlights the growing recognition of animal welfare as a critical issue on the global stage.

It is no longer viewed as peripheral but has become integral to discussions in regional and international policy forums.

This change is underscored by the emergence of an expanding framework of science-based standards, conventions, treaties, regulations, directives, and agreements.

### PDF version: https://animaljustice.org.nz/wp-content/uploads/2025/10/International-Considerations-Policy.pdf

AJP Policy Document

International Considerations
he shift in the international animal welfare and protection policy environment highlights
T
the growing recognition of animal welfare as a critical issue on the global stage.

I t is no longer viewed as peripheral but has become integral to discussions in regional
and international policy forums.

his change is underscored by the emergence of an expanding framework of
T
science-based standards, conventions, treaties, regulations, directives, and
agreements.

Key trends in this evolving landscape include:

1. Science-Based Frameworks: Policy decisions are increasingly guided by robust
s cientific research, which ensures that animal welfare measures are grounded in
evidence and best practices.
2. Global and Regional Agreements: International treaties and regional directives,
such as the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild
Fauna and Flora (CITES), the World Organisation for Animal Health (WOAH)
standards or EU directives on animal welfare, set benchmarks for practices
across borders.
3. Integration into Broader Agendas: Animal welfare is being linked with
sustainability, public health, biodiversity, and climate change, ensuring it receives
attention in broader policy contexts.
4. Stakeholder Collaboration: Governments, NGOs, scientists, and industry
players are collaborating more actively to develop and implement welfare
policies.

animaljustice.org.nz | party@animaljusticeparty.org.nz 1

---

his evolving framework not only reflects a growing ethical commitment to animals but
T
also acknowledges their role in sustainable development and human wellbeing. Global
animal protection is, however, a complex challenge requiring collaboration across
countries, cultures, and legal systems.

hile there are various treaties, conventions, and agreements addressing specific
W
aspects of animal welfare, there is no unified international instrument that broadly
regulates animal welfare across all contexts and provides holistic animal welfare
protections.

Key gaps include:

1. Limited Scope : Existing frameworks often prioritise conservation and
iodiversity rather than the welfare of individual animals. This leaves many
b
species, especially those not endangered or economically significant, without
legal protection.
2. Lack of Universal Standards and Jurisdictional Issues : Countries have
varying cultural, economic, and ethical views on animal welfare, making it difficult
to establish universally accepted standards. International frameworks may
conflict with national sovereignty, limiting their enforceability within domestic legal
systems.
3. Non-Binding Nature : Many international standards, such as the WOAH’s animal
welfare standards, are non-binding, leaving adoption and enforcement at the
discretion of individual nations.
4. Lack of Enforceability : Even binding agreements like CITES face challenges
with enforcement, as they rely on national governments to implement and
monitor compliance.
5. Species-Specific Gaps : Many frameworks focus on specific species or groups
(e.g., endangered species under CITES), leaving gaps in protection for other
animals, such as farmed or laboratory animals, despite these being the largest
groups of animals directly impacted by human activity.

elow is a proposed structure to guide the formulation of a policy to advocate for more
B
comprehensive and enforceable global animal protection frameworks:

1. Review of International Trade Law : Review New Zealand’s international trade
law and policy instruments and challenge any provisions that undermine animal
protection.

animaljustice.org.nz | party@animaljusticeparty.org.nz 2

---

2. Harmonising Standards : Creating internationally accepted benchmarks that
accommodate regional differences whilst maintaining high welfare standards for
imported animal products. As New Zealand has some of the most robust animal
welfare practices, compared to our trading partners, we have set the benchmark
for our primary industry and a framework for continuous improvement in animal
quality of life:
- AJP will campaign for uniform standards when importing animal products.
- AJP will continue to advocate for discussions with trading partners to
improve practices or find alternative suppliers.
- AJP will continue to push for a fairer and more equitable system.
- AJP will use this issue as a global platform to advocate for animals used
for agriculture.
3. Developing Binding Agreements : Evaluate international conventions and
agreements, advocate for an international treaty on animal rights, and support a
transition from voluntary guidelines to binding treaties with clear accountability
mechanisms.
4. Promoting Education and Advocacy : Building public awareness and fostering
a cultural shift toward valuing animal welfare globally.

International Considerations Policy | Created January 2025

animaljustice.org.nz | party@animaljusticeparty.org.nz 3

# Legislation and Regulation Reform for Animal Protection

> Archive note: Web text is the policy post body from animaljustice.org.nz/wp-json/wp/v2/policies; the PDF version linked from the page (if any) follows, extracted with pdftotext -layout.

## Full text (verbatim)

### Web page text

AJP supports legislation and regulation that prioritises the well-being, protection and rights of animals as sentient beings, ensuring they are not subjected to exploitation, harm or cruelty. It is imperative that animal welfare and protection legislation is adequately resourced and equipped with robust compliance monitoring, appropriate penalties and regulatory enforcement capabilities.

Animal welfare legislation should be drafted with the sole intention of recognising animal sentience and protecting animals, without influence from industries that profit from their exploitation. The principles enshrined in the Animal Welfare Act 1999 must be enforceable, without loopholes that allow industries to evade responsibility by self-regulation. Until adequate animal protection legislation is in place, AJP will also campaign to remove and prohibit exemptions and inconsistencies that allow animal cruelty to occur (for example, codes of practice for the “welfare” of farmed animals).

# Legislative Foundations

> Archive note: Web text is the policy post body from animaljustice.org.nz/wp-json/wp/v2/policies; the PDF version linked from the page (if any) follows, extracted with pdftotext -layout.

## Full text (verbatim)

### Web page text

To create a comprehensive and effective Animal Protection Policy, a new legislative framework must be established. This framework should address animal welfare, conservation, ethical treatment, and the enforcement of laws to ensure that animals are protected from cruelty and exploitation. Below is a proposed structure for legislative foundations that could guide the formulation of such a policy:

1. Define animal sentience in legislation

2. Strengthen legal protections recognising animals as sentient beings

3. Propose a new legislative framework with positive welfare obligations

4. Constitutional rights for nature: advocate for legal personhood for ecosystems and species

5. Abolish the legal classification of animals as property and grant animals legal rights

This will be achieved through dialogue, research, analysis and solutions-based reform proposals to inform legislative and policy change and to enable greater political accountability and more inclusive and just governance.

Law and policy reforms will be secured to create an animal welfare governance system that is transparent, in line with contemporary science and public expectations, and focuses on the wellbeing and protection of animals. These reforms in New Zealand will have the potential to set a precedent for the creation of large-scale change globally.

# Minimising Animal Suffering During Slaughter

> Archive note: Web text is the policy post body from animaljustice.org.nz/wp-json/wp/v2/policies; the PDF version linked from the page (if any) follows, extracted with pdftotext -layout.

## Full text (verbatim)

### Web page text

The Animal Justice Party Aotearoa NZ (AJP) is committed to protecting the rights and dignity of animals exploited in the agricultural system, including at the point of slaughter. We reject the idea that killing animals for products can ever be truly humane, as it inherently violates their right to life. While working towards the complete abolition of animal slaughter, we advocate for urgent reforms to eliminate the most egregious practices, improve transparency and enforcement in slaughter facilities, and reduce suffering where it still occurs.

AJP advocates for the elimination of all inhumane methods of slaughter, as existing practices often prioritise efficiency and profit over animal welfare. We believe that no animal should endure unnecessary pain, fear or distress at the end of their life.

# Mitigate natural threats to wild animals

> Archive note: Web text is the policy post body from animaljustice.org.nz/wp-json/wp/v2/policies; the PDF version linked from the page (if any) follows, extracted with pdftotext -layout.

## Full text (verbatim)

### Web page text

AJP recognises that wild animals often suffer from causes of natural origin. In many cases, intervention can be appropriate to protect wild animals from threats that they are not able to cope with.

There are many examples today of people and conservation agencies intervening to protect particularly endangered or charismatic species. For example, stranded whales or dolphins are often kept wet and efforts are made to refloat them; lost penguins are transported back to Antarctica; underweight yellow-eyed penguin/hoihoi chicks have been hand-reared until they can survive at sea; and following cyclone Gabrielle, wildlife stranded in mud and floodwaters were rescued. However, non-threatened and less charismatic species often suffer from similar threats. AJP wishes to see these existing efforts increased and expanded to other species. Research is also needed to understand the welfare of wild animals and how their flourishing can be ensured and legally protected.

**Key Objectives:**

1. Promote wild animal welfare science to better understand the lives of wild animals and how their flourishing and protection can be promoted.

2. Redefine the functions of the Ministry of the Environment to include the promotion of wild animal welfare.

3. Encourage other government and community agencies and local councils to consider the impacts of their policies on wild animal welfare where appropriate.

**Interim Measures:**

4. Establish protocols in local councils and environmental bodies for interventions to protect wild animals in the event of natural disasters.

5. Support volunteer groups that protect wild animals from natural threats.

6. Increase interventions to protect endangered species from natural threats.

7. Establishment of a national research institute for the study of wild animal welfare and the design and implementation of impact assessments and protection strategies.

Mitigate natural threats to wild animals
AJP recognises that wild animals often suffer from causes of natural origin. In many
cases, intervention can be appropriate to protect wild animals from threats that they are

protect particularly endangered or charismatic species. For example, stranded whales

understand the welfare of wild animals and how their flourishing can be ensured and
legally protected.
Wild animal populations are especially impacted by natural disasters. For example, the
Kaikōura earthquake disrupted marine ecosystems and seal colonies,5 while
increasingly frequent severe storms and flooding events have destroyed habitats and
nesting sites of birds like the endangered wrybill.6 Prolonged drought conditions have

# Overview – Protection of indigenous and non-indigenous wild animals

## Full text (verbatim)

### Web page text

The Animal Justice Party (AJP) recognises all wild animals (indigenous and non-indigenous) as individuals with unique needs and value. We believe that within Aotearoa New Zealand both native and introduced animals have a right to live their lives unimpeded and unharmed by human activities.

AJP recognises there can be conflicts between endemic and introduced animals, while emphasising the need for solutions that prioritise compassion and protection. We reject divisive language, hunting and the glorification of trapping and killing animals for conservation purposes. Fundamentally, wild animals deserve the same rights to liberty, health, and freedom from harm as domesticated animals, and this should be reflected in law by specifically including them under the protection of the Animal Welfare Act, rather than considering them “pests” for eradication.

**Key Objectives:**

1. **Use compassionate approaches to manage introduced species**. Implement non-lethal, humane and species-specific methods to address challenges posed by introduced animals while recognising their right to live without unnecessary harm.

2. **Protect and restore natural habitats.** Preserve and enhance the environments where wild animals thrive, using whole-ecosystem approaches that benefit both native and introduced species.

3. **Shield wild animals from human-caused harms**. Mandate practices that minimise the negative impacts of human activities, development and pollution on wild animals and their habitats.

# Pet Refuge Support for Domestic Violence Survivors

> Archive note: Web text is the policy post body from animaljustice.org.nz/wp-json/wp/v2/policies; the PDF version linked from the page (if any) follows, extracted with pdftotext -layout.

## Full text (verbatim)

### Web page text

The AJP is committed to eliminating barriers that prevent people from escaping domestic violence, recognising that the safety of beloved companion animals is often the deciding factor that keeps victims trapped in dangerous situations. We acknowledge that New Zealand has the highest rate of domestic violence among OECD countries, combined with one of the highest rates of pet ownership globally, yet we have only one pet refuge service operating in Auckland. We propose establishing a nationwide network of pet refuge facilities to ensure no family stays in danger because they cannot safely care for their animals.\
\
**Key Objectives:**

1. Advocacy for stronger legal penalties for those who threaten or harm animals as tools of domestic control.
2. Establish a nationwide network of pet refuge facilities ensuring every region has accessible, safe temporary housing for companion animals affected by domestic violence
3. Provide comprehensive support services including veterinary care, behavioural rehabilitation, and trauma recovery for animals who have experienced abuse
4. Create integrated referral systems connecting domestic violence services with pet refuge facilities to streamline support for families
5. Fund ongoing operations to ensure pet refuge services remain free for families escaping violence, removing financial barriers to safety
6. Establish a 24/7 emergency hotline for immediate pet refuge placement needs and rapid response protocols for situations where pets are in immediate danger
7. Develop and implement a comprehensive animal trauma rehabilitation programme that includes specialized behavioral therapy for abused animals, staff training in trauma recognition, and integrated therapeutic interventions that support the healing of both human survivors and their companion animals.

# Transition to a plant-based economy

> Archive note: Web text is the policy post body from animaljustice.org.nz/wp-json/wp/v2/policies; the PDF version linked from the page (if any) follows, extracted with pdftotext -layout.

## Full text (verbatim)

### Web page text

Policy category summary: The AJP is committed to transitioning to a wholly plant-based economy. We recognise that in Aotearoa New Zealand our economic model is currently deeply reliant on the use of animals for food, products and exports. And that for many New Zealanders there is a strong historic and cultural connection to animal farming. But this is now destroying our wildlife, polluting our water and changing our climate, as well as inflicting unnecessary suffering on millions of sentient beings. This model is inherently risky as an on-going economic strategy, as new technologies, consumer preferences, societal concerns and changes in global trade threaten to reduce long-term demand for animal products alongside increasing regulatory burdens.\

We appreciate this transition will take time, and that it must happen alongside financial and transitional support for farmers and the development of attractive and affordable alternatives for both farmers and consumers. There are, however, steps we can take now that will make a huge positive impact. These include banning factory farming, tougher laws, regulations and enforcement mechanisms, supporting farm livelihood transitions, supporting innovation in food tech, and promoting and incentivising more compassionate and healthy dietary choices.\

Shifting to a plant-based economy is the single most impactful change to reduce animal suffering, whilst addressing many of our most urgent economic, social and environmental challenges.

# Policy Summary

> Archive note: Web text is the policy post body from animaljustice.org.nz/wp-json/wp/v2/policies; the PDF version linked from the page (if any) follows, extracted with pdftotext -layout.

## Full text (verbatim)

### Web page text

Animals can’t vote, but their lives are shaped by decisions made in parliament every day. That’s why we exist: to bring animals into the conversation, and to show that what’s good for animals is usually good for people and the planet too. This is a plain-language summary of what we’re campaigning for. It’s more detail than our [election manifesto](https://animaljustice.org.nz/election-2026/election-manifesto/), and much shorter than our full policy platform, which sets out the evidence, legislation and reasoning behind every commitment.

We know change takes time, and that farmers, workers and communities need real support to get there. Nothing here is about punishing anyone. It’s about building something better, together.

### Ending the cruellest farming and fishing practices

New Zealand’s animal welfare rules are meant to protect animals, but in practice they’re often inadequate, poorly enforced, or simply ignored. We want to ban the most intensive and harmful practices first: intensive winter grazing, breeding fast-growing chickens, live exports, mutilations, and bottom trawling. Longer term, we support a full transition away from animal farming, done fairly and with proper support for the people who currently depend on it.

**We’ll push for:**

- An urgent ban on the cruellest, most intensive farming and fishing methods
- A funded transition scheme so farmers can move to plant-based or other work on their own terms
- Tighter standards and stronger enforcement of the Animal Welfare Act

### Recognising animals as sentient, not property

Animals in New Zealand are currently classed as property under the law, with no enforceable right to a decent life. We want animal sentience properly written into legislation, not just mentioned in passing, and the outdated property classification abolished.

**We’ll push for:**

- Legal recognition of animals as sentient beings, with real protections attached
- An end to codes of practice that let industries sidestep the Animal Welfare Act
- A future legal framework that treats animals as individuals, not commodities

### Making healthy, plant-based food the easy choice

Right now, animal-based foods dominate menus in schools, hospitals and other public places, even where health alone should point the other way. We want plant-based meals to be the default option everywhere they’re served publicly, clearer labelling so people know what’s really in their food, and GST removed from fruit, vegetables, legumes and nuts.

**We’ll push for:**

- Plant-based defaults in public institutions, with other options still available
- Fair, transparent food labelling, including clear health and environmental information
- GST removed from core plant-based foods to make healthy eating more affordable

### An independent Commissioner for Animals

Animal welfare policy is currently overseen by the same government agency responsible for growing farming exports. That’s a genuine conflict of interest. We want an independent Commissioner for Animals, similar to the Commissioner for Children, with real power to hold agencies to account and champion animal protection nationally.

**We’ll push for:**

- An independent Commissioner with investigative and enforcement powers
- Proper funding for animal welfare research and policy
- Accountability for the agencies currently responsible for enforcement

### Fixing our pound and shelter system

Thousands of healthy, adoptable dogs are euthanised in council pounds every year, often simply because of overcrowding, short reclaim windows, or fees families can’t afford. We want rehoming to be the default nationwide, not the exception, and euthanasia used only ever as a genuine last resort.

**We’ll push for:**

- Transparent public reporting from every council on outcomes for impounded animals
- Fairer, more flexible reclaim processes and fees
- Funded foster networks and widespread access to desexing

### Smarter, more compassionate conservation

We care deeply about protecting native wildlife, and we know introduced species do cause real harm. But we don’t believe mass killing is the answer, especially for cats, where there’s often no reliable way to tell a community cat from a wild-living one. Habitat loss is the biggest driver of native species decline, and that’s where solutions should start.

**We’ll push for:**

- An end to lethal, poison-based control methods for cats
- Investment in desexing, Trap-Neuter-Return, and habitat restoration
- Conservation policy guided by evidence, not by fear or blame

### Veterinary care people can actually afford

For many families, a sudden vet bill means an impossible choice. We want veterinary care treated as essential, not a luxury: GST removed from vet services, more publicly funded clinics in underserved regions, and funded desexing and wildlife care so access doesn’t depend on income or postcode.

**We’ll push for:**

- GST removed from all veterinary services
- A national network of publicly funded and mobile veterinary clinics
- Guaranteed funding for injured wildlife and desexing programmes

### Getting money out of politics

Industries that profit from animal exploitation have far more access to political decision-makers than ordinary people do. We want donation caps, real-time lobbying transparency, and cooling-off periods so industry leaders can’t move straight into government roles overseeing their own sector.

**We’ll push for:**

- Lower donation limits and stronger disclosure rules
- Public, real-time reporting of lobbying meetings with government
- Cooling-off periods between industry leadership and ministerial roles

### Making sure AI is used responsibly around animals

Artificial intelligence already manages hundreds of thousands of farmed animals in New Zealand, through automated monitoring, feeding and even virtual fencing, with no law written to account for it. We want animal welfare built into how these systems are designed and regulated, before harmful practices become locked in.

**We’ll push for:**

- Animal welfare requirements written into AI governance and the Animal Welfare Act
- A ban on AI systems that increase confinement or remove meaningful human oversight
- Independent validation of any AI system marketed as improving welfare

### Recognising companion animals as family

For many people, a companion animal is part of the family. We want statutory bereavement leave for the loss of a companion animal, and short paid leave when a new animal joins a household, so people aren’t forced to use sick leave to grieve or settle a new pet in.

**We’ll push for:**

- Up to five days’ statutory bereavement leave for the loss of a companion animal
- Up to three days’ leave when a new companion animal joins the family
- Emergency leave provisions that cover urgent animal care alongside human care

*This is a summary. Every commitment above is backed by detailed policy, evidence and legislative proposals in our full 2026 policy platform. If you’d like the short version of why we exist, start with our* [*election manifesto*](https://animaljustice.org.nz/election-2026/election-manifesto/)*.*\
*[This summary can be downloaded as a PDF.](https://drive.google.com/file/d/17bmtPsoUKDi05ugU50QkI7xTFoEgMTXh/view?usp=sharing)*

The AJP proposes to implement an absolute ban on the worst animal farming and fishing
practices.

We believe that all forms of animal farming and fishing should be phased out. There are steps
we can take now to eliminate the cruellest and most intensive practices, helping to move
towards our longer term objectives.

New Zealand’s Animal Welfare Act sets out obligations on people in charge of animals
(including farmed animals) to meet an animal’s physical, health and behavioural needs, and to
alleviate pain or distress. However in practice this does not happen. Minimum standards
contained in regulations and Codes of Welfare are inadequate, often out-dated and reviewed
according to the whims of Ministers, and frequently these minimum standards are not met. In
addition, monitoring and enforcement is stretched - the Ministry for Primary Industries (whose
main goals are productivity, export opportunities and food safety1) employs around 30
inspectors for more than 160 million farmed animals.2

We would undertake an urgent review of existing legislation, regulations and Codes of Welfare
and update these to strengthen a wide-range of requirements and minimum standards. This
would result in the following activities being banned:
- Intensive winter grazing (including feedlots and permanent indoor housing systems)
- Breeding fast-growing chickens
- Intensive animal farming
- Live exports and long-haul animal transport
- Mutilations
- Bottom and conventional trawling

For more detail on steps the AJP would take to raise standards for farmed animals, see our
policies on Protecting the Rights of Farmed Animals and Ensuring the Welfare and Protection of
Marine Life.

The AJP believes there is no place in our society for intensive animal farming and industrial
fishing and that these activities should be banned with urgency. This will be a critical step in the
transition to a plant-based economy, and will result in less animal suffering.

2. Strengthening the Animal Welfare Act
(Sentience & Rights)
2 key policies support this

Legislative Foundations
To create a comprehensive and effective Animal Protection Policy, a new legislative framework
must be established. This framework should address animal welfare, conservation, ethical
treatment, and the enforcement of laws to ensure that animals are protected from cruelty and
exploitation. Below is a proposed structure for legislative foundations that could guide the
formulation of such a policy:

1. Define animal sentience in legislation
2. Strengthen legal protections recognising animals as sentient beings
3. Propose a new legislative framework with positive welfare obligations
4. Constitutional rights for nature: advocate for legal personhood for ecosystems and species
5. Abolish the legal classification of animals as property and grant animals legal rights

This will be achieved through dialogue, research, analysis and solutions-based reform
proposals to inform legislative and policy change and to enable greater political accountability
and more inclusive and just governance.

Law and policy reforms will be secured to create an animal welfare governance system that is
transparent, in line with contemporary science and public expectations, and focuses on the
wellbeing and protection of animals. These reforms in New Zealand will have the potential to
set a precedent for the creation of large-scale change globally.

Sentience

The acknowledgement of animals as sentient in an amendment to the Animal Welfare Act 1999
(the “Act”) in 2015 was the first of its kind in a common law jurisdiction. However, its location in
the long title is telling – it simply states what the Act is about and is not defined or incorporated
into the offence sections. The New Zealand Government has openly stated it is a “symbolic”
change only and creates no legal or enforceable responsibility.3

Property

Domestic and wild animals are extremely vulnerable members of New Zealand society, and
therefore require stringent legal protection. They are entitled to the same level of protection and

rights under the law as humans and it is the antithesis of social justice that their vulnerability is
not adequately legally protected.

Currently classed as the property of humans, animals have no legal rights, and therefore require
AJP’s advocacy, to ensure that they receive the full protection of the law.

Interim measures, while we work towards legislative change, include:

- Communication with politicians to secure reform commitments, writing submissions and
reports to Select Committees, the National Animal Welfare Advisory Committee
(NAWAC) and the National Animal Ethics Advisory Committee (NAEAC) on Acts,
Regulations, Codes of Animal Welfare and other laws and policies affecting animals

- Reviewing current animal welfare laws and providing proposals to ensure modern
animal welfare policies and legislation, using available “best practice” models, and

- Drafting national strategies, regulations and/or codes of practice as necessary

- Developing deterrent penalties and more effective enforcement systems

Legislation and Regulation Reform for Animal
Protection
AJP supports legislation and regulation that prioritises the well-being, protection and rights of
animals as sentient beings, ensuring they are not subjected to exploitation, harm or cruelty. It is
imperative that animal welfare and protection legislation is adequately resourced and equipped
with robust compliance monitoring, appropriate penalties and regulatory enforcement
capabilities.

Animal welfare legislation should be drafted with the sole intention of recognising animal
sentience and protecting animals, without influence from industries that profit from their
exploitation. The principles enshrined in the Animal Welfare Act 1999 must be enforceable,
without loopholes that allow industries to evade responsibility by self-regulation. Until adequate
animal protection legislation is in place, AJP will also campaign to remove and prohibit
exemptions and inconsistencies that allow animal cruelty to occur (for example, codes of
practice for the “welfare” of farmed animals).

AJP supports a legal framework that reflects a societal commitment to valuing, protecting and
respecting animals, fostering responsible and compassionate treatment in all contexts and
industries. Without stringent, and enforceable, legal protection, animals remain vulnerable to
cruelty and exploitation, their welfare jeopardised by profit-driven motives. Empowering and
resourcing authorities to share information and enforce legislation and regulations is essential,
ensuring individuals and organisations are held accountable for infringements. Championing
animal-centric legislation paves the way to a more just and humane society where positive
animal welfare4 is legally recognised and animals are granted by the law the dignity and
protection they deserve.

Animal welfare has become a global concern, which first requires adequate regulation at a
national level.

There is an urgent need to overhaul New Zealand’s animal welfare governance system to
enable a paradigm shift in the value of animals and human responsibility towards them.5 It is
crucial that improved animal welfare and protection is prioritised by legislative reform and
strengthened regulatory enforcement to avoid ongoing exploitation and harm at human hands.

4

experience of predominantly positive mental states and the development of competence and resilience”
https://royalsocietypublishing.org/doi/epdf/10.1098/rsbl.2024.0382.

animals is extremely, or very, important to three in four New Zealanders.6

A Horizon Research poll conducted nationwide in June 2023 shows that 90% of New
Zealanders believe it is important to protect the welfare of animals farmed in New Zealand and
71% agree that the Government should do more to promote greater awareness of farmed

Purpose and Objectives of the Animal Protection Policy

AJP advocates for a new legal framework that recognises animals' right to live without suffering
harm from humans and ensures that their lives and well-being are protected by the
advancement of New Zealand’s legal system.

The core purpose of the animal protection policy is:

- To safeguard the welfare and well-being of animals
- To promote humane treatment of animals in all sectors (agriculture, entertainment,
research, etc.)
- To reduce instances of animal cruelty, neglect, and exploitation
- To foster public awareness and ethical responsibility regarding animal rights
- To protect endangered species and their habitats

AJP opposes all exploitation of animals and advocates for their ethical treatment in all
human-animal interactions. We stand against all practices that subject animals to stress and/or
harm. Our vision is for a society that places value on the well-being of animals and prohibits all
practices that exploit or harm them.

Our advocacy entails the development and promotion of policies that end harmful practices and
legally protect animals. Holistically, AJP policies promote a vision of a world where animals can
thrive in ways that respect their inherent needs and behaviours.

implementation, monitoring and enforcement of animal welfare and protection laws, to
coordinate and lead animal protection efforts (see separate policy Commissioner for
Animals).
2. Abolish the classification of animals as property and introduce consistent legislation that
defines and acknowledges animal sentience, ensuring legal protection from harm

3. AJP Overview for a Plant-Based Economic
Transition
The AJP is committed to transitioning Aotearoa New Zealand to a wholly plant-based economy,
where animal farming has been eliminated and no animals are used for economic gain. We
acknowledge the role of Māori as tangata whenua (people of the land) and recognise the
importance of kaitiakitanga, manaakitanga, and tino rangatiratanga in shaping a just transition.
This transformation must be guided by partnership with iwi and hapū, respecting mātauranga
Māori and supporting Māori economic aspirations through sustainable land-use practices. We
want to create a more prosperous, sustainable and secure economy that is underpinned by
compassion for all.

A transformation approach is required. We recognise that our current economic model is deeply
reliant on the exploitation of animals for food, other products and exports. And that for many
New Zealanders, including both Māori and Pākehā, have strong cultural and historical ties to
animal farming. For Māori, these ties are often rooted in whakapapa and a deep ancestral
relationship with the land, while for Pākehā, the connection has developed more recently
through settler-colonial history and generations of farming. Understanding these different
histories is essential as we navigate a just transition away from animal-based systems.

However, our current agricultural model has significant environmental impacts, including
biodiversity loss, freshwater degradation and greenhouse gas emissions, while also inflicting
unnecessary suffering on millions of sentient beings. It is also inherently risky as an on-going
economic strategy, as environmental tipping points, new technologies, consumer preferences,
societal concerns and changes in global trade threaten to reduce long term demand for animal
products alongside increasing regulatory burdens. New Zealand is currently in a ‘chaos and
emergence’ phase where existing systems are being questioned and new alternatives are
emerging.9

We appreciate transitioning to a plant-based economy will take time, and that to be sustainable
it must happen alongside support for farmers and the development of attractive and affordable
alternatives for both farmers and consumers alike. There are, however, steps we can take now
that will make a huge positive impact. These include banning factory farming, tougher laws,
regulations and enforcement mechanisms, supporting farm livelihood transitions, engaging with
Māori leadership, supporting innovation in food tech, and promoting and incentivising more
compassionate and healthy dietary choices. He ara kai pai ake mō te tinana, te wairua me te
taiao (healthier and more sustainable food pathways for the body, spirit, and environment).

Shifting to a plant-based economy is the single most impactful change we can make to reduce
animal suffering whilst also addressing many of our most urgent economic, social and

Four overarching objectives
Our policy for transitioning to a plant-based economy is focussed on shifting away from animal
agriculture and animal-based foods, and replacing these with sustainable and compassionate
alternatives. It is centered around four objectives, each supported by specific proposals:

1. Increase consumption of plant-based foods. Use a variety of policy levers to increase
consumption and market demand for healthier, kinder, more sustainable food options that
align with kai ora (healthy food) principles

2. Use land and water sustainably and compassionately. Use regulation and incentives
to shift from animal to plant-based farming and other sustainable land and water uses.

3. Support farmers, workers and communities to transition. Engage and collaborate to
support a fair and inclusive transition with economic opportunities for all.

4. Develop long-term economic alternatives. Invest in new technologies, products and
markets- to replace animal farming and provide prosperity and jobs.

To achieve these objectives, the Government should urgently develop a National Action Plan to
implement the proposals set out in this document. While animal agriculture currently remains
economically significant, there are both environmental and market pressures that suggest the
potential for transition. Given this context, transitioning to a plant-based economy should be a
national priority and the Government must play a critical role in making this happen.

The ‘value’ of animal exploitation to New Zealand’s economy
Despite its well documented negative impacts, animal agriculture occupies a prominent position
in New Zealand's economy and national identity. While agriculture is often described as the
foundation of New Zealand's economic prosperity, contributing to GDP, exports and
employment, the combined agricultural and fishing sectors represent approximately just 5% of
GDP.
The dairy sector accounts for 3% of this (>$11BN) and provides an estimated 55,000 jobs.
Dried milk powder is one of our most significant export commodities, with the dairy export trade
earning around $1 in every $4 of New Zealand’s foreign exchange income.10 However, the
expansion of dairy farming has led to economic vulnerabilities, including significant trade
imbalances and a high reliance on imports. It has also resulted in environmental challenges,
particularly regarding water quality.
Shifting away from these industries will be a significant challenge. New Zealand's agricultural
identity, established during colonisation as the dairy farm of the British Empire, continues to
shape its global economic position and national politics. A just transition requires redressing
these injustices by prioritising Māori leadership in land-use decision-making, ensuring economic
benefits are equitably distributed, and honoring Māori aspirations for self-determined food and
land systems. The close alignment between agricultural and state interests has historically been

It is imperative that we begin the transition to a plant-based economy with urgency. This is

opportunities to diversify, build resilience, food security, and secure long-term economic
prosperity.

Impacts on animals
Millions of farmed animals are slaughtered in New Zealand every year. Data from StatsNZ
reveals that around 27 million ‘livestock’ were killed in 2023, including 21 million lambs and
sheep, 4.6 million cows and 600,000 pigs, heifers, bulls, steers and calves. In addition, it is
estimated that 120 million chickens are slaughtered annually.12 Between 953 million to 5.94
billion wild-fish were killed for food (2016, Our World in Data), this estimate does not include
unrecorded fish capture, such as bycatch and discards. Farmed fish, including salmon, mussels
and oysters are killed in their hundreds of millions annually.
However, the impact on farmed animals cannot be captured by numbers alone. Poor conditions
and cruel practices are widespread. New Zealand’s animal welfare laws are inadequate even
when they are adhered to, but in practice we know that legal minimum standards are often not
met - with negative consequences for the sentient beings that are powerless to resist. Whilst
high welfare standards are better than low / no standards, ultimately the only ethically justifiable
course of action is to phase out animal farming altogether.

Impacts on the environment
Animal farming is a major driver of climate change. Globally it is responsible for between 10%
and 20% of global GHG emissions, and it is one of the leading causes of deforestation.13 48.6%
of New Zealand’s total emissions in 2022 came from sheep and cattle, of which 25.7% was from
dairy cattle, 12.4% from sheep and 10.5% from beef cattle.14 The inefficiency of producing food
through animals also means that shifting to plant-based foods has the potential to release large
tracts of land for ecosystem restoration and reforestation - critical parts of the solution to climate

Animal farming also has severe effects on rivers and waterways - degrading ecosystems, killing
animals and reducing water quality. Many Māori communities bear the brunt of these effects,
with degraded rivers, pollution, and land-use pressures disproportionately affecting Māori land
and resources. In New Zealand the Ministry for the Environment has estimated that 95% of
waterways whose catchments included areas of farmland exceed guideline values for water
turbidity or dissolved nutrients; and that 24% of total river length in those catchments had E. coli
levels that were greater than would be expected under natural conditions.17 Algal growth in
streams and rivers - caused by fertiliser runoff - is widespread, leading to impairment of water
for swimming, drinking and fish and other wildlife.

Impacts on human health

The rise in consumption of animal products over the past decades correlates with increasing
rates of chronic disease in New Zealand and globally. Research demonstrates clear
associations between high consumption of animal products and adverse health outcomes.
Specifically, red and processed meat consumption is linked to increased risk of colorectal
cancer, with the World Health Organisation classifying processed meat as a Group 1
carcinogen, alongside alcohol and tobacco.18 High consumption of animal products is
associated with increased risk of cardiometabolic diseases, certain cancers, and all-cause
mortality.19
Conversely, scientific evidence consistently shows that plant-based diets play both preventative
and therapeutic roles in managing major chronic conditions including cardiovascular disease,
type 2 diabetes, obesity, and certain cancers. Studies indicate that replacing animal-based
foods (such as red meat, processed meat, eggs, and dairy) with plant-based alternatives
(including legumes, nuts, whole grains, and olive oil) improves cardiometabolic health
outcomes.20
Plant-based diets are demonstrated to be safe and nutritionally adequate across all life stages,
from pregnancy and lactation through to elderly care, when appropriately planned.. Beyond
individual health benefits, transitioning toward plant-based agriculture could significantly reduce
the growing burden on our healthcare system. Shifting toward predominantly plant-based diets
is not only feasible but could substantially improve public health outcomes, reduce healthcare

Objective 1: Increase consumption of plant-based foods

Make plant-based foods the default option for
public institutions
The AJP proposes to increase the availability of plant-based foods in schools, hospitals and
other public institutions and events - by making nutritious plant-based foods the default option.

At the current time our public institutions offer little in the way of alternatives to animal-based
foods, even in settings like hospitals where health and nutrition alone should be a strong motive
for change. Increasing the availability and visibility of delicious plant-based foods is a low-cost
high-impact way of increasing demand for these products and supporting more sustainable,
healthy and compassionate consumer choices. This in turn has the potential to create a ripple
effect beyond public institutions by influencing broader community eating habits and private
organisations.

Similar initiatives have been implemented with success elsewhere in the world. For example in
New York in 2022 plant-based meals were made the default option across 11 public hospitals.
The initiative was introduced to address both health and environmental objectives. By early
2024 over 1.2 million plant-based meals had been served with an 80%+ satisfaction rate, and
with discharged patients receiving a free booklet of plant-based recipes to try at home. This also
led to an estimated 36% reduction in planet-heating greenhouse gas pollution, pointing to the
contribution these initiatives can make towards organisational carbon reduction efforts.34

To implement these initiatives in Aotearoa, we will also encourage the use of rooftops,
courtyards, and other green spaces in public institutions to create edible gardens. These
gardens can supply fresh, seasonal ingredients directly to institutional kitchens - the ultimate in
"farm to plate" - while also providing educational and therapeutic value. Patients, students, staff,
and visitors observing or participating in these gardens may be inspired to grow food at home,
creating a ripple effect beyond the institution. Globally, edible landscapes are being successfully
used in hospitals,35 schools,36 and community centres37 to reconnect people with food, promote
sustainability and enhance wellbeing.
To implement these initiatives effectively, we will work with hauora Māori (Māori health
providers), tohunga kai (food experts), and food suppliers to develop culturally appropriate
guidelines and menus that prioritise plant-based options. We will engage with communities to
cultivate buy-in and develop solutions that reflect the needs of all New Zealanders.

Ensure fair and transparent labelling
The AJP proposes to mandate fair and transparent food labelling that provides information
about the environmental, health and animal welfare impacts of food and drink products.

At the current time very little information is provided to consumers about the impacts of the food
and drink products they buy. Even when there is strong scientific evidence - for example that
processed red meats cause cancer - this is not communicated on packaging, in contrast to
other harmful products like tobacco. Furthermore, many of the marketing terms used on food
and drink products are not standardised (such as ‘natural’ and ‘less dairy’) - and thus can be
misleading to consumers.

By introducing a new mandatory system of labelling we will ensure that consumers have access
to the information they need to make more sustainable, healthier and compassionate choices.
This will also support producers who achieve higher standards and help to drive a broader
transformation of food supply chains.

Looking internationally, there are examples of good-practice approaches to labelling that
communicate information to consumers in a simple, transparent and high impact way. For
example in the UK a red-amber-green traffic light system is used to show nutritional information
such as levels of salts, fats and sugars. Research has found that this type of mandatory
labelling can be effective in encouraging healthier consumer choices.38

The AJP believes that consumers have the right to information about the health, animal welfare
and environmental impacts of the food and drink products they buy, and that standardised, fair
and transparent labelling has an important role to play.

Key Objectives:
1. Adopt a nutrition-based traffic-light labelling system for food and drink products.
2. Mandate the use of clear warnings of health risks where robust evidence exists e.g.
cancer warnings on processed red meats as per the World Health Organisation
rankings.39
3. Introduce greenhouse gas emission labelling on all food and drink products.
4. Develop standardised definitions and require mandatory labelling for terms such as
‘vegan’, ‘plant-based’ and related.
5. Ban the use of misleading terms such as ‘less dairy’.

Introduce plant-based eating initiatives and
improve guidelines
The AJP proposes to launch a range of plant-based, healthy eating initiatives that reduce harm
to animals by promoting the consumption of healthy plant-based foods and decreasing
consumption of animal-based foods. While improving public health is a valuable outcome, our
primary focus is on preventing animal suffering through dietary change. These initiatives will be
based on the best-available science, and communicate information in ways that promote
transparency and inspire change.

New Zealand's food environment poses challenges for promoting healthier, plant-based
choices. While the national dietary guidelines (last updated 2020) make some positive
recommendations around plant proteins and limiting red meat, they maintain a strong emphasis
on dairy products, likely reflecting industry influence. Educational initiatives like ‘Garden to
Table’ demonstrate the potential for teaching children about growing and preparing fresh food,
but operate in only a fraction of schools due to limited government funding.

Meanwhile, the public faces a constant barrage of meat-heavy fast food marketing, with major
chains dominating the advertising landscape through sports sponsorship, outdoor advertising
and prime-time TV spots. Children in particular are vulnerable targets for food companies, as
they struggle to distinguish marketing from fact. While adults are also susceptible to marketing
influence, children represent both current customers through their impact on household
purchasing decisions and valuable future customers. Adults ultimately control food budgets, but
research shows children significantly influence family food choices, making them strategic
marketing targets despite not having direct purchasing power themselves.40 The constant flow
of advertising makes it virtually impossible for young people to avoid unhealthy food marketing,
effectively normalising unhealthy consumption patterns.

First, we will launch public media campaigns to build awareness about the health benefits of
plant-based foods and the animal welfare concerns associated with animal products. These
campaigns will disseminate recipes and information on how to cook nutritious plant-based
meals, highlight ethical issues with animal-based foods, and reflect the diversity of New Zealand
society and current health inequalities.

Second, we will review and update New Zealand’s dietary guidelines to align with the latest
science, including the negative impacts of many animal-based foods. We will ensure it includes
guidelines for wholly plant-based diets and clearly articulates the evidence of the benefits these
can bring. In recent years many countries have amended their dietary guidelines to increasingly

Improve access to nutritious food
The AJP proposes to improve access to nutritious food for all New Zealanders through a
package of policy measures. While improving access to healthy food is a valuable outcome, our
primary focus is on preventing animal suffering through dietary change. These measures will
reduce costs, improve access to plant-based foods, support communities to take a lead role,
and tackle inequalities and health disparities.

Food access inequities exist across Aotearoa, disproportionately affecting Māori communities.46
Lower-income areas often have a higher concentration of fast food outlets and fewer fresh food
retailers, while transport barriers and distance to supermarkets create additional challenges,
particularly in rural areas.

Many communities rely on local dairies (convenience stores) which typically stock limited fresh
food at higher prices. These access issues are compounded by the high cost of healthy food.
Fresh fruit and vegetables are notably expensive with significant seasonal price fluctuations.
Studies of healthy food baskets consistently show that eating according to nutrition guidelines
requires a substantial portion of a low-income household's budget, while processed and
energy-dense foods remain cheaper per calorie than fresh, nutritious options.

New Zealanders are currently not eating the recommended servings of fruit and vegetables. In
2023/24, 47.1% adults ate the recommended amount of fruit and only 9.1% ate the
recommended amount of vegetables per day. For children aged 2 to 14 years the figures are
70.5% and 8.2% respectively47.
Food insecurity, “insufficient money or resources for a healthy diet; uncertainty about the ability
to obtain food; skipping meals or running out of food occasionally”,48 can lead to an average
educational achievement lag of up to four years for New Zealand teenagers,49 and poor health
outcomes and development difficulties for children, with potentially life-long impacts.50 In
2023/24 rates of food insecurity were higher in households where children were Māori, Pacific,
disabled, or living in the most deprived neighbourhoods.51

Healthy and sustainable food must be the most affordable options for households, and food
environments need to be actively re-shaped. We will:

The AJP seeks to address the environmental harm caused by agricultural practices while
supporting farmers to transition to more sustainable and plant-based alternatives. Through a
combination of regulatory reform, targeted taxation and funding mechanisms, we will create a
path forward that ensures polluters pay for the damage they cause. However, this will be no
substitute for action which other AJP policies will drive in order to reduce and eliminate the
pollution.

Animal farming is a major polluter in Aotearoa, on land and at sea. It is responsible for a 48.6%
of our planet-warming greenhouse gas emissions.58 It also causes effluent and fertiliser run-off
which is polluting our seas and rivers, making many of our waterways unfit for aquatic life as
well as for human swimming and drinking. Nutrient enrichment, from fish farm releases, leads to
eutrophication, promoting excessive algae growth that depletes oxygen levels and harms
marine ecosystems. Additionally, animal farming has resulted in the destruction of much needed
habitats for endangered species. This pollution is allowed to occur largely unchecked.
Regulations are insufficiently stringent, often ignored and rarely enforced.

The huge costs from this pollution are not borne by the polluter - the animal farming industry -
but by nature and society at large. This is in effect a subsidy for one of the dirtiest industries in
the country.

One of the most urgent measures needed is to include agriculture into an Emissions Trading
Scheme (ETS). We would adopt the Climate Change Commission’s advice that the current NZ
ETS should focus on fossil fuel emissions. A separate, new cap-and-trade ETS for biogenic
emissions (including forestry) should be established, which lowers gross methane emissions to
agreed long-term flow.59 This should be implemented as quickly as possible. We will also set
separate gross (total emissions produced) and net (emissions after offsets like forestry are

Provide financial incentives for good
environmental practices
The AJP will support more sustainable and compassionate uses of land and water through
financial incentives and regulatory reform. We will create a new Fund for Environmental and
Agricultural Transformation (FEAT) to support farm transitions, reduce pollution and harm, and
protect and restore natural habitats.

At the current time there are insufficient regulatory and economic incentives for farmers, fishers
and land managers to look after land and water sustainably. Initially funding for the Fund for
Environmental and Agricultural Transformation would occur by implementing the “polluter pays”
principle. Income would be raised from the biogenic Emissions Trading Scheme and the true
cost accounting of environmental impacts via pollution taxes. Examples of activities that will be
supported through this fund include:
- Support for farmers to shift towards plant-based farming systems and other sustainable
land uses (see our Farm Transition Scheme proposals).
- Tax breaks and grants for plant-based farming, including diversified, veganic farming
approaches that use regenerative, permaculture and natural principles to restore soil and
ecosystems, enhance food security and provide nutrient-dense foods.
- Payments for farmers who adopt practices that restore ecosystems and natural habitats,
promote biodiversity, enhance soil health, reduce nutrient run-off and pesticide use, and
build natural flood defences and resilience to climate change.
- Auditing and enforcement to ensure practices are enduring.
- Increased funding for marine reserves and marine habitat protection schemes.

In addition we will review and strengthen regulations to encourage the maintenance and
enhancement of natural ecosystems. National Policy Statements (NPS) would continue to set
the high-level policy direction, alongside National Environmental Standards, coupled with
flexible compliance mechanisms that accommodate different land uses and regional conditions
(Regional Policy Statements) without undermining the national goals.

Many other countries around the world have implemented schemes that offer financial
incentives for better environmental outcomes in the agricultural sector. Examples include the
UK’s Environmental Land Management Scheme (based on the principle of “public money for
public goods”) and the conditionality standards and eco-schemes under the EU Common
Agricultural Policy. In the Netherlands, 25 billion Euros has been budgeted to support herd
reduction to address water pollution from agricultural wastes.60 Whilst these programmes are far
from perfect, they offer different models and lessons to help inform the design of schemes in

Objective 3: Support farmers, workers and communities to transition

Introduce a farm transition scheme
The AJP proposes to create a new national scheme that provides direct support to animal
farmers who wish to transition to plant farming and other economic activities. This farmer-led,
government-supported initiative will build momentum and knowledge on viable approaches for
diversifying beyond animal farming, while recognising and honouring the unique considerations
of Māori land and agricultural practices.

At the current time there are practical, financial and cultural barriers that prevent animal farmers
from diversifying their activities and moving away from animal farming.61 Whilst there are
examples in Aotearoa of farmers making positive changes, they are fighting against the tide.
The system as it stands is stacked against them, legacy policies and institutional structures
favour incumbent systems,62 and current adaptation strategies often reinforce unsustainable,
high-input systems.63

There are also knowledge gaps in terms of the most economically viable, sustainable
alternatives to animal farming, both in New Zealand and elsewhere in the world, which need
addressing urgently as the global food system changes.

However, this concentration into dairying in particular, is a relatively recent phenomenon. Many
regions were previously much more diverse, growing crops as well as animals. Pig farming in
this country is facing significant challenges as farmers struggle to comply with new regulations
and compete with floods of cheap overseas pork from countries with lower animal welfare
standards. Similarly, sheep farmers are confronting problems due to climate change-induced
weather patterns, an aging farmer population, and decreasing value of mutton and lamb
exports. The reluctance of younger generations to enter these industries—including cattle
farming—represents a further challenge. These signs point to a broader decline in animal
agriculture, creating both urgency and opportunity for transition. The concentration of rural
production into animal agriculture means there is great opportunity for diversification in the
future.

Support for rural economies to thrive without
