The AJP will provide support to rural communities to develop and sustain strong local
economies that do not rely on animal agriculture and that are resilient to a rapidly changing
global context. We propose to introduce financial and other types of support to local councils,
community groups and businesses to shift towards economic activities that foster prosperity and
sustainability, and that deliver a just transition to a plant-based economy.

Given the current reliance of many of New Zealand’s rural communities on animal agriculture for
their economic well-being, it is essential that the transition to a plant-based economy includes a
proactive and locally-led approach to protecting rural economies; this would occur via the
proposed Farm Transition Advisory Network. Currently the interconnected web of services
creates a self-reinforcing economic ecosystem where feed suppliers, veterinary services,
equipment manufacturers, pharmaceutical companies and processing facilities are all
dependent on continuing intensive animal production, while also generating environmental and
social externalities that are often not fully accounted for in the economics of the system.64

There is an opportunity to develop more diversified local economies that are resilient to global
changes in climate, trade, technology and consumer demand. Potential economic opportunities
include horticulture, plant-based farming for emerging market demand (e.g. hemp, oats and
quinoa), plant-based food manufacturing, timber and fibre processing, tourism and energy.

We propose to establish a national rural economies programme, funded through our Fund for
Environmental and Agricultural Transformation with revenue raised from agricultural emissions
pricing and taxing agricultural pollution (see our ‘Provide financial incentives for environmental
good practice’ proposal). Likely activities funded by this Fund could include:
- Supporting local councils and Iwi to develop rural economic development plans
- Financial support for community-led initiatives and new or established businesses
- Investments in local infrastructure

Recent examples from other sectors provide useful lessons for a proactive approach to
long-term economic development and a just transition. In Queenstown, an Economic
Transformation and Resilience Fund supports diversification away from tourism aiming to
increase economic resilience and develop higher-paying jobs.65 In Taranaki, Transition Action
Plans address how the local economy can move away from oil and gas production. These
examples showcase efforts to build more resilient and diverse regional economies, reducing
dependence on single industries and fostering sustainable growth across multiple sectors.

5. Compassionate Pound and Shelter Reform
The Animal Justice Party Aotearoa NZ (AJP) advocates for a compassionate pound and shelter
system where rehoming and no-kill are the national default, not the exception. We believe every
dog is an individual with an inherent right to life, safety, and respect. Our policy tackles the root
causes of overcrowding while transforming pounds into transparent, well-funded spaces
dedicated to giving every dog the best possible chance of finding a home.

We challenge the current framework that allows thousands of dogs to be killed in the pound
system each year. This is happening across councils with varying resources and policies, and
largely out of public sight. In Auckland alone, 60%92 of dogs entering the pound system
between July 2024 and June 2025 were euthanised, that is 6,079 dogs. Behind every one of
those numbers is an individual who deserved better.

AJP calls for urgent legislative and operational reform that places the best interests of each
individual dog at the centre of pound policy. Every dog entering the pound system in Aotearoa
deserves to be treated as an individual, not a statistic. Our goal is straightforward: fewer dogs
killed, more dogs with a home.

Key Objectives:

1. Implement legislation that requires pounds to act in the best interests of the animals in
their care.
2. Ban the use of bolt guns entirely, with no exceptions.
3. Mandate consistent, transparent public reporting, including the number of animals
received and of that, how many are reunited with guardians, adopted or euthanised.
4. Strengthen reunification processes so guardians can quickly and easily locate missing
dogs
5. Remove financial barriers to reclaiming dogs through flexible fee payment options
6. Shift from traditional temperament testing to behaviour assessment in calm, home-like
foster environments
7. Enhance temporary animal housing conditions and capacity through increased funding
and support for rehoming facilities
8. Formalise relationships with rescues and shelters
9. Foster community-led animal welfare initiatives across Aotearoa
10. Promote and invest in widespread, accessible desexing programmes
11. End breed-based euthanasia and ensure all dogs are assessed as individuals

6. Cats, Conservation and Better Solutions
Why the Animal Justice Party opposes Predator Free 2050's inclusion of ‘feral’ cats

The Government has recently added ‘feral’98 cats to the Predator Free 2050 target species list.
We oppose this. Not because we are indifferent to native wildlife, but because we believe the
framing behind this decision is wrong, the actions and methods it encourages are cruel, and the
evidence for its effectiveness in strengthening indigenous biodiversity is weaker than its
proponents claim.
This is not a single-issue position. It reflects a consistent set of values that run across our entire
policy platform: that all animals matter, that killing is not synonymous with conservation, and that
Aotearoa can do better.

Our position at a glance
We support a greater focus on the introduction of science-based, ethical methods to manage
the genuine tension between introduced species, including cats, and indigenous species. We
believe the primary driver of indigenous species decline in Aotearoa is habitat loss, not
introduced animals, and that this must be honestly named and addressed proportionately.

What we believe: six policy pillars

1. All animals matter
Both indigenous and introduced species are sentient beings with a right to live unimpeded by
human activities. Cats did not choose to come here. Humans brought them.

2. Language shapes thinking
We call for an end to unscientific, emotive and dehumanising terms to describe introduced
animals that are not useful to us. Language that vilifies animals makes killing them easier to
ignore. NZ has no hate speech laws pertaining specifically to animals - while animals cannot be
hurt directly by the attribution of malice or intentional damage achieved by use of terms like
‘pest’, ‘invasive’, ‘stone-cold killer’, ‘utter killing machines’,‘killers for fun’, the effect is to
demonise and to make killing and cruelty more acceptable.

3. Lethal eradication is not conservation
We oppose the use of 1080 poison on cats. Animal welfare scientists have found 1080 causes
deaths averaging 9.5 hours of spasms and tremors. This is not humane. It is not acceptable.

4. Innovation over violence

Immunocontraceptives, in-ovo sex determination, gene drives are real, proven or emerging
solutions. We question the belief that pre-human ecologies can/should be restored right across
present day Aotearoa with its permanent and growing population and large scale agricultural
economy, and that mainland eradication of introduced predator and perhaps also competitor
species is achievable using available and even foreseeable technologies. We support a focus
on strengthening and augmenting an adequately sized, world class reserve system
encompassing multiple habitats above an unrealistic, overly-diffuse and ‘ad infinitum’ policy of
eradication.

5. Address the real driver
Habitat loss is the primary driver of native species decline in Aotearoa. Focusing on introduced
animals distracts from the human activities most responsible for ecological harm.

6. Accountability and transparency
An independent Commissioner for Animals and mandatory live cameras on traps would ensure
that animal welfare decisions are made free from commercial or political pressure.

7. Universal Veterinary Care - Ensuring
Wellbeing for All Animals

The AJP is committed to establishing veterinary care as a fundamental right for all animals,
recognising that access to medical treatment should never depend on their guardian's wealth or
their status as companion, free-living, or wildlife. We acknowledge that the current system fails
countless animals who suffer needlessly due to financial barriers, geographic inequities, and a
veterinary workforce pushed to breaking point by commercial pressures and inadequate
support. We propose comprehensive reforms to create a universal veterinary care system that
prioritises animal wellbeing over profit, ensuring no animal is denied treatment because of
economic circumstances.

The veterinary care crisis in Aotearoa reflects broader societal failures to value animal lives
equally. Countless companion animals live in households struggling with the cost of living,
where a sudden illness or injury forces impossible choices between veterinary bills and basic
necessities. Meanwhile, injured wildlife, including our precious native species, suffer without
treatment, and free-living cats and dogs continue breeding due to lack of accessible desexing
services, perpetuating cycles of suffering that overwhelm rescue organisations and community
groups.

This crisis is not inevitable, it is a direct consequence of treating veterinary medicine as a luxury
commodity rather than essential care. The current system concentrates services in wealthy
urban areas while rural and regional communities face severe shortages, leaving both animals
and their human carers without local access to critical treatment. Veterinarians themselves
suffer under this model, with crushing student debt, unsustainable workloads, and moral injury
from having to deny care based on payment capacity driving concerning rates of burnout and
mental health struggles within the profession.

The economic barriers are deliberately constructed. GST on veterinary services treats animal
healthcare as discretionary spending, while limited university places and high fees create
artificial scarcity that drives up costs and restricts workforce growth. Emergency procedures can
cost thousands of dollars, forcing people to choose between insurmountable debt or
euthanasia, while preventative care like desexing remains financially out of reach for many
households, particularly in communities already facing economic hardship.

The connection to animal justice is fundamental and inseparable. Every animal who dies from a
treatable condition because their carer couldn't afford treatment represents a failure of our
society's values. Every injured kererū, kākā, or kiwi who suffers without veterinary intervention
because there's no guaranteed funding for wildlife care reveals the hollowness of our claimed
concern for biodiversity and our taonga species. Every free-living cat or dog who continues
breeding because desexing is unaffordable perpetuates suffering across generations and
threatens our native wildlife.

This policy also addresses the exploitation of veterinary professionals themselves. The current
system transforms dedicated animal carers into gatekeepers of treatment based on payment,

Beyond individual animals, lack of accessible veterinary care undermines community resilience

The current model also perpetuates inequality between communities. Whānau in rural areas,

gatekeeping. This is not charity, it is recognition that animals' right to medical care should not
depend on economic circumstance or postcode.

8. Getting Money Out of Politics - Restoring
Democratic Equality
The AJP is committed to creating a democracy where all voices are heard equally, regardless of
wealth or corporate connections. We acknowledge that money currently dominates our political
system, giving wealthy industries, particularly those that exploit animals, vastly superior access
to decision-makers compared to ordinary citizens and community advocates. We propose
comprehensive reforms to eliminate financial advantages in politics, ensuring democratic
participation is based on ideas and community support rather than economic power.

Unregulated lobbying creates a two-tier democracy where wealthy interests dominate
decision-making while ordinary citizens and advocacy groups are shut out. The revelations in
August 2025 about the then Fisheries Minister Shane Jones receiving over $100,000 from
fishing industry donors while rolling back environmental protections illustrate this problem
perfectly.102 Companies like Talley's Group strategically split donations to avoid disclosure
thresholds, while fishing baron Craig Boote admitted to spending $30,000 across parties before
securing exclusive access to ministers.103 This isn't democracy - it's a system where money
buys policy outcomes.

Although Federated Farmers does not make direct political donations,104 influence can flow
through other channels. Andrew Hoggard’s career path illustrates the concern: after nearly a
decade in Federated Farmers leadership roles, including serving as president until May 2023,
he joined ACT New Zealand the very next day.105 Following the 2023 election, he was appointed
Minister for Biosecurity and Food Safety, and Associate Minister of Agriculture (Animal Welfare,
Skills)106 and for the Environment, portfolios directly affecting farming and animal welfare. This
revolving door between industry leadership and political office underlines the urgent need for
reform: mandatory lobbying registers, cooling-off periods, and stronger transparency rules to
ensure that public decision-making serves the wider public interest.
The connection to animal welfare is direct and profound. Industries that exploit animals (factory
farming, commercial fishing, entertainment using animals) rely heavily on political influence to
maintain harmful practices. By eliminating their financial advantages, we create space for
evidence-based policy that considers animal welfare alongside human and environmental
concerns.

When wealth can't buy political influence, policy debates focus on ideas, evidence, and
community values rather than corporate interests. This creates conditions where animal welfare
advocates can participate on equal terms with industry representatives, leading to policies that
reflect genuine public concern for animals rather than industry profit margins.

9. Artificial Intelligence and Animal Welfare
Introduction
The Animal Justice Party of Aotearoa New Zealand (AJP) recognises that artificial intelligence
(AI) is rapidly transforming how millions of animals are managed across farming, aquaculture
and introduced species control in Aotearoa New Zealand. While AI technologies offer potential
to improve animal welfare through enhanced monitoring and early disease detection, they also
risk entrenching harmful practices and creating new forms of harm if deployed without adequate
governance systems.

AJP does not endorse the continued expansion of animal agriculture. Any use of AI in these
systems must demonstrate responsible development and genuine prioritisation of animal
welfare and harm minimisation. We oppose AI technology systems designed purely for
economic efficiency that treat animals as units of production rather than as sentient individuals
with inherent value.

AJP calls for immediate integration of animal welfare and protection considerations into AI
governance frameworks before harmful practices become economically entrenched and
impossible to reform. The long-term policy direction of AI must prioritise transition away from
animal farming, not the technological optimisation of it.

Context
The Scale of AI Deployment
AI technologies are already deployed across Aotearoa New Zealand's animal management
systems at unprecedented scale. Over 400,000 cattle are currently managed using AI-powered
virtual fencing systems, whilst millions more animals in dairy, beef, sheep, chicken, aquaculture
systems and introduced species control are increasingly likely to be subject to AI-driven
management decisions.
AI systems are being rapidly integrated into the management of these animals, making
autonomous decisions about their welfare, health and lives.

Current AI applications include:
- Virtual fencing and herding: AI-integrated wearable technology using sounds and
vibration to control animal movement, with systems learning and predicting individual
behaviour patterns
- Slaughterhouse automation, Computer vision, machine learning and robotics for carcass
grading, meat inspection, automated restraint, and cutting, optimising yield and
throughput.
- Health monitoring: Computer vision and machine learning analysing gait patterns, body
condition and behaviour to assess welfare
- Automated feeding and milking: AI-optimised systems managing nutrition and dairy
production
- Aquaculture management: Machine learning for biomass measurement, feeding
optimisation and water quality monitoring

animaljustice.org.nz | party@animaljusticeparty.org.nz 55

---

- Introduced species control: AI-powered cameras in traps using species recognition, and
autonomous drones identifying and poisoning target animals

The Regulatory Gap
The Animal Welfare Act 1999 was enacted before AI technology existed and contains no
provisions for AI-driven animal management and welfare. This creates a critical regulatory time
lag where technology is reshaping human-animal relationships faster than legislation and
regulation can adapt.

Aotearoa New Zealand's AI Strategy (July 2025), positions agriculture as a key adoption sector
but contains no animal welfare considerations. The accompanying Responsible AI Guidance for
Businesses covers cybersecurity, privacy and intellectual property whilst omitting animal welfare
entirely. The Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment has been explicit that “unlike EU
regulatory approaches, our approach is dispersed. The Government doesn't intend to put in
place an overarching AI Act. AI risks should be managed in relevant legislation as they arise”
(email correspondence Oct 2025).

This dispersed “light touch” approach is already being implemented in other sectors. 2025
changes to the Commerce Act, address AI-facilitated anti-competitive conduct, ensuring
companies are liable for AI actions. Additionally, a Members Bill was introduced (2025) to
amend the Harmful Digital Communications and Crimes Act 1961 to address AI-generated
harms such as deepfakes. These examples confirm that rapid, targeted legislative response is
possible.

Animal welfare requires the same urgency. Without explicit action to integrate welfare
considerations into relevant existing Acts, AI governance will continue to treat animal welfare as
a low-priority externality rather than a core consideration.

Without explicit regulatory requirements, AI systems will inevitably be designed solely for
economic efficiency rather than animal welfare and protection. Market forces alone cannot
ensure welfare and safety outcomes; only regulation can mandate that AI development
prioritises animals' behavioural, physical and mental needs rather than subordinating them to
economic and productivity metrics.

Case Study: Virtual Fencing Regulatory Lag
Virtual fencing technology demonstrates the pattern of regulatory lag that affects AI systems
deployment. Despite operating commercially since at least 2020 and affecting hundreds of
thousands of cattle:

- Circa 2021: The National Animal Welfare Advisory Committee (NAWAC) recommended
safeguards for virtual fencing in its Code of Welfare Evaluation Report on Dairy Cattle,
stating these "should have more generic application than only virtual fencing and apply to
any future technology proposed for animal management"
- Early 2024: A petition called for a parliamentary inquiry into virtual fencing technology

animaljustice.org.nz | party@animaljusticeparty.org.nz 56

---

- December 2024: Veterinarians for Animal Welfare Aotearoa announced development of a
code of ethical conduct for virtual fencing, demonstrating industry concern whilst
government action remained pending
- April 2025: The Petitions Committee recommended inclusion of guidance in the Code of
Welfare: Dairy Cattle update
- July 2025: The government noted that virtual fencing presents "an opportunity to review
the standards" but provided no timeline for implementation
- Late 2025: NAWAC's work programme plans to provide a revised recommendation, with
no certainty about when actual regulatory guidance will be implemented

This five-year lag between commercial deployment and potential regulatory guidance illustrates
the systematic failure to apply anticipatory regulation principles to animal welfare contexts,
despite on-going advocacy by the Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals (SPCA).
Without proactive intervention, each new AI technology will follow this same pattern: commercial
deployment, widespread adoption, entrenchment in industry practice, then belated regulatory
consideration of animal welfare and safety.

Global Context and Market Pressures
Globally, most AI governance frameworks have overlooked animal welfare. The OECD's AI
Principles and most national AI strategies focus exclusively on human-centred concerns such
as privacy, bias, transparency, data integrity, accountability and safety.

However, a significant breakthrough occurred in July 2025, when the EU's General-Purpose AI
Code of Practice explicitly listed “risk to non-human welfare” as a systemic risk, alongside
threats to democratic processes, financial stability and environmental harm. This represents the
first time a major jurisdiction has formally recognised that AI governance must consider animal
welfare, achieved through successful advocacy by animal welfare organisations during the
drafting stage.

Beyond the EU, Serbia's AI framework explicitly states AI systems “must be in line with the
well-being of humans, animals, and the environment.” These examples demonstrate that
inclusion of animal welfare in AI governance is both achievable and is increasingly being
recognised as necessary.

The AI animal health market is projected to grow from approximately $1.4 billion in 2024 to over
$8 billion by 2034, with the farmed animal sector expected to see the fastest growth. This rapid
investment is occurring without systematic regulatory oversight of welfare outcomes, creating
substantial risk that AI systems will entrench rather than improve current harmful practices.

Welfare Risks of Unregulated AI
- Intensification of harmful practices: AI technology makes existing harmful practices
more efficient rather than more humane. It integrates best with intensive, cage-based
systems that have the worst welfare conditions, enabling higher stocking densities and
more intensive confinement, whilst appearing to ensure individualised care.

animaljustice.org.nz | party@animaljusticeparty.org.nz 57

---

- Economic prioritisation: Data collection prioritises economic metrics over welfare
indicators. AI systems optimise measurable parameters (e.g. milk yield, growth rate, feed
conversion) whilst potentially missing qualitative welfare aspects such as emotional
wellbeing, behavioural freedom and social relationships.
- Reduced human oversight: Fewer human caregivers enable larger-scale operations,
removing human-animal relationships and reducing opportunities for animals to receive
individualised attention and compassionate care.
- Degraded human-animal relationship: humans become algorithm supervisors rather
than carers risking moral injury and loss of empathy. Sentient beings are viewed as data
streams.
- Technological dependency: System failures could leave animals without care. Farms
become vulnerable to hacking, sabotage and corporate espionage. Adverse weather
conditions may impact camera-based systems.
- Welfare washing: AI systems create the appearance of individualised care whilst
facilitating intensive systems. Companies can claim “precision welfare” or “AI-monitored
health” whilst maintaining fundamentally harmful practices.
- Automated lethal control: AI-powered introduced species control technologies operate
without direct human oversight of individual animal deaths, making life-or-death decisions
autonomously. This raises serious ethical questions about delegating such decisions to
algorithms designed for efficiency rather than compassion.

Economic Scale and Digital Divide
High AI technology implementation costs will create a digital divide where smaller operations
cannot access technologies that larger commercial operations use for both efficiency and
welfare monitoring. This risks creating a two-tiered system where animal welfare outcomes
depend on economic scale rather than consistent regulatory standards, with larger operations
able to demonstrate compliance through AI systems monitoring, whilst smaller farms lack
resources for equivalent compliance systems.

The Window for Action
Despite AI technology deployment already underway across Aotearoa New Zealand's animal
management systems, the window for proactive policy intervention still remains open. While
systems already affect hundreds of thousands of animals, harmful practices have not yet
become so economically entrenched that reform is impossible.

The government has demonstrated capacity for rapid legislative response when circumstances
require it. In May 2025, Parliament passed the Wildlife (Authorisations) Amendment Bill under
urgency to clarify authority for killing protected wildlife during development projects, responding
within months to a High Court decision. This swift action demonstrates that regulatory speed
depends on political prioritisation rather than legislative capacity.

Connection to Existing AJP Policies
Several existing AJP policies already provide a foundation for addressing AI systems and
improving animal welfare:

- Worker Rights and Safety: Existing policies on Health and Safety at Work align with the

- Transparency and Whistleblowing: Policies protecting those who expose cruelty

 - Mandatory public reporting of AI deployment scale, including the number of
animals affected and the types of systems used
 - Accessible data on welfare outcomes, system failures and interventions
 - Clear pathways for reporting, and addressing, welfare concerns related to AI
systems
 - Protection for whistleblowers who expose AI systems-related welfare failures
 - Public registers of validated AI welfare management systems
 - Consolidated national statistics on introduced species control methods, kill
numbers and welfare outcomes to enable comprehensive assessment of both
traditional and AI-enabled systems
8. Prohibit AI applications that:
 - Enable increased stocking densities or more intensive confinement
 - Reduce human-animal contact below minimum welfare standards
 - Make autonomous lethal decisions without human oversight
 - Prioritise economic optimisation at the expense of animal welfare and protection
 - Conceal or normalise practices that would otherwise be recognised as harmful or
cruel
9. Ensure AI governance frameworks address sentience comprehensively:
 - Expand explicit species coverage in animal welfare legislation to reflect current
scientific understanding of sentience, including cephalopods, decapods, fishes
and other invertebrates (as outlined in existing AJP policy on animal sentience
and legal status)
 - Regulate AI systems affecting aquaculture and commercial fishing with the same
rigour as terrestrial animal systems
 - Require that AI design processes acknowledge and respond to positive
species-specific behavioural and cognitive needs

Interim Measures
While comprehensive legislative amendments are developed and implemented, AJP supports
immediate actions to reduce harm:

animaljustice.org.nz | party@animaljusticeparty.org.nz 61

10. Issue urgent guidance under existing legislation to all research facilities, farms and
conservation operations using AI systems, requiring:
 - Immediate risk and animal impact assessments of current AI deployments
 - Enhanced human oversight protocols
 - Mandatory reporting of welfare failures related to AI systems
 - Suspension of AI systems that cannot demonstrate welfare benefits
11. Implement emergency protocols for deployed AI systems:
 - Mandatory backup systems ensuring animal care safely continues during
technological failures
 - Clear escalation and resolution procedures when AI systems indicate welfare
problems
 - Regular audits of AI systems decision-making to identify and rectify harmful
patterns
 - Immediate intervention and resolution requirements when AI systems recommend
actions contrary to animal welfare.
12. Fast-track regulatory capacity building by establishing an AI literacy programme for
Ministry for Primary Industries inspectors and Department of Conservation staff, a rapid
response team with expertise in both AI technology and animal welfare and interim
assessment tools for currently deployed AI systems.
13. Prioritise virtual fencing regulation as a test case for broader AI governance:
 - Implement NAWAC's recommended safeguards immediately through the Code of
Welfare: Dairy Cattle (on the assumption they are reasonable in relation to the
code of ethical conduct developed by the Veterinarians for Animal Welfare
Aotearoa)
 - Require independent welfare validation of existing virtual fencing systems
 - Establish clear standards for appropriate use, system maintenance and animal
conditioning
 - Prohibit use near milking sheds and in situations where animals cannot retreat
from stimuli
14. Conduct comprehensive AI systems deployment mapping across all animal management
sectors to identify the current scale and scope of AI systems use, assess the welfare
risks, prioritise regulatory intervention and establish transparent baseline data for
measuring regulatory effectiveness.
15. Establish interim consultation processes ensuring:
 - Animal welfare organisations are consulted on AI technology development and
deployment
 - Welfare and protection considerations are integrated into industry AI systems
adoption decisions
 - Public input is sought and integrated for AI technologies affecting animals
 - Affected communities, including farmers and conservation practitioners, contribute
to ongoing regulatory development.

10. Companion Animal Bereavement and
Parental Leave

The AJP is committed to recognising the profound emotional bonds between humans and
companion animals, acknowledging that these relationships provide immense psychological,
emotional and social benefits that mirror many aspects of human family connections. We
acknowledge that current employment law fails to recognise the grief and care needs
associated with companion animals, forcing people to use sick leave or holiday entitlement
during some of their most vulnerable moments.

We propose establishing statutory rights to bereavement and parental leave for companion
animal guardians. Leave entitlements should be flexible blocks that employees can use to care
for who they consider family, whether parents, children, or companion animals. This approach
avoids additional administrative burden for businesses while reflecting the reality of modern
family life.

Half of pet owners say their animal is a member of the family, equal to humans, reflecting the
deep emotional connections that have developed over thousands of years of co-evolution.
Anyone who has ever loved a pet knows: they're not "just animals" - they're family. They're the
wagging tail that greets us after a hard day, the purring companion during late-night work
sessions, and the loyal friend who never judges our worst moments.

Some forward-thinking employers have already recognised this reality. Google, Starbucks,
United Airlines and Walmart have embraced a so-called "pet-conscious workplace",107 while pet
ownership surged during the pandemic,108 and more workplaces have become pet-friendly.109
The concept of "pawternity leave", time off (paid or unpaid) for staff who have recently brought
home a pet, is gaining recognition internationally.110

Currently, pet leave isn't a legal right, but some businesses offer it.111 This creates inequality
where workers in progressive companies receive support while others must navigate grief and
companion animal care using inappropriate leave categories or risk job security. The absence of
statutory rights means many people cannot properly grieve the loss of beloved companions or
adequately care for newly adopted animals during critical bonding periods.

Policy Framework

- Bereavement Leave

 - Up to 5 days paid leave available as a single entitlement for use following the
death of a close human family member or a companion animal.
 - Flexible timing to cover funerals, tangihanga, memorials, veterinary appointments,
or grieving.
 - Self-declaration only, no burdensome paperwork.

- Parental (“Pawternity”) Leave

 - Up to 3 days paid leave available when a new family member joins the household,
whether a baby or an adopted companion animal.
 - Additional unpaid leave (up to 2 weeks) available for animals with special needs or
trauma histories.

- Emergency Care Leave

 - Employees may take reasonable time off to respond to urgent medical
emergencies, end-of-life decision-making, or intensive care needs - for human or
animal family members.

This policy reflects our core belief that recognising the sentience and emotional value of animals
creates a more compassionate society overall. When we acknowledge the grief people feel for
companion animals, we validate the emotional lives of those animals and reinforce that all
beings deserve consideration and respect.

The AJP believes that establishing companion animal bereavement and parental leave is a
compassionate step that can be taken now to support the millions of New Zealanders who
share their lives with animal family members. This policy will reduce workplace stress, improve
employee wellbeing, and strengthen a compassionate culture in Aotearoa New Zealand.

Key Objectives:

1. Establish statutory bereavement leave (up to 5 days) for family members, human or
nonhuman animals
2. Create "pawternity leave" entitlement of up to 3 days for new family members, including
companion animals
3. Extend emergency leave provisions to cover urgent care for both human and nonhuman
family
4. Ensure leave entitlements apply equally to all recognised forms of family life.

# Protect and restore natural habitats

> Archive note: Web text is the policy post body from animaljustice.org.nz/wp-json/wp/v2/policies; the PDF version linked from the page (if any) follows, extracted with pdftotext -layout.

## Full text (verbatim)

### Web page text

AJP supports greater protection and restoration of natural habitats and ecosystems. We recognise that the destruction or degradation of habitats and ecosystems causes direct harm to wild animals, and that both humans and wild animals are sustained by natural habitats and ecosystems.

63% of Aotearoa’s land area has now been converted for human use, with animal agriculture being a primary historical cause of habitat destruction. By 1930, 39% of New Zealand’s land area had been cleared and transformed to make way for pastoral farming. This transformation of land involved destroying forests, draining wetlands and disrupting waterways, causing significant harm to natural ecosystems and free living animals, whose habitats were obliterated or disrupted. As of 2021, this remains largely unaddressed, with 42% of land converted for farming and 8% converted for forestry. In order to reverse this process, AJP would enable greater protection of native ecosystems along with the restoration of ecosystems, especially in areas currently used for animal agriculture. Pastoral farming is a highly inefficient use of land for food production, using far more land compared to other crops, but producing a fraction of the calories. Moving towards a plant-based food system and away from animal agriculture would allow us to free up significant areas of land to re-wild.

**Key Objectives:**

1. **Restrict** further habitat destruction, of both terrestrial and aquatic ecosystems.

2. **Ban** bottom trawling

3. **Restrict** seabed mining

4. **Redirect** funds away from animal agriculture, through taxes and regulations, and towards plant-based agriculture and habitat restoration projects and practices, as outlined in our ‘*Introduce tighter standards and enforcement for agricultural pollution’ and ‘Provide financial incentives for good environmental practices’ sub-policies under Objective 2 in our ‘Just Transition to a Plant-Based Economy’ policy*. This redirection of funds would enable: \
a. Reserves: Stronger protection of, and creation of more, land and marine reserves (including more Highly Protected Marine Areas) \
b. Restoration: Roll out restoration projects to restore habitats, including mangroves, peat bogs, forests, marine habitats and other natural ecosystems. Subsidise farmers and landowners actively restoring the land and associated ecosystems. \
c. Subsidise green community projects \
d. Create wildlife corridors (link to Objective 3: *Protect Wildlife From Anthropogenic Harms*)

5. **Implement** educational programmes in schools, universities, and communities to promote awareness of the importance of living within our ecological limits, for the purpose of avoiding, remedying and mitigating the destruction of natural environments in which animals live. *See Compassionate Education policy.*

# Protect wildlife from anthropogenic harms

> Archive note: Web text is the policy post body from animaljustice.org.nz/wp-json/wp/v2/policies; the PDF version linked from the page (if any) follows, extracted with pdftotext -layout.

## Full text (verbatim)

### Web page text

Wild animals are frequently harmed due to the design of urban structures, roads, and the activities of people who are often unaware of their impacts. To address these issues, AJP wishes to see greater integration of wildlife considerations into urban planning, road design and signage by way of impact assessments. This would require greater collaboration between local councils, urban planners, conservation groups and communities to develop wildlife-friendly infrastructure.

**Key Objectives:**

1. Require animal welfare impact assessments to be carried out in the design of all roading and urban development projects. Enact stricter regulations mandating designs that better protect wild animals, especially where they are particularly vulnerable.

2. Raise awareness of impacts on wild animals through education and public engagement, encouraging more compassionate wildlife-friendly behaviour and fostering community-led conservation efforts.

3. Promote rewilding projects in urban areas, using native species where possible, and the connection of existing habitats through wildlife corridors.

4. Fund scientific research to better understand the impacts of roads and urban structures on wild animals, and the development of solutions to mitigate these impacts.

### PDF version: https://animaljustice.org.nz/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Protect-wildlife-from-anthropogenic-harms.docx.pdf

Protect wildlife from anthropogenic harms
Wild animals are frequently harmed due to the design of urban structures, roads, and
the activities of people who are often unaware of their impacts. To address these issues,
AJP wishes to see greater integration of wildlife considerations into urban planning,
road design and signage by way of impact assessments. This would require greater
collaboration between local councils, urban planners, conservation groups and
communities to develop wildlife-friendly infrastructure.
Many wild animals, native and introduced, inhabit towns and cities and are frequently
harmed by their human-centric design. For example, windows can be made with glass
that is more visible to birds, thereby reducing collisions.1 Human-wildlife conflicts can be
addressed in nonviolent ways, such as through nonviolent population control of pigeons,
rather than using spikes to restrict perching.2 Generally speaking, by considering
animals in the design of urban structures and areas, harms to wild animals can be
reduced or avoided altogether. This may often require collaboration between local
councils, urban planners, conservation groups and communities.
This is particularly important in the design of roads, which frequently kill and injure wild
animals. Measures such as wildlife crossings, barriers, and lower speed limits can
reduce these harms,3 and research into wildlife movement patterns can inform road and
urban planning that prioritises animal safety. While the Wildlife Act 1953 requires
permits for developments that may disturb or kill protected species, its focus remains on
species conservation and habitat protection rather than the welfare of individual
animals, leaving a gap between conservation law and animal welfare.
An important aspect of making urban areas friendly to wild animals is by the integration
of habitat. This may involve planting native species, connecting fragmented habitats

# Protecting the rights of farmed animals

> Archive note: Web text is the policy post body from animaljustice.org.nz/wp-json/wp/v2/policies; the PDF version linked from the page (if any) follows, extracted with pdftotext -layout.

## Full text (verbatim)

### Web page text

Policy category summary: The AJP believes that all forms of animal farming are ethically and morally unjustifiable and unnecessary. Nevertheless, we recognise that certain uses of animals inflict greater suffering than others, prompting our focus on addressing and alleviating these specific harms through our policies. The AJP actively focuses on safeguarding the rights of farmed animals, particularly during the ongoing societal transition towards a plant-based economy. While ideally aiming for a world without animal farming, we acknowledge the urgency of addressing the challenges currently faced by farmed animals and advocate for humane treatment, improved living conditions, and overall well-being.

The AJP recognises that the shift towards a plant-based economy is pivotal in reducing the need to farm animals, and will endeavour to guide this transition with compassion and practical solutions.In envisioning a society that places value on the lives of farmed animals, and seeks non-animal alternatives to food products, we advocate for policies and practices that protect the rights of these animals fostering compassion, responsible farming practices, and the overall improvement, and advancement, of conditions in the evolving landscape of sustainable agriculture.

# Regulatory Oversight and Enforcement

> Archive note: Web text is the policy post body from animaljustice.org.nz/wp-json/wp/v2/policies; the PDF version linked from the page (if any) follows, extracted with pdftotext -layout.

## Full text (verbatim)

### Web page text

AJP believes that animal welfare and protection is a social justice issue intrinsically linked to other areas where the vulnerable are exploited, for example, human rights, labour rights and environmental justice.

There are several Commissions and Commissioners in New Zealand dedicated to improving these societal issues, such as the Human Rights Commission, the Climate Change Commission and the Children’s Commissioner. They provide independent information and recommendations to the Government.

Currently the regulation of the welfare of animals is the responsibility of the Minister of Primary Industries and the Minister of Agriculture. New Zealand does not have a Commissioner for Animals who is independent to the Government and who can advocate independently on animal welfare and protection issues.

# Ban Rodeo

> Archive note: Web text is the policy post body from animaljustice.org.nz/wp-json/wp/v2/policies; the PDF version linked from the page (if any) follows, extracted with pdftotext -layout.

## Full text (verbatim)

### Web page text

In New Zealand, approximately 30 rodeo events are held every summer, featuring activities such as bareback bronc riding, saddle bronc riding, bull riding, steer wrestling, barrel racing, team roping, and calf roping. These events involve significant risks to animal welfare, resulting in injuries and fatalities.

\
Rodeos inherently involve cruelty, and we believe that they cannot be made safe through regulation. These events promote and normalise violence against animals, dulling society’s sensitivity to animal suffering. This is particularly concerning for children who learn a skewed perception of “acceptable” animal treatment, shaping their long-term attitudes towards animal welfare.

AJP advocates for non-violent, community-friendly entertainment that aligns with society’s progressive concerns and higher ethical and moral principles, and does not exploit and undermine animals’ well-being.

**Key Objectives:**

1. Ban all forms of rodeo activities involving animals.

*Interim measures, while we work towards the ban, include:*

2. Change advertising practices to remove ‘family-friendly’ messaging.
3. Implement a rapid phase-out of all rodeo events within a specified timeframe to eliminate this source of animal cruelty.
4. Increase funding and support for cruelty-free community sporting events.

Policy category summary: Te Tiriti o Waitangi holds profound significance for Aotearoa New Zealand, shaping the nation’s foundation and fostering principles of justice, inclusivity, and cooperation. The AJP embraces this treaty and acknowledges its importance in guiding a compassionate, just and equitable relationship with animals. A just transition to a plant-based Aotearoa New Zealand reflects the essence of Te Tiriti o Waitangi, promoting harmony and respect for all beings within the nation’s diverse tapestry. Test

# The environmental impacts of animal-based research

> Archive note: Web text is the policy post body from animaljustice.org.nz/wp-json/wp/v2/policies; the PDF version linked from the page (if any) follows, extracted with pdftotext -layout.

## Full text (verbatim)

### Web page text

### The Animal Justice Party of Aotearoa New Zealand (AJP) aims to ban all harmful forms of animal experimentation. AJP commits to promoting the use of compassionate research.

Animal-based research isn’t just an ethical issue. It also has significant environmental impacts that demand attention. The environmental cost of maintaining these practices contradicts commitments to sustainability and climate action.

### Key Objectives:

#### Interim measures, while we work towards the AJP Policy Ending Animal testing, include:

1. AJP will encourage the minimisation of the environmental impacts of animal-based research by requiring all research facilities, laboratories, and institutions engaged in animal research and testing, including academic, governmental, and private-sector organisations, to implement sustainable practices, reduce waste, and ensure compliance with relevant environmental regulations.\
 \
2. AJP will support the adoption of the following measures by all research facilities and institutions:\

- *Reduce, Refine, Replace (3Rs):* Prioritise alternatives in order to replace animal testing where possible, refine methods to minimise environmental impact and reduce the number of animals used. Strengthen the adherence to the 3Rs.\
- *Waste Management:* Reduce reuse and recycle materials wherever possible, properly dispose of hazardous and biological waste in compliance with regulations and implement sustainable alternatives for animal bedding and feed where feasible.\
- *Energy and Resource Efficiency:* Utilise energy-efficient equipment and lighting in animal research facilities and optimise water usage in cleaning, animal care and laboratory operations.\
- *Sustainable Procurement:* Source laboratory supplies, animal feed and equipment from environmentally responsible suppliers and prioritise biodegradable or recyclable materials in research processes.\
- *Reduction of Greenhouse Gas Emissions:* Reduce transportation-related emissions by consolidating supply shipments and using local vendors when possible, implementing practices that minimise the release of harmful substances into the air and water.

# The Future of Zoos and Aquariums

> Archive note: Web text is the policy post body from animaljustice.org.nz/wp-json/wp/v2/policies; the PDF version linked from the page (if any) follows, extracted with pdftotext -layout.

## Full text (verbatim)

### Web page text

The Animal Justice Party (AJP) advocates for a fundamental reorientation of zoos and aquariums away from entertainment-driven models toward facilities that exist to serve the interests of animals themselves. Facilities that currently exhibit animals for public display must transition toward roles centred on rescue, veterinary care, rehabilitation and, where necessary, the provision of lifelong sanctuary.

Where animals cannot be returned to the wild, their environments must be designed to approximate natural conditions as closely as possible, prioritising autonomy, social needs and behavioural expression. Public access, if permitted, must be strictly managed to ensure that it does not compromise animal wellbeing.

To find out more download the full policy PDF.

### PDF version: https://animaljustice.org.nz/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/The-Future-of-Zoos-and-Aquariums.docx.pdf

AJP Policy Document

The Future of Zoos and Aquariums
The Animal Justice Party (AJP) advocates for a fundamental reorientation of zoos and
aquariums away from entertainment-driven models toward facilities that exist to serve
the interests of animals themselves. Facilities that currently exhibit animals for public
display must transition toward roles centred on rescue, veterinary care, rehabilitation
and, where necessary, the provision of lifelong sanctuary.

Where animals cannot be returned to the wild, their environments must be designed to
approximate natural conditions as closely as possible, prioritising autonomy, social
needs and behavioural expression. Public access, if permitted, must be strictly
managed to ensure that it does not compromise animal wellbeing.

The AJP recognises that many species are not suited to captivity under any
circumstances. As such, the long-term objective is to significantly reduce and, where
appropriate, eliminate the keeping of animals in traditional zoo settings. Technological
alternatives, particularly immersive and virtual experiences, should replace the use of
live animals for education and entertainment.

Key Objectives:

1. Transition to Animal-Centred Models
Phase out practices that prioritise exhibition and profit, supporting the evolution
of zoos and aquariums into rescue, rehabilitation and sanctuary-focused
facilities.

2. Restrict New Zoo Establishments
Prohibit the establishment of new private zoos and aquariums. In exceptional
circumstances where approval is considered, require rigorous pre-licensing
assessments, including detailed evaluation of operator suitability, financial
capacity and contingency planning for animal care.

animaljustice.org.nz | party@animaljusticeparty.org.nz 1

---

3. End Breeding for Display
Ban captive breeding except where it forms part of independently assessed
conservation programmes that demonstrably benefit both species survival and
individual animal welfare.

4. Euthanasia Standards
Clear distinction between euthanasia conducted in an animal’s best interests and
that undertaken for management reasons, so that healthy animals are never
killed due to management failure or financial constraints.

5. Mandatory Exit and Transition Planning
Require all facilities to maintain legally enforceable exit strategies that specify
how animals will be rehomed, transferred or cared for in the event of closure or
operational change.

6. Financial Assurance Requirements
Introduce mandatory financial assurance mechanisms to ensure that adequate
funds are available for the ongoing care, relocation or rehabilitation of animals if
a facility ceases operation.

7. Develop Exit Pathways for Existing Animals
Implement coordinated strategies to relocate animals currently held in zoos and
aquariums to accredited sanctuaries or appropriate environments wherever
feasible.

8. Promote Non-Exploitative Alternatives
Support the development and accessibility of virtual reality and other immersive
technologies as humane alternatives to live animal displays.

9. Strengthen Transparency and Accountability
Mandate full disclosure of animal origins, health status and life histories and
prohibit the commercial import and export of live animals for profit.

10. Regulate Sanctuaries
Establish clear legal definitions and accreditation systems to distinguish genuine
sanctuaries from commercial enterprises, ensuring animal interests are
paramount.

11. Enhance Welfare Standards

animaljustice.org.nz | party@animaljusticeparty.org.nz 2

---

Introduce stringent, enforceable welfare standards, particularly for animals
exposed to public viewing, recognising the stress associated with human
interaction.

12. Prohibit Animal Performances
Ban the use of animals in performances, displays or interactive experiences that
compromise their wellbeing.

13. Redirect Public Investment
Prioritise support for wildlife rescue organisations, veterinary services, and
rehabilitation programmes over traditional zoos.

14. Support Ethical Transition Pathways
Provide assistance to operators seeking to transition toward non-exploitative
models, including the adoption of virtual and educational alternatives.

15. Promote Ethical and Sustainable Practices
Encourage facilities to align all operations, including food provision, with
principles of animal justice and environmental sustainability through adopting
plant-based options.

Background and Rationale

Zoos and aquariums may unintentionally communicate that it is acceptable to confine
wild animals in small or unsuitable enclosures - sometimes in isolation from their own
species - for human education or entertainment. Yet such conditions can cause
significant harm, as many animals are unable to engage in their natural, species specific
behaviours.

The AJP’s approach is grounded in the moral significance of individual animals. Whilst
biodiversity and ecosystem protection are important, they must not be pursued at the
expense of the lives and wellbeing of individual sentient beings. Practices such as
forced breeding, confinement in inadequate conditions and the treatment of animals as
interchangeable components of conservation strategies are ethically indefensible.

Effective conservation must prioritise the protection and restoration of natural habitats.
Without suitable environments for animals to return to, captive breeding programmes
offer limited value and may, in some cases, perpetuate harm. Moreover, zoos tend to

animaljustice.org.nz | party@animaljusticeparty.org.nz 3

---

favour highly visible or charismatic species,1 neglecting the broader ecological
relationships necessary for functioning ecosystems.

The AJP envisions a future in which human engagement with animals is guided by
respect, responsibility and non-exploitation. Transforming zoos and aquariums is a
critical step toward this goal, ensuring that animals are no longer used for entertainment
purposes, but are instead protected as individuals with intrinsic value.

Defining Zoos and Sanctuaries

Facilities that house animals vary widely in purpose and practice, often using
overlapping terminology that obscures important ethical distinctions.

- Zoos and aquariums are typically commercial enterprises that display animals
to paying visitors, sometimes incorporating conservation or educational activities
alongside entertainment functions.

- Sanctuaries, by contrast, are dedicated to the protection and care of animals,
without breeding, trading, or exploiting them for profit. Whilst some may allow
visitors, animal interests must always take precedence.

Given the blurred boundaries between these categories, regulatory focus should be
directed toward the underlying purpose of the institution - whether it exists primarily for
animals or for commercial gain.

Conservation Considerations

Although zoos often claim to contribute to conservation, and prevent some species from
extinction, evidence suggests that only a small proportion of their resources is directed

1
Contributions of zoos and aquariums to reintroductions: historical reintroduction efforts in the context of
changing conservation perspectives - Gilbert - 2017 - International Zoo Yearbook - Wiley Online Library

An analysis of zoo visitors' favourite and least favourite animals - ScienceDirect

animaljustice.org.nz | party@animaljusticeparty.org.nz 4

---

toward meaningful conservation outcomes.2 Furthermore, most animals held in captivity
are not endangered and reintroduction programmes are limited in scope and success.3

Captive environments cannot replicate the complexity of natural ecosystems and
animals bred in such conditions frequently struggle to survive when released.4 This
raises serious questions about the effectiveness and ethical justification of captivity
based conservation models.

Animal Welfare Concerns

Confinement in artificial environments can lead to significant physical and psychological
harm. Many captive animals exhibit signs of distress, including repetitive behaviours,
self-harm, and abnormal aggression. In some cases, these symptoms are managed
pharmacologically rather than addressed at their source.5

Additionally, practices such as the killing of “surplus” animals highlight the
commodification inherent in zoo systems.6 Even in well-resourced facilities, captivity
restricts animals’ ability to engage in natural behaviours, form social bonds and exercise
autonomy.7

Education and Public Engagement
Claims that zoos provide meaningful conservation education are not strongly supported
by evidence.8 Visitor engagement is often driven by leisure and social interaction rather
than learning and any educational benefits are typically limited.

Emerging technologies offer a more effective and ethical pathway. Virtual and
immersive experiences can foster understanding of animals and ecosystems without
subjecting animals to captivity.9 These approaches also allow for broader accessibility
and adaptability.

To maintain credibility as educational institutions, facilities must also align their
practices, such as food offering, with principles of sustainability and animal protection.

# Towards a Cruelty Free and Sustainable Fashion Industry

> Archive note: Web text is the policy post body from animaljustice.org.nz/wp-json/wp/v2/policies; the PDF version linked from the page (if any) follows, extracted with pdftotext -layout.

## Full text (verbatim)

### Web page text

The Animal Justice Party Aotearoa NZ envisions a future where fashion is free from animal exploitation and environmental harm. We recognise that the use of animal-derived materials such as leather, wool, fur, down and exotic skins perpetuates cruel and unsustainable practices. Animals exploited for fashion, like those farmed for food or fibre, are sentient beings with their own personhood and rights, and their lives must not be commodified for human use.

‭animal‬ ‭exploitation‬ ‭and‬ ‭environmental‬ ‭harm.‬ ‭We‬ ‭recognise‬ ‭that‬ ‭the‬ ‭use‬ ‭of‬
‭animal-derived‬ ‭materials‬ ‭such‬ ‭as‬‭leather,‬‭wool,‬‭fur,‬‭down‬‭and‬‭exotic‬‭skins‬‭perpetuates‬
‭cruel‬ ‭and‬ ‭unsustainable‬ ‭practices.‬ ‭Animals‬ ‭exploited‬ ‭for‬ ‭fashion,‬ ‭like‬‭those‬‭farmed‬‭for‬
‭food‬ ‭or‬ ‭fibre,‬ ‭are‬ ‭sentient‬ ‭beings‬ ‭with‬‭their‬‭own‬‭personhood‬‭and‬‭rights,‬‭and‬‭their‬‭lives‬
‭must not be commodified for human use‬

‭Key Positions:‬
‭1.‬ ‭Complete Phase-Out:‬‭Ban on production, sale and import‬‭of:‬
‭●‬ ‭Leather and exotic skins‬
‭●‬ ‭Wool and possum fur‬
‭●‬ ‭Down and feathers‬
‭●‬ ‭Animal-derived accessories (bone, horn, pearls)‬
‭2.‬ ‭Industry Transition Support:‬
‭●‬ ‭Financial assistance for businesses transitioning to ethical alternatives‬
‭●‬ ‭Research funding for sustainable materials‬
‭●‬ ‭Training programs for workers in affected industries‬
‭3.‬ ‭Te Tiriti Partnership:‬
‭●‬ ‭Consultation with Māori textile experts‬
‭●‬ ‭Support for traditional, cruelty-free fibre practices‬
‭●‬ ‭Investment in Māori-led sustainable textile initiatives‬
‭4.‬ ‭Interim Measures:‬
‭●‬ ‭Mandatory labeling of animal-derived materials‬
‭●‬ ‭Import restrictions from countries with poor animal welfare‬
‭●‬ ‭Transparency requirements for production methods‬

## Full text (verbatim)

### Web page text

## Urgently addressing climate change

The AJP is the only political party in Aotearoa New Zealand with a serious commitment to tackling major sources of emissions in ways which are credible, compassionate and aligned with climate science.

\

Policy category summary: We support a rapid reduction in animal agriculture (which is responsible for around half of Aotearoa New Zealand’s emissions) by transitioning to a plant-based economy, supporting farmers to grow produce instead of farming animals and addressing the profoundly detrimental impact of climate change on animals. Additionally, animals are extremely vulnerable to the storms, flooding and fires we continue to see in Aotearoa New Zealand as a result of climate change.

We support policies that reduce emissions, avoid unnecessary animal suffering, improve human and non-human animal health, and restore and expand our waterways, forests and wildlife. We reject ineffective solutions that aim to perpetuate the status quo. We are committed to supporting animals of all kinds to adapt to the changes in climate that are already underway, and that which are predicted, in order to create a sustainable future.

# What Shapes Our Policy

## Full text (verbatim)

# What Shapes Our Policy

### Our Policy Documents

Our policies aren’t just words - they’re blueprints for change. Backed by experts and evidence, our Policy Framework sets out the values behind everything we do, while our Policy Directory brings those principles to life with specific, practical policies across every area we work on. These comprehensive documents lay out our path to a world where animals and nature thrive alongside humans.

[Policy Framework Document](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1hgQ3Zo3HU9XhjS1_RJ9v66_uD78HDIV9/view)[Policy Directory Document](https://drive.google.com/file/d/15IUFRZw04B6DanyzXQUXLdCjylN9lJ53/view?usp=drive_link)

### Policy Documents

Each policy supports actionable campaigns that bring our vision to life: a healthier planet where all beings are protected and respected. They have been developed by our Policy Committee, often via engagement with experts and members, and all include clear short- and long-term objectives.

### Positions

Animal advocacy is our passion, but we don’t live in a single-issue world. At times we may need to take a stand on a wider range of topics. Our position statements give you a clear snapshot of where we stand on these diverse issues. Always guided by our core values of compassion, non-violence, equality, sustainability and a just transition, these statements show how our animal-friendly philosophy shapes our approach to every aspect of society.

[Browse Policies](https://animaljustice.org.nz/policy/our-policies/)
